title: An-Nisa
label: Plain-English commentary
intro:
The fourth surah of the Qur'an is called An-Nisa, "The Women", a name it earned from the number of its rulings that concern women: who may marry whom, what a bride is owed, how inheritance is shared between sons and daughters, and how a marriage in trouble is repaired or ended. It came down in Madinah, where the new community had to be built household by household, and one hundred and seventy-six verses make it in large part the community's book of family law. Around that core it gathers much else: the orphans' property, prayer in danger, the duties of government, fighting in Allah's cause, the hypocrites, the People of the Book and the truth about ʿĪsā (Jesus).

The surah opens by addressing all people, not only the believers, with a command to be mindful of the Lord who created them from a single soul. That word, taqwa (being mindful of Allah), is the thread of the whole surah, because most of what it commands cannot be enforced by any court. A judge can order a seller to return what he sold. No judge can make a guardian love the orphan in his care, or make a husband deal gently with his wife. Rights of that kind are held together by the fear of Allah and the Day of Judgement, and that is why the surah that carries them begins with the command of taqwa.

### Where and when it was revealed

An-Nisa is a Madinan surah. Al-ʿAwfī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said it was revealed in Al-Madinah, and Ibn Marduwyah recorded the same statement from ʿAbdullāh ibn az-Zubayr and from Zayd ibn Thābit, two Companions who were among those charged with collecting the Qur'an. The reports agree with the surah's own character: its laws assume a settled community with orphans, estates, marriages and courts, not a persecuted band of believers.

### Its virtues

ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd prized five verses of this surah above everything the world contains. In the report al-Ḥākim recorded in his Mustadrak, he said: "There are five verses in Surat An-Nisa that I would prefer to the life of this world and all that is in it." The five are the assurance that Allah does not wrong anyone by even the weight of an atom (4:40), the promise that if the believers avoid the great sins they will be forgiven their misdeeds and admitted honourably (4:31), the declaration that Allah does not forgive the setting up of partners with Him but forgives whatever is less than that to whom He wills (4:48), the call to those who wronged themselves to come to the Prophet ﷺ and seek forgiveness (4:64), and the assurance that whoever does evil or wrongs himself and then turns to Allah in forgiveness will find Him forgiving and merciful (4:110).

Ibn ʿAbbās went further. Al-Ḥākim recorded him saying: "Ask me about Surat An-Nisa, for I learned the Qur'an when I was still young." He had taken the Qur'an to heart as a boy, and he offered himself as a teacher of the surah to anyone who would ask. Al-Ḥākim graded the report ṣaḥīḥ by the standard of the two Ṣaḥīḥs, though those two collections did not include it.

### How it connects to the surah before it

Āl ʿImrān closed with an exhortation to taqwa. An-Nisa opens with the same word, now in the form of a command. The earlier surah had spoken of battles, of how antagonists are to be treated, and against misappropriation in the battle spoils. This surah turns from the enemy outside to the people inside the community: the rights of one's own people, the rights of the servants of Allah, which orphans, relatives and wives hold over those who have charge of them.

Those rights are of two kinds, and the difference explains the surah's method. Some can be taken to court: buying and selling, leases, tenancy and wages can be settled by agreement and arbitration, and if a party falls short, the law can retrieve what is owed. But the rights of the people in one's own charge, children, parents, husband and wife, orphans and the wider family, are different. Their fulfilment depends on civilized behaviour, respect, loving care and a heartfelt wish to do good. They cannot be weighed on a scale or written into a contract. For them there is no method of enforcement except the fear of Allah and the fear of what happens in the life to come. That is taqwa, and it is a stronger guarantee than the combined powers of government and law.

This is also the surah's way of teaching. It does not issue its rulings like cold print, the way governments publish statutes. It brings each law together with the training of minds and hearts, so that the person bound by the rule wants to keep it even when no one is watching.

### The opening verse at weddings

The first verse of the surah has a fixed place in Muslim life. The Prophet ﷺ used to recite it as part of his address when a marriage was solemnized, and reciting it in the khutbah of nikah, the marriage address, has remained a living sunnah ever since. It is a fitting opening for a marriage: the verse calls on everyone to fear the Lord from whom the whole human family descends, and to honour the ties of kinship, at the very moment two families are being joined and a new set of mutual rights begins.

### What the surah covers

The surah moves from creation to the family, and from the family out to the community and its enemies. It begins with the foundation of human society: one Lord who made all people from a single soul, the ties of kinship, and God-consciousness (verse 1). Then come the laws of the household: the protection of orphans and their property (2), justice between wives and the rights of brides to their dowries (3 and 4), and the responsible management of what belongs to dependents who cannot manage it themselves (5 and 6).

The longest run of rulings concerns inheritance: the shares of children, parents and spouses, the share of a brother or sister on the mother's side, the warning against those who would consume an inheritance wrongfully, and the limits Allah has set (7 to 14). The surah then turns to unlawful relationships and the door of repentance (15 to 18), to the protection of wives from financial abuse, the prohibition of taking back what was given, and the gravity of the marriage covenant (19 to 21), and to the list of relatives a person may not marry, together with the provision made for those who cannot afford marriage (22 to 25).

A passage of grace follows: Allah's wish to make clear the way and bring people out of darkness into light, His forgiveness and mercy, and the weakness of the human being who must not despair (26 to 28). Then come the prohibitions of exploitation, envy and self-harm, contentment with Allah's distribution of provision, and the rights of heirs (29 to 33), and the two verses on the household itself: the responsibility of husbands for its order, the admonition and reconciliation of a wife whose conduct is feared to be unfaithful, and the arbitration to be used when a couple are close to breaking apart (34 and 35).

The middle of the surah widens to worship and society: the call to worship Allah alone and do good to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy and the traveller, with warnings against stinginess and hypocrisy in charity (36 to 38), Allah's perfect fairness and generosity (39 and 40), the witnesses who will be brought forward on the Day of Judgement (41 and 42), and the purity, physical and spiritual, required for prayer, including the concession of tayammum in travel and illness (43).

Next the surah addresses those who received scripture before: the scholars who distort Allah's words for a small price, the Jews who took trust and mockery in place of faith, and the People of the Book who are summoned to believe in what was sent down confirming what they have (44 to 47). It states the one sin Allah does not forgive, the associating of partners with Him (48), and exposes the self-righteousness, false claims and envy of those who praise themselves and resent the favour Allah gives to whom He wills (49 to 55), before setting the two destinations side by side: those who reject the signs in the fire, and those who believe and do good in gardens with rivers flowing beneath (56 and 57).

The community's public life follows: the command to hand over trusts to those entitled to them and to judge with justice, the call to obey Allah, the Messenger and those in authority and to refer disputes back to Allah and His Messenger (58 and 59), and a long unmasking of the hypocrites, who claim faith while turning away from judgment, whose double standards are laid open in scene after scene (60 to 63). The surah then holds up the opposite: true faith as complete submission to the Prophet's judgment, with no resistance in the heart, and the reward of those who obey Allah and the Messenger, the company of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous (64 to 70).

A long section on fighting runs from there to the middle of the surah's second half: readiness and the exposure of those who hang back (71 to 77), the inescapability of death and the truth that every event, good and evil, comes from Allah (78 and 79), obedience to the Messenger and the hypocrites' whispered opposition (80 to 82), the verification of reports, the call to fight and the etiquette of greetings (83 to 87), the treatment of the hypocrites in arms (88 to 91), the ruling on killing a believer by mistake or deliberately (92 and 93), caution before striking in the confusion of battle (94), the rank of those who strive with their wealth and lives (95 and 96), the fate of those who failed to emigrate from oppression (97 to 100), the shortened and combined prayers of travel and danger (101 to 103), and perseverance in pursuit (104).

The closing run returns to law and belief: judging justly and not pleading for the deceitful (105 to 109), the door of repentance open to every individual (110 to 112), Allah's protection of His Prophet from deception (113), the value of good speech and private counsel (114), the severe consequence of opposing the Messenger (115), shirk and Satan's deceptions exposed (116 to 121), the believers' reward as Allah's true promise (122), salvation through deeds rather than wishful thinking (123 and 124), and the way of Ibrāhīm (Abraham), the one who submitted himself wholly to Allah (125 and 126).

The surah ends as it began, with women, orphans and the household: the rights of women and orphans in marriage (127), the reconciliation of marital disputes and the justice owed between wives when love is uneven (128 to 130), Allah's sovereignty over everything in the heavens and the earth (131 to 134), the command to stand firm for justice even against oneself or one's parents (135), the pillars of true faith (136), the wavering and the hypocrites (137 to 147), the ethics of speech (148 and 149), the requirement to believe in all the prophets without distinction (150 to 152), the demands and transgressions of the Children of Israel and the truth about ʿĪsā (Jesus), who was Allah's Messenger, His word and a spirit from Him, raised to Him and not killed (153 to 162), the line of messengers ending with Muhammad ﷺ (163 to 166), the fate of those who reject and obstruct (167 to 173), and the conclusive proof and the light that has come from Allah (174 and 175). The final verse answers a question about a man who leaves neither child nor parent, and closes the surah with the law of the brother and sister on the mother's side (176).

### In short

- An-Nisa, "The Women", is a Madinan surah of 176 verses named for its many rulings about women, marriage, dowry and inheritance.
- Ibn Masʿūd said five of its verses (4:31, 4:40, 4:48, 4:64 and 4:110) were dearer to him than the life of this world and all it contains, and Ibn ʿAbbās invited people to ask him about the surah he had learned in his youth.
- It takes up the call to taqwa with which Āl ʿImrān ended and makes it the foundation of the rights of orphans, relatives and wives, the rights no court can enforce.
- Its opening verse is recited in the marriage address, following the practice of the Prophet ﷺ.
- From the family it widens to inheritance, purity for prayer, the People of the Book, the hypocrites, fighting and justice, and it ends with another inheritance ruling.

1.text:
The surah opens with an address to the entire human race: "O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord Who created you from a single soul". No tribe and no era is left out. The command is taqwa (being mindful of Allah), and it is the foundation stone of everything that follows, because this surah is a book of rights: the rights of orphans, wives, children and relatives, the rights that no court can enforce. The verse gives two reasons for the command in the same breath. Allah is the Lord who made every person from one soul, and He is the One whose name people invoke when they claim something from one another. Both truths ask for the same answer. The God who made you, and the God you call upon over your neighbour's conscience, deserves to be obeyed.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O humanity!"** The address is general, and it can also be read as particular. In its wide sense it takes in all human beings, men and women, those alive when the Qur'an came down and everyone still to be born until the Day of Judgement. In its narrower sense it was spoken to the people of Makkah. Either way, the verse is not addressed to believers only. It speaks to people as people.

**"Be mindful of your Lord"** translates the command ittaqū, guard yourselves against acting against your Lord. To have taqwa of Allah is, first of all, to worship Him alone, with no partner. To fear Allah is to fear His punishment, and the way to fear it is to obey. The name chosen here is Rabb, Lord, picked from the fairest of Allah's names, and the choice carries a lesson. The One totally responsible for a person's nurture, whose care he witnesses every moment of his life, deserves all the awe a person can feel. The mere thought of rising against Him in defiance is dangerous.

**"Who created you from a single soul"** identifies the soul as Ādam (Adam), the father of all human beings. Allah could have created people in more than one way. He chose one way and one form: every human being from one man, so that the whole race is tied together in a strong bond of brotherhood. One reported reading adds that Ādam's soul alone is meant, with the soul of Ḥawwā (Eve) already contained in it, her creation being the drawing out of what was in him.

**"and from it He created its mate"** names Ḥawwā (Eve), the mother of humankind. She was created from Ādam, from a rib on his left side, taken from his back while he slept. When he woke and saw her, he was drawn to her and loved her, and her feeling matched his. An authentic hadith draws a lesson for married life from the manner of her creation:

> Woman was created from a rib. The most curved part of the rib is its upper part. If you try to straighten it, you will break it. If you leave it as it is, it will remain crooked.

**"and through both He spread countless men and women"** means that from Ādam and Ḥawwā came generation after generation, spread throughout the world in different shapes, characteristics, colours and languages. In the end their gathering and their return will be to Allah. Read inwardly, the phrase is a display of perfect power and lordhood. From the offspring of one upright individual came thousands upon thousands of creatures, each with its own colour, nature, character and state, its own form and its own aspiration. No two people are alike in nature and face. Glory to the One whose decrees have no end and whose knowledge reaches beyond all limits.

**"And be mindful of Allah—in Whose Name you appeal to one another"** points to a habit of speech that was current then and is still current now. A person pressing a claim says, "I ask you by Allah", or "for the sake of Allah", or "I ask you by Allah, and then by the womb that joins us", a manner of appeal reported from Ibrāhīm, Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan. Ad-Daḥḥāk applied it to trade: fear the One you invoke when you conduct your transactions and contracts. The grammar was weighed closely. The verb can be read tassā'alūna, where the first letter of the doubled form has merged into the next, or tasā'alūna, you ask one another. Both readings give the same scene of two people, one saying to the other, "I ask you by Allah." The command makes the appeal a mirror. Whoever expects others to fear Allah when they owe him something must fear Allah himself in what he owes them.

**"and ˹honour˺ family ties"** turns to the wombs, al-arḥām. They are to be revered by not cutting the ties of kinship but keeping and honouring them. This is how Mujāhid, Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrimah explained it, and al-Ḥasan, ad-Daḥḥāk and ar-Rabīʿ said the same. On one variant reading the word joins the name of Allah that precedes it, as though the verse said: fear Allah, and fear the wombs. People did indeed implore one another by ties of kinship, as they implored by Allah's name. A third rendering takes the phrase as a plain command: keep the ties of kinship, and do not sever them.

**"Surely Allah is ever Watchful over you"** means He watches all your deeds and sees your every circumstance. The Qur'an says the same elsewhere: "And Allah is Witness over all things" (58:6). An authentic hadith turns the doctrine into a way of standing before Him:

> Worship Allah as if you see Him, for even though you cannot see Him, He sees you.

Nothing escapes Him. He takes every act into account and repays it. A Watcher, in the language of this reading, is One who gives ear to hearts without having to investigate, who is aware of deeds without asking, and who never needs to rest from striving. He is also a Protector: He will ask about the acts of obedience He commanded, and about the kinship He told people to keep.

### One family from one soul

All human beings are one and the same by birth. Every person alive can trace his origin to the same man and the same woman, Ādam and Ḥawwā. That single origin makes the human race one extended family, and it ought to live with fairness and goodwill, the members of one household. No one may treat race, caste, colour or language as the measure of good or bad, nobility or meanness. Those differences are real, but they are never the standard by which people are judged. What the shared origin tightens in the human family it tightens further in the family itself: the closer the blood, the higher the duty of decent behaviour among kin.

The verse also states, in passing, why dealings with other people are never only human business. Everyone stands under the Great Almighty God, who is the Reckoner for all, who will decide the eternal future of every human being in the Hereafter and repay each according to what he did in this world. A person should therefore not treat his dealings with others as a matter between man and man. They are a matter between man and God. He should fear God's grip and keep within the bounds God has set, to save himself from His wrath.

There is a further sign in the pairing. The Lord who created everything created it as a pair, and He made a spouse appear for everyone, joining each with a likeness and attaching each to what resembles it. Unity and solitariness belong to Him alone. It is His due and worthy of Him. It is narrated in one of the books that Allah said: "I have given the things mates so that My unity will be inferred." Even the division of creation into pairs points back to the One who has no partner.

### The blessing of kinship, and the warning against cutting it

The word al-arḥām is the plural of raḥm, the womb, the child's home until it is born. Since the womb is where blood relationship begins, keeping that relationship alive is called silatur-raḥm in Arabic, literally the umbilical bond. Its opposite, indifference toward the ties of blood, is qaṭʿur-raḥm, cutting the bond. The hadiths on this subject are many and strong.

The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever wants his livelihood made plentiful and his term extended should keep good relations with his near of kin. The reward of the Hereafter is promised, and this life sees a share of the benefit too: provision widens, and the years are blessed. ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām said that when the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah aṭ-Ṭayyibah, the very first words he heard from him were these:

> O men, make a practice of greeting each other with salām, feed people for the pleasure of Allah, treat your near relations well, and pray by night while people sleep. You will enter Paradise in peace.

Maymūna, the Mother of the Faithful, once freed a bondwoman and told the Prophet ﷺ about it. He told her that had she given her to her maternal uncle, her reward would have been greater. Freeing a slave is one of the finest acts of merit in Islam, and still the fair treatment of relatives was put above it. In the same spirit he said that charity to a needy person is charity, while to a near relative it is twofold: charity and kinship. A simple change in where the charity goes earns two rewards at once.

The warnings on the other side are stern. The Prophet ﷺ said that a breaker of blood relationships shall not enter Paradise, and that mercy does not come down upon any people among whom lives someone who has severed the bonds of kinship. According to a hadith in which Allah Himself speaks, He proclaimed: "I shall associate Myself with one who strengthens the ties of kinship, and detach Myself from one who severs them."

These reports show what the verse is testing. A person's attachment to Allah is measured by his relations with other human beings. Whoever fears Allah while dealing with the rights of others is the one who truly venerates Him, and whoever loves other human beings is the one who really loves his Creator. Fair dealing and compassion are general requirements of any society, but for family relations they are so vital that they stand second in importance only to Allah Himself.

### Three degrees of godwariness

Read inwardly, the opening command is an address to the centre of the human being: "O centre of human nature, make godwariness your shelter and cling to it, for the life of the servants is through it and the deliverance of the travellers is in it." Godwariness means that the servant makes the commands of the sharīʿah, the law Allah has laid down, into his shield, so that the arrows of prohibition cannot reach him. It has three levels. First, take refuge in the sentence of tawḥīd, the oneness of Allah, and avoid every kind of associationism. Second, take refuge in obedience and step away from the path of disobedience. Third, take refuge in caution and flee from what is ambiguous. Whoever climbs these way stations with truthfulness will without fail reach deliverance, for the Qur'an itself gives the report: "God will deliver those who were godwary" (39:61). And it promises: "Whosoever is wary of God, He will appoint a way out for him and He will provide for him from whence he never reckoned" (65:2-3). Whoever takes hold of godwariness finds the road of deliverance made easy from every suffering, and provision sent from where he had no hope of it.

Scruple of this fineness has its own story. The sister of Bishr al-Ḥāfī went to see Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and said: "O Imam of the Muslims, I spin thread on the roof of my house. When the torch of the Ṭāhirids passes by, I may join my threads by its rays. Is that permissible or not?" Aḥmad asked her first who she was, and whether she belonged among people able to carry such godwariness. When she said she was the sister of Bishr al-Ḥāfī, he wept and said that godwariness like this is permitted only in the household of Bishr al-Ḥāfī, that it was not worthy of her, and that she should emulate her brother so that perhaps she might become like him. Then, if she wanted to spin by the light of the Ṭāhirids' torch, her hand would not obey her. Her brother had reached a degree where his hand refused to obey him whenever he reached for food touched by the slightest suspicion.

For those drawn all the way in, the verse opens onto Allah's own care. Muṣṭafā ﷺ narrated from his Lord that when Allah knows that what dominates His servant's heart is being occupied with Him, He turns the servant's appetite toward supplicating Him and conversing with Him. The servant gains passion for Allah, and Allah for him. And when such a servant then desires to be negligent, Allah comes between him and his negligence. These are His friends in truth, His champions, the ones for whose sake He removes from the earth those they desire to be punished. For the servant who wants only Him, knows only Him and belongs only to Him, Allah turns the face of His heart toward him. He shuts against him the doors of desires, appetites and wants, removes all others from his heart, and lets passion for speaking with Him and listening to Him rule his spirit. He gives him ease on the carpet of passion and holds over his head the sword of a jealousy that predates creation, so that looking at another, craving another, doing business with another, is not allowed. "I will make night into day and day into night in your work. I will ruin your business with the world's creatures." When Allah wants such a servant, He knows how he must be plundered. Today He entrusts him to the policeman of godwariness, keeping him under the protection of His sharīʿah, which gives his movements and his stillnesses the condition of courtesy. Tomorrow He gives him a place in the seat of truthfulness (54:55), within the Presence of At-ness, the state of being with Him alone.

The end of the road is pictured as a market day. At the resurrection it will be said to godwariness: "Come, for today is the day of your bazaar. Whoever has a portion of you, settle him in a dwelling in the measure of his portion." Those familiar with godwariness are settled in the Presence of At-ness, for it was decreed from before time: "Surely the godwary will be in the midst of gardens and a river, in a seat of truthfulness, at an Omnipotent King" (54:54-55).

### The Prophet's ﷺ use of this verse

In his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim records the account of Jarīr ibn ʿAbdullāh al-Bajalī. A delegation of Mudar came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he saw the state they were in: striped woollen cloaks, worn thin by poverty. After the Zuhr prayer the Prophet ﷺ stood up and gave an address in which he recited this verse to its end. He also recited: "O you who believe! Have taqwa of Allah. And let every person look to what he has sent forth for the tomorrow" (59:18). Then he called on them to give charity, saying that a man gives ṣadaqah from his dinar or his dirham, from a saʿ of wheat or a saʿ of dates, and so on through the report. Aḥmad and the compilers of the Sunan collected the same narration from Ibn Masʿūd. The choice of this verse for that day is itself a reading of it. The Prophet ﷺ reached for it when he wanted to stir the conscience of the poor toward giving: first the fear of the Lord who made one family of them all, then the spending that such fear produces. He also used to recite it in the khutbah when a marriage was solemnized, which is why it is still recited at weddings, and that use suits it equally, for a marriage is where two families' mutual rights begin.

### How the verse opens the surah

The verse is the doorstep of everything the surah commands. Its purpose is to stop people from becoming usurpers of the rights of Allah and of His servants, and to do it by reminding them that they are all children of one father. That reminder sets love, mutual sympathy and concern as the working basis of common life, so that the rights of relatives, orphans and married couples are fulfilled from the heart, at the root, where no law can reach. The last sentence of the verse, that Allah is watchful, is what keeps the fulfilment honest. Divine watchfulness reaches intentions, scruples and motives, everything hidden in human hearts. Acts done halfheartedly, or for form's sake, or out of fear of embarrassment, without any genuine desire to serve, remain unacceptable to Allah. The Qur'an does not bring its laws in cold print the way governments publish statutes. It teaches them the way a teacher or a parent teaches, joining each rule to the training of minds and hearts.

### In short

- The verse commands taqwa of all humanity: be mindful of the Lord who made every person from one soul, Ādam (Adam), and created from him his mate Ḥawwā (Eve), then spread the two of them into countless men and women.
- Since people appeal to Allah's name when claiming their rights from one another, whoever invokes that name must fear Allah in the rights he owes.
- Family ties are never to be cut. Keeping them brings plentiful livelihood and blessed years in this world and Paradise in the next. Cutting them keeps a person out of Paradise and withholds mercy from his whole people.
- Godwariness has three degrees: tawḥīd without any associationism, obedience instead of the path of disobedience, and caution against the ambiguous. Its promise is deliverance and a seat of truthfulness with an Omnipotent King.
- Allah is Watcher over everything. He sees deeds, hears what hearts contain, and repays every act. Worship Him as if you saw Him, for He sees you.
- The Prophet ﷺ recited this verse to move a poor delegation to charity and in the marriage address. It opens the surah because the laws that follow stand on the fear of the One who watches.

2.text:
The first ruling of the surah follows straight from its opening address. Humanity was told to fear the Lord who made one family of all people, and the first members of that family to be protected are the ones with no father to protect them: "Give orphans their wealth ˹when they reach maturity˺, and do not exchange your worthless possessions for their valuables, nor cheat them by mixing their wealth with your own". The verse assumes what was common: a guardian, usually a relative of the child, holding property that belongs to an orphan. It commands him to guard it honestly, to hand it over whole when the child grows up, and to leave it alone in the meantime. The closing words leave no room for bargaining: "For this would indeed be a great sin".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Give orphans their wealth"** takes up the duty of the guardian. Whether he was appointed by the orphan's father before his death, or by the government, the property and the child are in his charge. He may meet the costs of the orphan's maintenance and upkeep, but he must not place the property itself in the hands of an immature minor, who could lose it somewhere. The handover is to happen at the right time, and the surah returns to it in verse 5, where the property is to be given once the orphan is mature and can tell what is good from what is not. Read in that light, the command to give is, before anything else, a command to protect: keep the property sound and whole so that it can be handed over intact when the time comes.

**"˹when they reach maturity˺"** gives the timing. The property is released when the orphan comes of age and shows sound judgement, not at a fixed number of years alone.

**"and do not exchange your worthless possessions for their valuables"** forbids the neat trick that kept the count right while robbing the child. People would leave the number of items owned by the orphan untouched, but take a good one out and put a bad one of their own in its place. A weak animal of the guardian's must not be swapped for a fat animal of the orphan's, as Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and az-Zuhrī explained it. Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī and ad-Daḥḥāk put it generally: nothing of bad quality may be given for something of good quality. As-Suddī painted the scene: a caretaker of orphans takes a fat sheep from their property and leaves one of his own weak sheep in its place, saying, "a sheep for a sheep". He takes a sound dirham and hands over a counterfeit one, saying, "a dirham for a dirham". The excuse would be that nothing was taken, only exchanged. The answer of the Qur'an is that this exchange is taking, and it is forbidden. The prohibition reaches further than direct swaps: any deal the guardian makes with anyone else that ends in a loss for the orphan falls under it.

**"nor cheat them by mixing their wealth with your own"** strikes at the commonest form of the abuse. The guardian holds the orphan's property together with his own, spends from the pooled stock, and lets the orphan do the same. No separate accounts are kept. Even a religiously careful Muslim could fall into thinking there was no sin in such an arrangement. Hence the explicit prohibition. Either the orphan's property is kept absolutely separate and spent from separately, or, if a joint household expense is unavoidable, the accounts must be so clear that the guardian can be sure he has spent nothing of the orphan's on himself or on his own interests. The question of guarding orphan property is treated in detail where the Qur'an takes it up in Surah al-Baqarah (2:220), in section 27 of that discussion.

**"For this would indeed be a great sin"** closes the warning. The word translated "great sin" is ḥūb. Ibn ʿAbbās said it comes from the Ethiopian language and means a major sin, and Arabic uses it with that meaning. The same judgement is reported from Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan and Ibn Sīrīn, from Qatādah and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, from ad-Daḥḥāk and Abū Mālik, and from Zayd ibn Aslam and Abū Sinān. Adding the orphan's property to one's own is a grave sin and a major mistake. The sternest warning of all comes a few verses later, where those who consume the property of orphans are told what awaits them (4:10).

### Who counts as an orphan

The word for orphans, al-yatāmā, is the plural of al-yatīm, which literally means the lone one or the unique one. A pearl that sits alone in its shell is called ad-durr al-yatīm, the orphan pearl. Islamic law gives the name yatīm to a child whose father has died. Among animals, by contrast, the word is used for an offspring whose mother has died. The status does not last forever. A hadith states that orphanhood ends with puberty, so once a child reaches maturity the legal protections aimed at orphanhood give way to ordinary adulthood.

### The occasion: a fortune withheld in Ghatafan

The verse came down over a real case, and the case shows exactly the abuse it targets. Muqātil and al-Kalbī said it was a man of Ghatafan who held in his hands a great fortune belonging to his orphaned nephew. When the nephew reached puberty he claimed what was his, and the uncle refused to give it up. So they took their dispute to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this verse was revealed. The uncle at once said: "We obey Allah and we obey His Messenger. We seek refuge in Allah from the great peril." And he handed the wealth over to his nephew. The Prophet ﷺ then said that whoever is saved from the stinginess of his own soul and hands over what he was holding back in this way will abide in Allah's Garden.

The story has a coda. The young man, once he had his fortune, spent it in the way of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The reward is confirmed, but the sin still persists." Those present asked how a sin could persist when the wealth was being spent in Allah's way. He answered: "The reward is confirmed for the youth, but the sin persists for his father."

### Every use of the orphan's property is "eating"

The verse speaks of not eating the orphan's property along with one's own, because eating is the most common end-use of what a person possesses. In the usage of the Qur'an, however, "do not eat up" covers every kind of impermissible use: using, consuming, exhausting. Spending anything from an orphan's property unlawfully, by whatever means, is absolutely ḥarām (forbidden).

The manner of the prohibition carries a quiet rebuke. Those who misappropriate the property of orphans are usually people who own property of their own. They have lawful means at hand and still stoop to consuming what belongs to a fatherless child. The verse names that for what it is, a shameful act.

Orphans, boys and girls, are the weakest members of any family or society. Dealing with them as they deserve is therefore the hardest test of whether a person truly fears Allah. They are owed justice and compassion together, and their rights deserve the strongest protection. It counts as a major sin, for instance, to divide a jointly held property so that some receive valuable shares and others receive worthless ones, with the only aim being to make the listed items tally.

### The guardian's true opponent

There is a sharper way to read the verse, and it turns the guardian's eyes upward. Whoever is given charge over others and then acts unjustly toward those in his charge makes an adversary of his Lord. Allah avenges His servants in a way He does not avenge for His own sake. The protector of an orphan who acts with justice and kindness finds his own right protected by Allah. The one who behaves badly and aggressively finds Allah himself standing opposite him, taking the orphan's side.

### In short

- Orphans, children whose fathers have died, are to receive their property in full once they reach maturity and sound judgement. Until then the guardian protects it so it can be handed over whole.
- Swapping bad possessions of one's own for good ones of the orphan's, even with the counts matching, is forbidden taking, and so is any deal that loses the orphan money.
- The orphan's property is to be kept separate, or under accounts so clear that nothing of it is spent on the guardian.
- Every unlawful use of an orphan's property is "eating" it, and every form of it is forbidden. It is a great sin, in the Ethiopian-derived word ḥūb that Ibn ʿAbbās explained.
- The verse came down when an uncle of Ghatafan refused his nephew's fortune, and he surrendered it the moment he heard it. Whoever is saved from his own stinginess in that way abides in Allah's Garden.
- An unjust guardian makes Allah his adversary, for Allah avenges those under charge as He does not avenge His own cause.

3.text:
The verse before this one guarded the property of orphans. This one guards the orphan girls themselves, and then opens into the marriage law of the Qur'an: "If you fear you might fail to give orphan women their ˹due˺ rights ˹if you were to marry them˺, then marry other women of your choice—two, three, or four. But if you are afraid you will fail to maintain justice, then ˹content yourselves with˺ one or those ˹bondwomen˺ in your possession". The verse moves in three steps. It warns guardians away from marrying orphan girls for gain. It permits marriage to other women, up to four. And it commands a man who cannot be just between wives to stop at one. The closing words, "This way you are less likely to commit injustice", are the measure of the whole permission.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If you fear you might fail to give orphan women their ˹due˺ rights ˹if you were to marry them˺"** sets the test before the act. The verse does not wait for the wrong to be done. A guardian who suspects in himself the temptation to skimp on an orphan girl's dowry or her upkeep must drop the idea of marrying her and look elsewhere. The same standard reaches further than guardians. Just as people feared being unfair with the wealth of orphans, they were told to fear being unfair with women, for women stand with orphans in weakness and lack of power. Whoever cannot fulfil a wife's rights should not marry her.

**"then marry other women of your choice—two, three, or four"** opens a wide door and then frames it. Women other than the orphan girls under a man's care are many, and the believer is not restricted to one of them. The permission names a ceiling, not a target. Read with the practice of the Prophet ﷺ, it sets the limit of marriage at four wives at one time, and no more.

**"But if you are afraid you will fail to maintain justice"** names the condition on which the whole permission rests. The justice in question is the kind a man can deliver: equal spending on maintenance, and an equal share of nights and turns with each wife.

**"then ˹content yourselves with˺ one or those ˹bondwomen˺ in your possession"** gives two exits for the man who fears he cannot be fair. He keeps to a single wife. Or he stays with what his right hand owns, since bondwomen do not carry the same rights as wives. With them equal apportionment is not owed, and even the waiting period does not apply, so falling short of parity there carries no sin as it would between free wives. One caution belongs here. The ownership the verse speaks of can only come about through its own narrow conditions, conditions that generally do not exist in our time. No one may live with a woman outside marriage by simply declaring her his property. That claim is invalid and plainly unlawful.

**"This way you are less likely to commit injustice"** closes the verse with a word of nearness and a word of tilt. The word for "more likely" comes from a root meaning nearness: this arrangement brings a man nearer to safety. The word for injustice here comes from a root meaning to lean, an inclination that grows until it becomes outright wrongdoing. Following the verse, one wife or a bondwoman, keeps a man away from that lean. It does not by itself make him innocent of every wrong, for reasons the verse itself points to at its end.

### The abuse the verse answers

In the days before Islam the guardian of an orphaned girl held all the power and none of the accountability. A guardian would notice a girl in his charge who had good looks or valuable property. He would then marry her himself, or arrange her marriage to his son. He fixed the dower himself, and it was usually the lowest possible. He kept her in whatever manner suited him, for who was there to object? Her father, the one man who would have weighed every aspect of her future happiness in a marriage and made sure she was well provided for, was in the grave.

The Qur'an answers this with the command that every excuse, device and stratagem used to get at an orphan's property is impermissible. The rights of the orphan must be protected honestly. The verse came down over cases of exactly this kind. In the report of Muslim, ʿĀʾishah said it was revealed about a custodian in whose care was a female orphan with some wealth and no one to defend her. Out of greed for her money the custodian refused to give her in marriage, and he harmed her and treated her badly. The verse tells such a man to marry other women, lawful to him, and leave her alone.

Al-Bukhārī records ʿĀʾishah's account of a case that arose in the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ. A man had an orphaned girl in his guardianship who held a share in his fruit farm. He married the girl, though he did not really desire her, and instead of giving her a dower from his own pocket he took possession of her very share in the farm. Her money was mixed with his, and he kept her portion from her. The verse was revealed about his case. ʿUrwah ibn az-Zubayr asked ʿĀʾishah what the verse means, and she answered: it concerns the orphan girl who shares her guardian's house and his property. Her wealth and her beauty may tempt him to marry her without giving her the adequate dower that another suitor would have given. Such guardians were therefore barred from marrying them except with full justice and the most suitable dower. Otherwise they were told to marry other women.

That was not the end of the question. People went on asking the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about marrying orphan girls, and another verse came down: "They ask your instruction concerning the women" (4:127). There the words "yet whom you desire to marry" describe the guardian who does not want to marry the orphan girl in his care precisely because she has neither wealth nor beauty. A guardian who would not touch a poor plain girl but reaches for a rich pretty one is not choosing a wife. He is choosing property.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Qatādah, ar-Rabīʿ, ad-Daḥḥāk and as-Suddī read the verse against the habits of the time. People had become careful about the wealth of orphans after the earlier command, yet they took liberties with women and married whoever they liked, sometimes treating them fairly and sometimes not. When they asked about the orphans and the verse about their property came down, this verse came down with it: as you fear to deal unfairly with the orphan, so fear to deal unfairly with women. Marry only as many as you can fulfil the rights of. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās in the narration of al-Wālibī.

### Why the limit is four

The permission "two, three, or four" was read against a verse about angels: "Who made the angels messengers with wings, two or three or four" (35:1). That verse does not mean no angel has more than four wings, for there is proof that some do. The marriage verse is different. It specifies what men are allowed, as Ibn ʿAbbās and the majority of scholars stated. Had more than four wives been permitted, the verse would have said so. And the Prophet ﷺ applied the number as a hard limit in real cases.

A man named Ghilān ibn Salamah ath-Thaqafī had ten wives when he accepted Islam, and they accepted it with him. The Prophet ﷺ told him: "Choose any four of them, and divorce the rest." Ash-Shāfiʿī, at-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah, ad-Dāraquṭnī and al-Bayhaqī recorded the hadith up to those words, and only Aḥmad collected the full version. That version carries the rest of the story. In the reign of ʿUmar, Ghilān divorced his remaining wives as well and divided his money among his children. ʿUmar concluded that the devil, from what he overhears, had brought Ghilān word of his coming death, and he told him so. Then he gave him a choice: take back your wives and your money, or I will seize all of it and order your grave to be stoned, as the grave of Abū Righal was stoned. Abū Righal belonged to Thamūd, and he had been safe from their punishment only while he stayed within the sacred area. The moment he stepped out of it, the torment took him as it had taken them. Ghilān complied.

The argument from these reports is a fortiori. If the Prophet ﷺ did not let a new Muslim keep more than four of the wives he already had, then marrying more than four from the start is even more clearly barred. Two more cases seal it. Qays ibn al-Ḥārith al-Asadī accepted Islam with eight wives and mentioned it to the Prophet ﷺ, who told him: "Keep four of them and divorce the rest." Abu Daud records it. And Nawfal ibn Muʿāwiyah ad-Daylamī accepted Islam having five women in his nikah and was told to divorce one, in a report from the Musnad of Imam al-Shāfī, found in the Mishkāt with reference to Sharḥ al-Sunnah. The consistent practice of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions shows what the verse means: joining more than four women in marriage at one time is ḥarām (forbidden).

### Plurality of wives before Islam

More than one wife at a time was permitted in every religion of the world before Islam, and no law had drawn a line. The custom ran through Arabia, India, Iran, Egypt and Babylon. The Jews knew it, the Christians knew it, the Hindus and Aryans knew it, and the Zoroastrians knew it. The Vedic teachings allowed an unlimited number of wives at once, in tens, in thirteens, even in twenty sevens, and Shri Krishna, a greatly revered figure among Hindus, is said to have had hundreds. Among Christian writers there has always been a school, never the loudest, that defended plurality from the Bible as a blessing rather than a blot, and names such as Davenport, Father Nixon, John Milton and Isac Taylor have argued it.

The modern West set out to do away with plural marriage, and the result, on this reading, was not fewer women in men's lives but more of them outside marriage: a spread of kept mistresses and girlfriends with no bond at all. The euphemisms multiply, "relationship", "affair", "consenting adults", "partner", while the thing itself remains. A society that forbids a man to marry two women and winks at his taking two lovers has said no to marriage and yes to adultery, which is a strange place to stand. There is also the plain arithmetic of certain times and places, where women outnumber men. Where lawful plurality is closed, the alternative is not chastity but prostitution, or so the argument runs.

None of this is a defence of what Arabia actually did with the permission. Before Islam men took as many wives as they liked, some nine or ten, and Qays ibn al-Harth alone had eight. They satisfied greed first and discovered justice never. Wives lived like prisoners held in the chains of marriage. The darling of one season became the forgotten woman of the next, and the very idea of standing rights for wives did not exist. It was the Qur'an that stepped into this and stopped a great injustice: four at most, and equality made a binding duty, with a stern warning against contravention.

### What "of your choice" means

The words "of your choice" translate an Arabic expression whose literal sense is "what you like". Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Ibn Jubair and Ibn Mālik read it as meaning what is lawful: women who are permitted to you. Others kept the literal sense, women you like. There is no quarrel between the two. Together they say: women you are drawn to by natural inclination, who are also lawful for you under the rules of the sharīʿah.

### The marriage of orphan girls who are minors

The word for orphans in this verse covers orphaned girls, and in the terminology of the sharīʿah a yatīm is a boy or girl who has not yet reached puberty. From this the jurists drew a ruling: the guardian of an orphaned girl does have the authority to give her in marriage while she is still a minor, but only on condition that the decision is made with wisdom and her future welfare in view. Without that condition the door opens to abuses seen in some communities, where a grown girl is married to a child with no regard for the gap in their ages and no inquiry into the boy's circumstances or character.

An orphaned girl who has reached puberty has, without question, the right to choose her husband freely. In practice, though, young women are often too modest and shy to speak out on their own marriages, even when the right is theirs, and they accept in good faith what their guardians arrange. That very trust makes the guardian's duty heavier. He must not use it to step on her rights.

The verse therefore lays down a rule of total vigilance over the marital rights of orphaned girls. Enforcement is not left to government alone, as ordinary statutes are. The command is addressed to conscience first: fear Allah, and if you see injustice in yourself where an orphan girl is concerned, marry elsewhere. To that, the verse adds the ordinary arm of the state. The agencies charged with enforcement must watch that no such violation occurs in society, and where it does, they must use the force of law to see the rights fulfilled.

### The Prophet's ﷺ own marriages

Any talk of the four-wife permission invites the question of the Prophet's ﷺ own marriages, and the material answers it at length. His purpose in life was to carry the call of Islam, purify people and teach the Qur'an, and he taught by deed as much as by word. There is no corner of human life that did not need his guidance, from the congregational prayer to the treatment of wives, the upbringing of children and the etiquettes of the call of nature. What he did inside the walls of his house, how he dealt with his wives, how he answered the women who came to ask: all of it is recorded in the books of hadith, and much of it reached the community through his wives themselves.

That last point is the heart of the matter. His marriages created the setting in which the community could learn its religion from the inside of his household. Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah alone is the one from whom some two thousand and ten narrations are reported, covering the explanation of Qur'anic injunctions, questions of law and answer, morals and manners, and the Prophet's ﷺ life itself, and through such reports the Muslim ummah received guidance no other setting could have supplied. From Sayyidah Umm Salmah come three hundred and seventy eight. Ibn al-Qaiyyim observed that if the rulings Umm Salmah gave after the Prophet's ﷺ death were collected, they would make a treatise by themselves. ʿĀʾishah taught as the beacon light of religious knowledge for forty eight years after his death, and her students alone number around two hundred.

The calumny that his marriages served desire is answered by the plain record of his life, which his enemies watched for fifty years and never caught. Before the eyes of the Quraysh of Makkah he married, at twenty five, a widow older than himself who had lost two husbands and had children, and he stayed with no one but her for twenty five years. In those years he would leave home for a month at a time and sit in the cave of Hira, given to the remembrance of his Lord. Every one of his other marriages came after the age of fifty. His enemies called him magician, sorcerer, poet, madman, liar, fabricator. They used every arrow in the quiver. Not one of them, not once, said a word casting doubt on his chastity, because there was nothing to say.

The chronology strips the charge of everything. Khadijah was his only wife until he was fifty. Then came his marriages to Saudah and ʿĀʾishah, and Saudah came to his house while ʿĀʾishah, being young, stayed at her father's until the second year after the Hijrah, when she joined him in Madinah. He was fifty four then, with two wives. Hafsah came a year later. Then Zainab bint Khuzaymah, who died eighteen months after the marriage, or three months by one report. Umm Salmah he married in year four, Zainab bint Jahsh in year five, when he was fifty eight and had four wives, though he could have taken four the moment the permission was revealed, and never did. Juwayriyyah came in year six, Umm Habibah and Safiyyah in year seven, and Maymunah later in the same year. In sum: one wife until fifty four, four at fifty eight, and the rest within two or three years after that, in old age. Of all his wives, only ʿĀʾishah aṣ-Ṣiddīqah came to him a virgin. All the others were widows, with the single exception of Zainab bint Jahsh, and some had already lost two husbands. His Companions would have laid down their lives at his word. Had desire been the motive, nothing stopped him from marrying only virgins, or from changing wives every month or two. He never did.

And there is a verse to close the argument. Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ was a true prophet of Allah, and a prophet does not follow his own desires. What he does, he does by the leave and will of Allah, and once prophethood is granted, that is the whole account. But for the one who insists on the smear, there is a fact to face: the Prophet ﷺ proclaimed against himself a restriction never laid on another Muslim, "It is not lawful for you to take more wives after this" (33:52). A man chasing desire does not close his own doors.

Three of these marriages show their purpose in detail. Umm Salmah had lost her husband Abū Salmah, and she came to the Prophet ﷺ a widow with her children, whom he raised in his house with love and concern, demonstrating by his own conduct how stepchildren are to be brought up. Had none of his wives brought children, this whole area of guidance would have gone undemonstrated. Her son ʿUmar ibn Abī Salmah said he grew up in the lap of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Once, eating with him, the boy kept dunking his hand all over the bowl. The Prophet ﷺ told him: "Say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is in front of you." Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record it.

Juwayriyyah came to him as a prisoner of jihād, fallen to the share of Thābit ibn Qays or his cousin. She made an agreement with her master to buy her freedom for a sum, then came to the Prophet ﷺ asking his help with the payment. He said to her: "Shall I not tell you something much better than this? That I pay on your behalf and marry you?" She agreed with pleasure, and he paid and married her. Then came something no law could have produced. Hundreds of her people had passed into the ownership of the Companions as prisoners. When the Companions learned that the Prophet ﷺ had married her, they freed their slaves, one after another, unable to keep in bondage people now joined to the Prophet's ﷺ household by marriage. ʿĀʾishah said of it: "One hundred families of Banū al-Muṣṭaliq became free because of his marriage with Juwayriyyah. I know of no other woman who proved a greater blessing for her people."

Umm Habibah had accepted Islam in Makkah in the early days and migrated to Ethiopia with her husband. There her husband turned Christian and died soon after. The Prophet ﷺ proposed to her through the Negus, the emperor of Ethiopia, who gave her in marriage to him there. She was the daughter of Abū Sufyān, at that time the leader of the camp whose declared aim was hostility to Islam. When Abū Sufyān learned of the marriage, the words escaped him involuntarily: "He is a man of valour. His nose cannot be cut off." A man of honour is not easily disgraced, and there, under his own nose, his daughter had become the Prophet's ﷺ wife. The marriage worked as psychological warfare: it watered down the ambitions of the leader of the unbelievers, and the political gain for Islam and the Muslims can hardly be denied. God's far-sighted and wise Messenger, in all likelihood, had that in sight. Those who want the fuller picture will find it in the treatise devoted to the plurality of his marriages, and still more in the books of hadith and the Prophet's ﷺ life read from their own sources rather than from the books of those who set out to trap Muslims with golden snares.

### Justice between wives

The permission ends where injustice begins. More than one wife is allowed and fitting only on condition that the equality required by the sharīʿah can be maintained and the rights of all the wives fulfilled. A man who cannot do that must keep to one wife, or to what his right hand owns. Whoever thinks of marrying more than one should first look hard at himself, weigh his means and his character, and ask honestly whether he can treat several wives justly without failing any of them. If the strong likelihood is that he cannot, then stepping into a second marriage is a thoughtless plunge into grave sin. Human condition being what it is, one wife is enough for most.

The law behind it is exact. A marriage beyond four wives contracted in a single offer and acceptance is void from the start, since no one has the right to more than four. Within the limit of four, the marriages are valid, but it is obligatory, wājib, to maintain justice and equality between the wives, and falling short is a grave sin. A wife whose rights are infringed can take the matter to an Islamic court and obtain redress.

The Prophet ﷺ pressed the duty with warnings and lived it to the outer edge. In a hadith he said that a man with two wives who cannot fulfil their rights equally and justly will be raised on the Day of Doom with one shoulder drooping. He himself treated his wives with full equality in everything within his control, even in matters where equality was not mandatory, and then he prayed:

> O Allah, this is my equalizing in what I control. So do not hold me to account for what You control and I do not.

For the equality demanded of a man runs only through what is in his power: the spending on each wife's upkeep, and the parity of nights and turns. The tilt of the heart is not in his power, and no one is taken to account for what is not his choice, on one binding condition: the heart's tilt must never leak into the things he does control. The Qur'an says plainly that perfect equality between wives is beyond a man: "You will never be able to do perfect justice between wives even if it is your ardent desire" (4:129). Love cannot be portioned by rule. But even that involuntary tilt is not left uncorrected, for the same passage forbids the full tilt: a man who loves one wife more may not therefore turn from the other in total indifference. If something even an infallible Messenger cannot claim, the heart's exact equality, is written as a duty, it is because the duty covers only the part a servant can reach.

### The apparent contradiction with 4:129

Some readers set the two verses side by side and stumble. This verse commands one wife if perfect justice is feared impossible. The later verse declares perfect justice impossible outright. Does it not follow that more than one wife is forbidden altogether?

The answer lies in what each verse is measuring. The first verse speaks of justice in matters of choice: spending, maintenance, turns, the things a man does or refuses to do. That justice is commanded, and discrepancy in it is a grave sin. The second verse speaks of love and the heart's inclination, which no man commands. Had Allah meant the verses to abolish plural marriage, the details would be pointless. Why say "marry women of your choice, two, three, or four" at all? Why say "if you fear you will not be just", when on that reading the injustice would be certain and fear would have no meaning? And the words and deeds of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, generation after generation, show more than one wife, up to four, was never treated as forbidden. The two verses contradict nothing. They divide the field: the hand is commanded to equality, the heart is excused its preference, and neither verse voids the other.

### Why "closer" and not "safe"

The verse ends by saying one wife is "closer" to not doing injustice, and the choice of word was itself discussed. A man with one wife has no second wife to wrong. Why not say the arrangement makes him safe outright? Because there are men who inflict every kind of injustice on even one wife. Not marrying a second time does not by itself cure a man of injustice. What the single marriage does is remove the likeliest occasion and bring him nearer to fairness. Complete deliverance from wrong comes only when the one wife's rights are given in full, generously, her shortcomings forgiven and her difficult ways borne with patience. That is the standard for one wife as much as for four.

### In short

- A guardian who fears he cannot give an orphan girl her full rights, her dower and her due, must not marry her. He should marry other women, who are many.
- Marriage is permitted up to four wives at one time, no more. The Prophet ﷺ had new Muslims with ten, eight and five wives keep four, or release one, and that practice fixed the limit.
- Plurality of wives was unlimited in every religion before Islam and unrestricted in Arabia. The Qur'an capped it at four and made equal treatment a binding duty.
- The orphan girl who is a minor may be given in marriage by her guardian only on the strength of wisdom and her future welfare. A grown orphan girl chooses for herself, and her trust makes the guardian's duty heavier, not lighter.
- The Prophet's ﷺ marriages came after fifty, mostly to widows, and served the teaching of the community, the freeing of prisoners, ties with opposing camps, and the raising of stepchildren. ʿĀʾishah alone transmitted some two thousand and ten reports.
- Justice between wives is obligatory in spending and turns, which a man controls. The heart's tilt he does not control, is not punished for, and may not act on. If he cannot keep the justice he controls, the rule is one wife.

4.text:
The previous verse removed one injustice against women, the injustice of marriage without justice. This one takes up a particular right, the mahr (dower): "Give women ˹you wed˺ their due dowries graciously. But if they waive some of it willingly, then you may enjoy it freely with a clear conscience". The dower is the payment the husband owes the bride herself. The verse commands that it be given, and that it be given gladly, and then names the one case in which a husband may take any of it back: when the wife, truly of her own will, hands it over.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Give women ˹you wed˺ their due dowries graciously"** states an obligation from Allah, and the adverb carries half the law. The dower is the wife's right, and the husband is to pay it himself, into her hands, as one gives a gift, with a good heart. The word translated "graciously" is niḥlah, which in Arabic usage means giving something cheerfully. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥā reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the niḥlah of this verse is the dowry itself. Ibn Isḥāq narrated from az-Zuhrī, from ʿUrwah, from ʿĀʾishah, that niḥlah means obligatory. Muqātil, Qatādah and Ibn Jurayj said the same, and Ibn Jurayj added the sense of specified. Ibn Zayd said that in Arabic niḥlah refers to what is necessary, so the command is: do not marry unless you give the wife something that is her right. After the Prophet ﷺ no one may marry a woman without the required dowry, nor by giving false promises about one. Since every obligatory right is to be discharged cheerfully, the dower is no exception: give it, and give it in good cheer.

**"But if they waive some of it willingly"** opens the single exception. The words "of their own accord" are pinned to the women themselves, not to circumstance. It is their own selves that must be pleased to let the husband have some of the dowry.

**"then you may enjoy it freely with a clear conscience"** permits what the earlier hesitation had questioned. Some people had been uneasy about a husband taking back any part of the dower, and the verse was revealed in answer to them. If the waiver is genuine, taking what is given is lawful, with no blame and no harm in the Hereafter. The two words of the ending are worth their weight. One, haniʾan, describes what comes without labour or pain, the way good food is eaten, digested easily and turned into health. The other, mariʾan, from a root meaning to be wholesome, says nearly the same, and the two are so close that some translators render both with one word. What is taken freely from a willing wife sits well. What is squeezed from her does not.

### The three old injustices

Before Islam, the dower was wronged in three ways, and the verse answers all three.

First, the dower was simply taken by the girl's guardians instead of given to her. The command is addressed to husbands so that they themselves put the dower in the wife's hands, and to guardians so that whatever passes through them on the way reaches the girl intact and untouched for personal use without her permission.

Second, the dower was paid, but sourly, as a penalty is paid, by a man with no way out. The word niḥlah cuts that attitude out of the transaction. What is owed by obligation is still to be given with cheer.

Third, husbands used the wife's powerlessness to press her into forgoing the dower altogether. The verse answers that exacting a waiver by pressure achieves nothing. Nothing is forgiven that way. A waiver counts only when the wife herself elects it, out of free choice in its most genuine sense, whether she forgoes part of the dower before taking it or returns part after having it in hand. Then, and only then, it is permissible and correct for the husband.

These abuses peaked in the Jāhiliyyah, and the shame is that traces of them survive among Muslims in some tribes and regions to this day. Before Islam men used to marry without giving any dowry at all. Every such practice is to be left behind.

### What counts as willing

The restriction to the wife's own sweet will is not decoration. It rests on a principle the Prophet ﷺ stated once and for all:

> Beware, do no injustice. A person's property is not lawful for another unless it be through his sweet will.

From that one rule many details flow. Consider the woman of our own time who doubts she will ever see her dower. She expects that asking for it will displease everyone, so, like it or not, she lets it go. That kind of forgiveness is not to be trusted. The real touchstone, as Ashraf Thanavī used to teach, is to place the dower in the wife's hands first, as its owner. What she then returns to the husband, freely and without pressure, is truly given. The same test governs inheritance. It is common enough, after a father's or mother's death, for sons to take over the whole property and leave the girls their share only on paper. If such brothers feel a twinge of conscience, the most they do is go and excuse themselves before their sisters, who, knowing they will not be paid anyway, forgive against their will. That forgiveness is worthless, and withholding the share is open usurpation. The widow's share, and especially the stepmother's, is treated the same way. The one exception is a forgiveness that is genuinely glad.

The text says the whole self must be willing, not merely the heart. Men who pay bribes or interest do so after calculation and with apparent gain, but no one would call that glad giving. Probe such a man's conscience and his self would flatly refuse. That is why good cheer and sweet will are given the deciding role. The rule runs beyond family. Donations sought for mosques or religious schools are lawful only when the giver gives freely and gladly. A donation squeezed out by tribal, social or legal pressure may not be accepted or used. It goes back to the giver.

### Why the dower is called ṣadaqah

The verse calls the dower ṣaduqāt, the plural of ṣaduqah. The words ṣaduqah and ṣudaq both signify the dower of women, and the name is a small sermon. The root ṣadaqa signifies truth, and the dower shows the true attitude of the husband toward his wife, which made the name fit. Mulla ʿAlī Qārī notes this in his commentary on the Mishkāt.

### The food of the generous

Read inwardly, the ending of the verse says something about people at table. What the generous set before others is wholesome, because they feed from good-heartedness. What the miserly serve is spoiled food, for they look only to themselves and feed out of obligation. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The food of the generous is a remedy, while the food of the miser is a disease." What a man takes from a wife's free gift is of the first kind. What he grinds out of her is of the second.

### In short

- The dower is the wife's right, owed by the husband personally, and it is to be paid gladly, not as a ransom. Niḥlah, the word for this gladness, was explained by Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿĀʾishah and others as meaning the dowry itself, and as obligatory and specified.
- No marriage is valid without the required dower, and false promises about it do not count.
- A waiver of the dower is valid only when the wife's own self, not just her resignation, gives it freely. Pressure-produced forgiveness forgives nothing.
- The same rule governs property of every kind: nothing of another person's is lawful without their glad consent, which is why shares of inheritance and pressured donations must also be returned or honoured.
- Taken from a willing wife, what is given back is wholesome enjoyment. The food of the generous is a remedy, the food of the miser a disease.

5.text:
The previous verses ordered the property of orphans returned and the dowries of women paid in full. This verse adds the other half of the rule: "Do not entrust the incapable ˹among your dependants˺ with your wealth which Allah has made a means of support for you—but feed and clothe them from it, and speak to them kindly". A right to property is not the same as an ability to manage it. Where the person entitled is not yet capable, the property stays in the hands of the one who can guard it, while the incapable person is fed and clothed from it and treated with gentleness.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do not entrust the incapable ˹among your dependants˺ with your wealth"** forbids the handover. The word behind "the incapable" is the foolish, the weak of judgement. Who exactly is meant was answered in several ways. Ad-Daḥḥāk reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that it refers to children and women. Ibn Masʿūd, al-Ḥakam ibn ʿUyaynah, al-Ḥasan and ad-Daḥḥāk said women and boys. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said the unwise are the orphans. Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah and Qatādah said they are women. In one reading the foolish are the squanderers found among men, women and children alike. Behind the disagreement stands a shared idea: whoever is likely to spend wrongly, whether from immaturity or inexperience, is not to be given free use of wealth.

**"which Allah has made a means of support for you"** explains the stakes. Property is what stands people up, the beam the household rests on. The words can also be read as "that by which property is valued", and both readings say the same thing: this wealth is the substance of livelihood, for the guardian and for the children alike, and it must not be wrecked.

**"but feed and clothe them from it, and speak to them kindly"** gives the guardian his alternative duty. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: do not give to your wife or children the wealth Allah has made your responsibility and your means of sustenance. Keep the money in your own care, look after it, and let the spending on their food, clothes and provision come from you. If they demand the property, explain honestly and gently, in a way that neither breaks their heart nor wastes the wealth. Ibn ʿAbbās gave the very words a father might use: "All this is there for you. Just grow up a little more and you will have it all." The same explanation is reported from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, and al-Ṭabarī adopted this view. The kind words are part of the command itself: Mujāhid read the closing phrase as kindness and the keeping of good relations. Where there is nothing to give at the moment, even a promise to clothe and provide, spoken kindly, is within the verse.

### Who the ruling covers

The immediate setting is the orphan, but the words are general. The verse reaches all children, orphaned or not, and all whose judgement is weak, and the form of address, "your wealth", carries a deliberate breadth. It includes the property of the guardians themselves and, for as long as the orphans remain immature, the property of the orphans too, which stays in the guardian's safe custody and under his responsibility as though it were his own. Verse 2 has already settled the ownership beyond doubt, that the orphan's property goes to the orphan alone, so no confusion arises.

The same rule extends past childhood. It applies in insanity and erratic behaviour, in weakness of intellect or of religious practice, and in bankruptcy, where creditors ask that the property of a man who cannot pay his debts be placed in escrow. Wherever handling fails, custody holds.

### Why property is guarded so strictly

Property is meant neither for luxury nor for display. It is the means by which a person lives, and its protection matters. Human love can do the very thing greed does: out of natural affection, people hand properties to inexperienced children or ill-informed women, and the usual result is waste and the quick poverty that follows it. A person who squanders what was supporting a household has torn a hole in the arrangement by which Allah gives His servants their livelihood, and that is true whoever the owner is. When the property belongs to an orphan, the weakest member of society, the duty of protection is at its strongest and the dealing must be fair and just.

### The worth of lawful wealth

A cluster of reports fixes the value the verse places on property. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever is killed defending his property is a shahīd (martyr), counted with the martyrs in divine reward, just as the one killed defending his life earns the great reward of shahādah (martyrdom). Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record it. He also said that the best asset a good man can hold is property that is good and clean, and that being rich does no harm to one who fears Allah, because such a person keeps his wealth away from sin. The anti-wealth sayings of many saints apply only to wealth earned in lust and spent on sin, which becomes its owner's punishment. Still, since people who grow rich tend to drift from moderation, the earliest generations earned about what they needed, gave thanks, and were glad to be spared the final audit of every dirham. In an age when people care little for faith and will drop it rather than fall out with a passing fashion, lawful earning and careful conservation matter all the more. The Prophet ﷺ said that poverty can push a person to the edge of disbelief. Sufyān al-Thawrī put the two sides together: once, keeping wealth was thought blamable, but today wealth is the shield of the believer. Whoever holds wealth in such times should make it serve him well, for when a need presses, a person without means is liable to spend his faith to meet it.

### The inner reading

Read inwardly, the foolish are whoever turns a servant from the Real and busies him away from the Lord: the dependents and children who prefer their worldly portion over the rights of Allah most high. The wealth assigned as your maintenance is to be handled without the disgrace of begging and contriving: better to stay with pleasing actions, generosity over withholding, patience over grasping. Rather than form the intention to beg, or make yourself and your dependents a burden on others, hold on to a sufficient amount of what Allah has assigned you, and be generous with what exceeds your needs. Two further counsels follow. If you have more than enough to help your dependents today, do not withhold what you know they need out of fear of future poverty. And if your hand is too tight to support them, do not let your tongue loose in speaking ill of them. When the lower self calls a person to spend in a useless way, that person is the most foolish of the foolish, and should not yield to it.

### In short

- The incapable, whether understood as children and women, as women and boys, as orphans or as squanderers of any kind, are not to be given free use of wealth, theirs or anyone's.
- The guardian holds the property, spends from it on their food and clothing, and speaks to them gently, promising good without breaking hearts.
- The rule extends to every kind of weak judgement: insanity, erratic behaviour, weak intellect or religion, and bankruptcy escrow.
- Property is the means of livelihood, not luxury or pride. Squandering it is a sin, defending it can earn martyrdom, and wealth in God-fearing hands does no harm.
- Read inwardly, the foolish are whatever pulls a servant from his Lord, and the command is to hold enough, give the excess, help today, and never spend uselessly.

6.text:
The surah now comes to the moment of return. The orphan's property, guarded through childhood, must go back at the right time and in the right way: "Test ˹the competence of˺ the orphans until they reach a marriageable age. Then if you feel they are capable of sound judgment, return their wealth to them. And do not consume it wastefully and hastily before they grow up ˹to demand it˺. If the guardian is well-off, they should not take compensation; but if the guardian is poor, let them take a reasonable provision. When you give orphans back their property, call in witnesses. And sufficient is Allah as a ˹vigilant˺ Reckoner". The verse was revealed over a real question. Rifāʿah died leaving his son Thābit ibn Rifāʿah al-Anṣārī very young, and the boy's uncle came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to ask what was lawful for him from his orphan nephew's wealth and when he should hand it back. The answer came as this verse: test, then return, with witnesses, and Allah watching.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Test ˹the competence of˺ the orphans"** is a command of practical education.
