What is tested is intelligence, in the words of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, as-Suddī and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, and the test is conducted by doing: the child is given small assignments of buying and selling well before maturity, and the guardian watches how he manages himself in actual transactions.

**"until they reach a marriageable age"** is the age of puberty. When a child has become eligible for marriage through the signs of adulthood, the special assessment begins. The majority of scholars hold that puberty arrives with the first wet dream.

**"Then if you feel they are capable of sound judgment, return their wealth to them"** names the true finish line, which is not a birthday but demonstrated judgement. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said it means finding them good in their religion and wise with their money, and the same was reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and others among the leading scholars. The scholars of fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence) therefore state that when a child becomes sound in religion and competent with money, the money kept for him is surrendered.

**"And do not consume it wastefully and hastily before they grow up ˹to demand it˺"** warns the guardian against two distinct sins while he waits: spending above the orphan's normal needs, and spending early, in a hurry, as though racing the day the boy grows up and the property must leave the guardian's hand.

**"If the guardian is well-off, they should not take compensation"** makes guardianship an unpaid duty for the rich man. The service is an obligation on him, and receiving payment for it is not permissible.

**"but if the guardian is poor, let them take a reasonable provision"** permits the poor guardian a share. He may consume from the orphan's property in fairness, a measure just about right to cover his basic needs, or, as some added, in proportion to the work he does for the estate, or as a loan he intends to repay.

**"When you give orphans back their property, call in witnesses"** protects both sides. The handover happens in front of reliable witnesses so that no one can later deny receiving what he received, and the guardian stands absolved with a clear proof.

**"And sufficient is Allah as a ˹vigilant˺ Reckoner"** closes the account. Allah is enough as Witness, Reckoner and Watcher over the guardians' work, whether the property they return is complete and whole or deficient and less. He knows all of it. A small point of the wording carries the emphasis: the preposition in the phrase is extra, and the verse means, plainly, Allah suffices as the One who counts everything.

### How the testing works

Children move through three stages in these verses. First, minority, before puberty. Second, after puberty. Third, self-reliance and discretion in conducting one's own affairs, rushd as opposed to safāḥah, sound judgement as opposed to folly. In the first stage the guardian educates and trains the child with hands-on experience, letting him grow smarter through small dealings in buying and selling on his own. That is what the command to test the orphans means. From it Abū Ḥanīfah deduced the ruling that transactions of buying and selling entered into by minor children with their guardian's permission are sound, valid and operative. In the second stage, when the child is mature and of marriageable age, the guardian examines his growth in experience, intelligence and dealing. When it is clear that the child understands his profit and his loss and handles his affairs satisfactorily, the property is handed over.

### When a child counts as grown

Real maturity, the verse indicates, is not tied to a count of years but to the indicators and signs of adulthood. When those signs show and the person is fit to marry, maturity is established, even at thirteen or fourteen. Puberty by wet dream is the marker held by the majority. ʿAlī said he memorized from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ the words: "There is no orphan after the age of puberty, nor vowing to be silent throughout the day to the night." Abū Dāwūd recorded it. Another hadith from ʿĀʾishah and other Companions says that three kinds of person have no deeds recorded by the pen: the child until he reaches puberty, the sleeper until he wakes, and the senile until his mind returns.

Where the signs do not appear, age steps in. The two Ṣaḥīḥs record Ibn ʿUmar saying that he was presented to the Prophet ﷺ on the eve of Uḥud at fourteen and was not allowed to join the battle, and presented again on the eve of al-Khandaq, the battle of the Trench, at fifteen, and was allowed. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbdul-ʿAzīz, when this hadith reached him, said: "This is the difference between a child and an adult." Fifteen completed years is also the mark fixed by al-Shāfī. Muslim jurists differ where signs never appear: some set eighteen years for boys and seventeen for girls, some fifteen for both, and the Ḥanafī ruling, given as the operative fatwa, is that boy and girl are both considered mature under Islamic law once they have completed their fifteenth year, whether or not the signs of maturity are found.

One further sign was debated: pubic hair. The correct opinion is that it does count as a sign of adulthood, and the sunnah supports it. Imam Aḥmad recorded from ʿAṭiyyah al-Quraẓī that on the day of Quriẓah the captives were presented to the Prophet ﷺ, and whoever had grown pubic hair was executed while whoever had not was left to go free. ʿAṭiyyah was one of those set free. The four compilers of the Sunan recorded something similar, and at-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.

### Sound judgement, and how long to wait

The Qur'an commands the handover when proper understanding is perceived, but sets no final age for it. Some jurists leaned toward holding the property until full understanding is certain, keeping it in the guardian's custody for life if need be. Abū Ḥanīfah, however, verified the issue differently: the absence of rushd that the verse speaks of is the effect of childhood, and that effect is gone within ten years after maturity. Fifteen years for bulūgh, maturity, and ten years for rushd bring the age of presumed understanding to twenty five. By then the barriers of childhood are past, and the property goes over.

The verse also says "sound judgement" in an indefinite form, and the indefiniteness softens the standard. Perfect sense is not an absolute condition. A reasonable measure of understanding is enough, on the strength of which the property is given. Some people remain simple, innocent, slow and shy in their practical dealings their whole lives, and they are not to be deprived of their property for it. Only the totally insane fall under a separate rule: such a person stays in the category of the immature child, and his property is never handed over unless his mind returns, even if his whole life passes in insanity.

Read inwardly, to perceive maturity in someone is to perceive decency and integrity in him: generosity and the preservation of honour, keeping company with elders, striving toward good and performing acts of devotion as the command decrees. The rashīd, the mature one, is a person whom Allah has guided to his Lord, so that when a need presses on him he leans neither on his own strength and power, nor on his own plans and choices.

### The two temptations of the waiting guardian

The verse names the guardian's two temptations precisely. The first is extravagance, spending above the orphan's normal needs out of the property in one's care. The second is haste, starting to spend from the orphan's property long before there is any need, as if in a race against the boy's growing up, the day the property would have to be returned and the guardian's control would end. One reported reading of the phrase hears the guardian's own fear in it: consuming in haste lest they grow up and put a stop to the devouring of their wealth. Both are forbidden, and the boundary is simple: the orphan's wealth is used only when there is genuine need.

### The guardian's wage

May a man who spends his time and labour raising an orphan and protecting his property take payment for it from that property? The rule comes in the verse's own words. The rich guardian, who can meet his needs by other means, takes nothing, because the service is an obligation already on him. The poor guardian, who has no other livelihood, may consume from it in fairness, an amount just about right for his basic needs. ʿĀʾishah said that the verse about the rich abstaining and the poor consuming fairly concerns the orphan's guardian, and covers whatever labour he performs for the orphan's estate. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded it and al-Bukhārī collected it. A man once told the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he had no money but had an orphan in his care. The answer was:

> Eat from your orphan's wealth without extravagance or wastefulness, without mixing it, and without saving your own money by spending his.

Imam Aḥmad recorded it in the report of ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb from his father from his grandfather.

### The same rule for public trusts

The verse yields a wider juristic principle by extension. It covers those who supervise awqāf (religious endowments and trusts), manage mosques and religious schools, head the institutions of Muslim states, or render similar service to country and community, service known in Islamic terminology as fard ʿalal-kifāyah, an obligation that absolves the rest when some discharge it. The superior conduct for such people, if they have the means to maintain their families, is to take nothing from those institutions or from the public treasury. If they lack means of their own and give their earning time to the service, they may take from it in proportion to their need. The condition is exactly that: proportion to need. Plenty of people fix a small official salary to satisfy the letter of the law and then spend on themselves and their families by a dozen other routes far beyond it. For that there is no remedy except the fear of Allah, and the verse's last words are addressed to everyone alike, ruler and ruled: the man untouched by unlawful acquisitions is the man who fears the final accounting.

### Witnesses, and the Reckoner

When the testing is done and the property goes back, witnesses are called to be present, so that no dispute can arise later and the guardian's responsibility is honourably discharged with a clear proof. Some add that the settlement should be recorded in writing as well, which serves the same purpose. The person whose affairs are being settled may be weak and unable to defend himself, but the Arbiter is not weak. Allah will catch hold of everyone who administered another's affairs unjustly on the Day of Reckoning and punish the unjustified settlement severely. None can escape it.

For all of that, the true Guardian of the orphan is Allah. In his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim records the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying to Abū Dharr:

> O Abū Dharr! You are weak, and I love for you what I love for myself. Do not become a leader of two, and do not assume guardianship of an orphan's property.

### In short

- Orphans are tested for competence through real dealing, small buying and selling, from before maturity. Abū Ḥanīfah deduced from this that a minor's transactions with the guardian's permission are valid.
- Maturity comes by its signs, the wet dream, or pubic hair, or by age: fifteen, the age at which Ibn ʿUmar was allowed at al-Khandaq, and the mark fixed by al-Shāfī and by the Ḥanafī ruling.
- The property is returned when sound judgement appears, good religion and competence with money. By the Ḥanafī reckoning the latest presumption is twenty five, since the word "sound judgement" is indefinite and a reasonable measure suffices. The permanently insane never take charge of property.
- Wasteful and hasty spending from the orphan's wealth while waiting is forbidden. The rich guardian takes no wage. The poor guardian takes according to need, or the measure of his work, and the same rule governs everyone paid from public trusts.
- The handover is witnessed, so no right is lost and no dispute remains, and Allah is sufficient as Reckoner, for even the weak orphan's cause is in His hands.

7.text:
The surah now arrives at inheritance, and its first sentence overturns a whole social order: "For men there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave, and for women there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave—whether it is little or much. ˹These are˺ obligatory shares". Before this verse, women and children in Arabia did not inherit at all. After it, every relative named by the law holds a fixed, compulsory share that no one may enlarge or shrink.

### Phrase by phrase

**"For men there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave"** states the right of inheritance in general. Two words carry the system. "Parents" points to the bond of birth between children and their father and mother. "Close relatives" covers every kind of family tie: birth, the wider kinship, and the bond created by marriage. Parents are named separately only because of their importance. The same word also fixes the operating principle of the whole law: mere kinship is not enough, the heir must be the nearest in kinship. If nearness were not the standard, the estate of every deceased person would have to be split across the entire human race, since everyone descends from one father and mother, Ādam (Adam) and Ḥawwā (Eve). Each person would receive a particle worth nothing. So when choosing among relatives, the nearer excludes the farther. And where several relatives are equally near, though in different ways, they share together: the father, the mother, the children and the wife are all nearest, each in their own mode.

**"and for women there is a share in what their parents and close relatives leave"** repeats the right in a second, independent sentence. The repetition is deliberate. The two entitlements could have been merged into one sentence, but the Qur'an states each on its own, to emphasize that a woman's right in inheritance stands on its own and matters as much as a man's. Kinship is the same in a boy and a girl. Both are born to their parents. If inheritance hangs on kinship alone, nothing justifies cutting out a small child or a girl.

**"—whether it is little or much"** corrects another old custom. Some people would assign particular items, a horse or a sword, to young males alone as a matter of right and deprive everyone else of them. The verse sweeps that away: in everything the deceased owned, big or small, every inheritor holds a standing right, and no inheritor may set anything aside for himself before the estate has been formally distributed.

**"˹These are˺ obligatory shares"** closes the foundation. The shares are determined, apportioned by Allah Himself. Nobody may add to them, delete from them, change them or transpose them by personal opinion or analogical deduction. The word also makes the transfer of ownership automatic and compulsory. It does not depend on the heir's acceptance, consent or satisfaction. Even if he declares that he will not take his share, he is its owner in the sight of the sharīʿah. Once he owns it, he may gift it, sell it or give it away under the rules of the sharīʿah if he wishes.

### The world before this verse

The pre-Islamic Arabs lived by a plain principle: the one who deserves inheritance is the one who rides a horse, fights the enemy and collects the battle spoils. Women and children self-evidently could not live by that principle. So only a grown young man could inherit. A girl was out of the question, minor or grown, and a boy too young to fight was passed over as well. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Qatādah said exactly this: the idolaters used to give adult men a share and deprive women and children of it, and this verse came down against them. Nor was the injustice local. The nations around the world left these two weaker members of society without their natural rights, and none of their laws recognized the rights of orphans and women as such. Even where a right was conceded in words, no power existed to wrest it from the strong and hold it safe. Islam championed their cause, legalized their rights and built the safeguards around them.

### The occasion of the verse

The reports centre on the family of Aws ibn Thābit al-Anṣārī. He died leaving his wife, Umm Kujjah in one report and Umm Kuhhah in another, and children: two daughters, or three, and in one account a young son as well. Two paternal cousins, named in one report as Suwayd and ʿArfajah, came and took the whole estate into their possession, following the old custom that women and children do not inherit. They gave nothing to the widow or the children. Ibn Marduwyah reported from Jābir that Umm Kujjah came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah! I have two daughters whose father died, and they do not own anything." In the fuller report she said that their father had left a considerable fortune now held by the two cousins, who fed her nothing and cared for the children not at all. The cousins were summoned and defended themselves: her children cannot ride a horse, bear responsibility or harm an enemy. The Prophet ﷺ told them to leave for now, that he would wait for what Allah related to him concerning the matter. He did not yet have a verse. In one account the widow even suggested that the cousins marry the two orphaned daughters, to relieve her of the burden of providing for them, and they refused that too.

Then this verse came down, and after it the verses that detail the shares. The Prophet ﷺ divided the estate by the Qur'an. The wife received her one-eighth. Of the rest, half went to the son and half was shared between the two daughters. The cousins, farther in kinship than the children, received nothing.

### Not need, but nearness

The verse teaches that distribution is not based on need but on nearness of kinship. The nearest relative outranks a poorer, needier one. This is not hardness but law. Need is a shifting thing: conditions change, levels change, and a rule built on need or usefulness could never settle into solid law, for the claimants would multiply and the settlement would never end. Nearness is fixed. One hard case is answered directly: the orphaned grandson. If his father died before the grandfather, the grandson may be poorer and needier than anyone, but in the presence of a son of the deceased he is not the nearest, and he does not inherit. The entire Muslim ummah has held this, clarified by the Qur'an and the hadith, and only some contemporary westernized modernists have argued otherwise. The need of such a grandson is not forgotten. It is met by the very next verse, which opens the estate to those excluded from it.

### The inner reading

Read inwardly, the fixing of inheritance carries a lesson about gifts. Inheritance does not vary with virtue or good qualities, nor is it reduced by fault, defect or sin. A man dies leaving two sons: their rights are equal even where one son is God-fearing and the other disobedient and wicked. The good one receives nothing extra for his fear of Allah, and the bad one loses nothing for his badness. The deeper meaning is that inheritance is a gift from Allah that comes before any action of the heir, so the pious and the wicked share it alike. The same is true of faith itself, which is a gift given before any action or virtue. Allah said: "Then We bequeathed the Book to those of Our servants whom We chose. Yet some of them are those who wrong themselves, and some of them are moderate, and some are those who take the lead in good works by the leave of God. That is the greatest favor" (35:32).

### In short

- Men and women both inherit from parents and near kin, in everything the deceased owned, whether little or much. The two rights are stated separately on purpose.
- Before Islam, only fighting adult men inherited in Arabia, and much of the world was no better. The verse came down after the cousins of Aws ibn Thābit seized his whole estate, leaving his widow and daughters nothing.
- Inheritance follows nearness of kinship, not need. The nearer excludes the farther, and equally near relatives of different kinds share together.
- The shares are fixed by Allah. No one may change them, and ownership passes automatically, whether or not the heir consents.
- Read inwardly, inheritance is a gift that precedes action, like faith itself, shared alike by the pious and the wicked.

8.text:
The rule of nearness excludes some people from every division of an estate: the distant relative, and sometimes the poor who happen to be standing there. This verse catches them on their way out: "If ˹non-inheriting˺ relatives, orphans, or the needy are present at the time of distribution, offer them a ˹small˺ provision from it and speak to them kindly". The excluded are not to be shooed away from the table. They are to be given something from what is being divided, and spoken to well.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If ˹non-inheriting˺ relatives, orphans, or the needy are present at the time of distribution"** paints the scene. The relatives meant are those of kinship who cannot inherit, and the orphans and the needy are those present before the division is effected. They watch each eligible person assume a share while they stand desperate, receiving nothing.

**"offer them a ˹small˺ provision from it"** is the command of kindness. Those who are receiving shares without any effort of their own, simply through the mercy of Allah, should let their hearts beat with the urge to give. What they hand over becomes charity, rewarded by Allah, and it compensates something of the sense of deprivation the onlookers carry. It also covers the orphaned grandson excluded under the rule of nearness: his uncles and aunts should be glad to give him something each from their own shares. One caution bounds the command. The gift must come from the shares of the adult inheritors present. Gifts from the shares of minors and of those absent are not allowed.

**"and speak to them kindly"** handles the harder case. If the excluded are not satisfied with what they receive and start demanding a share equal to everyone's, the demand is unjust and contrary to the sharīʿah, and there is no way to satisfy it. Even then, no rudeness. The rule itself is explained to them politely: they have no share under the law of inheritance, and what they were given was a gift. Where the heir is himself a minor, the guardian makes a goodly promise on his behalf: "when the child grows up, we will tell him to give you something."

### Command, counsel or abrogated?

Is this giving obligatory? The reports divide. Ibn Jarīr recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that the verse still applies and should be implemented. Ath-Thawrī narrated from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, that implementing it is required of those who have anything to inherit, paid in whatever portions their hearts are satisfied to give away. Among those reported with a similar explanation are Abū Mūsā and Ibn Masʿūd, ash-Shaʿbī with Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr and al-Ḥasan. A second group went further and called the payment obligatory: az-Zuhrī and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, Ibn Sīrīn with Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Makḥūl, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ and Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī. Others said the verse refers to the bequest a person makes at the time of death. Others said it was abrogated, and others again that it was never prescribed, only encouraged, and that people simply neglected it because it was counsel rather than command. Weighed against these, the ruling given is that the instruction is commendatory, not obligatory: a moral obligation on those who receive, answered in the spirit of the Qur'an's own arrangement, which presses the rule of nearness with one hand and tends the disappointment of the excluded with the other. The Qur'an teaches the same generosity at harvest: "Eat of the fruit when it bears fruit, and give away the due of the poor on the day of harvest" (6:141).

### The inner reading

There is a subtle allusion in the verse for those who have sinned. At the division, those present with no legal portion are still granted something. So too, on the Last Day, when the Real forgives the obedient and hands them the rewards of their deeds, the sinners of the family of faith, ahl al-īmān, will not be turned away without pardon, if God wills. They were not there when the shares were fixed and hold no prior entitlement. His favor made them deserving anyway, though He knew beforehand the lapses their states would carry.

### In short

- Non-inheriting relatives, orphans and the needy present at a division of inheritance are to be given something from it and spoken to kindly.
- The gift comes from the shares of the adult inheritors present, never from the shares of minors or the absent.
- If they demand an equal share, the law is explained politely, and where the heir is a child, a promise is made on his behalf.
- The strongest reports make the giving obligatory or at least required in proportion to what the heart is satisfied to give. Others read it as bequest, or abrogation, or encouragement. The settled ruling is that it is a moral obligation, not a legal one.
- Read inwardly, the verse is a picture of pardon: sinners arrive at Allah's court with no entitlement, and His favor provides for them anyway.

9.text:
The verse turns from the estate to the deathbed: "Let the guardians be as concerned ˹for the orphans˺ as they would if they were to ˹die and˺ leave ˹their own˺ helpless children behind. So let them be mindful of Allah and speak equitably". It addresses everyone who stands near a man about to die, and everyone who administers what the dead leave behind, and it gives them a single test: treat other people's children the way you would want yours treated.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Let the guardians be as concerned ˹for the orphans˺ as they would if they were to ˹die and˺ leave ˹their own˺ helpless children behind"** builds the test on a natural fear. Every person who leaves behind weak offspring, young children unable to fend for themselves, is afraid for them, afraid they will be ruined. The verse says: let that same fear govern how you handle the children of others, and how you guard the orphans in your care. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the verse refers to a man near death who dictates a will damaging the rights of his heirs. Whoever hears such a will must fear Allah, turn the dying man toward what is right and fair, and guard those heirs as jealously as he would guard his own children. A similar report comes from Mujāhid and several others.

**"So let them be mindful of Allah"** names the standing motive. The guardians of orphaned children must protect the property and hand it over in full at maturity, taking pains over the trust, never letting negligence touch the duty. What a Muslim should accumulate for his dependents is not wealth. It is taqwā (the fear of Allah) and ṣalāḥ (righteousness). The verse does not say: let them gather their wealth, multiply real estate for them, leave behind household goods. It says: let them fear Allah, for He looks after the righteous. Deal with the orphans of others as you would have others deal with your children after you, and Allah will bring it about that your own are treated well.

**"and speak equitably"** is the bedside duty. In the days before this verse, people would visit the dying and press them to bequeath their property to this person and that, until nothing was left for their own children. The practice is what the verse closes down. The one who sits with a dying man speaks the pertinent words to him: enjoin on him the voluntary almsgiving of no more than a third of the estate, and the remainder for the inheritors, so that they do not end up as dependants begging from others. Nor should the one making his will deprive himself of this good deed by leaving none.

### Saʿd's one-third

The living application is recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim, the two Ṣaḥīḥs. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to visit Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās during an illness, Saʿd said: "O Messenger of Allah! I am wealthy and have no inheritors except a daughter. Should I give two-thirds of my property in charity?" He said: "No." Saʿd asked: "Half?" He said: "No." Saʿd said: "One-third?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "One-third, and even one-third is too much," and added that it is better to leave one's inheritors wealthy than to leave them poor, begging from others. The ruling is recorded in the Mishkāt in its chapter on bequests, Bāb al-Waṣāyā. Had the whole or half been given away as ṣadaqah, the inheritors' share would have been consumed or curtailed, and that is what the verse and the Prophet's ﷺ answer both prevent.

### In short

- Whoever hears a will that harms the rightful heirs must fear Allah, intervene, and protect those heirs as if they were his own children.
- Guardians protect the orphan's property and hand it over whole at maturity, treating the orphans of others as they would want their own children treated after them.
- What to store up for one's dependents is not wealth but taqwā and righteousness, for Allah looks after the righteous.
- The dying are to be spoken to justly: no more than a third in voluntary almsgiving, as Saʿd was told, and the rest for the heirs, so no child is left begging.

10.text:
The section on orphans ends with its most terrible sentence: "Indeed, those who unjustly consume orphans' wealth ˹in fact˺ consume nothing but fire into their bellies. And they will be burned in a blazing Hell". One report ties the verse to Hanzalah ibn Shamardal. What it says is not a metaphor dressed as a threat. It is a description of what the eaten property already is.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, those who unjustly consume orphans' wealth"** covers every form of taking. The verb is "eat", but the usage, as elsewhere in the Qur'an, embraces eating, drinking, consuming and utilizing. Using an orphan's property in whatever manner, without right, is totally unlawful and a sure cause of divine wrath.

**"˹in fact˺ consume nothing but fire into their bellies"** states the identity. Many have read this metaphorically: eating the orphan's property is like stuffing one's stomach with fire, because that is what awaits the person in the Hereafter. Others, with deeper insight, refuse the figure of speech. What is eaten from the orphan's property unlawfully is, in reality, fire, though it does not look like fire at the time. A man may call the matchbox in his hand a fire, and the piece of arsenic a killer. Handling the matchbox does not burn the hand, and holding arsenic in the mouth does not kill. But a little friction proves the first name right, and once the arsenic goes down the throat, the second. So with the wrongfully eaten wealth: its true form appears on the Day. The Qur'an's own generalizations support this. Whatever deeds a person does, good or evil, those very deeds are the trees, flowers and fruits of Paradise, or the embers of Hell, in a different form here, transformed into their true forms on the Day of Doom: "On the Day of Doom, they shall find what they did, present" (18:49).

**"And they will be burned in a blazing Hell"** completes the sentence. On the Day of Resurrection, the fire kindles in their stomachs. In some narrations, those who devour the property of orphans unjustly are raised with flames issuing from their bellies by way of the mouth, the nostrils, the ears and the eyes. The Prophet ﷺ said that a people will be raised on that Day with their mouths erupting with fire. His Companions asked who these could be. He said: "Have you not read it in the Qur'an? Those who eat up the property of the orphans unjustly." A detail of the closing word carries two readings, an active and a passive form, both ending in a blaze: a fierce fire in which they burn.

### The One who takes the orphan's side

Behind the warning stands a portrait of Allah: the majestic compeller and great Lord, the renowned keeper of servants, clement and generous, loyal and tremendous, the lord of all and the carrier of everything, the One who takes the weak by the hand and joins them to Himself in love. In this verse He caresses the weak and shows love to the orphans. Toward the wrongdoers, those who stab the orphan's liver and drink the blood of the destitute, He turns with a fearful punishment. He makes Himself the deputy of the helpless and takes up their dispute against their wrongers. He is the companion of the weak and the helper of the despairing. He answers the distressed when they call, and hears the voice of the grieved. And He loves a particular kind of servant: the one who, beaten down, helpless and destitute, breathes a cold sigh, lets warm tears fall, and lifts a pair of empty hands toward his Lord, asking once more to be excused.

The same passage presses the sinner toward exactly that excuse. In one tradition a man was praying:

> O Lord, O Lord! You have written, You have measured out, and You have decreed. All that was, is and shall be is what You want, what You bring about, and what You write for the creatures. None of it lies outside Your predestination.

A call came in his secret core: "That is tawḥīd. Where is servanthood?" What he had said was pure oneness, fitting for Godhood. What, then, was the mark of his servanthood? The man answered:

> O Lord, surely I have disobeyed, I have sinned, and I ask. I have broken the covenant and have no loyalty. Greed has made me all grasping claws. I am all war with the Apportioner's apportioning.

That is the confession the verse seeks from the one whose hand is in an orphan's property.

### The seven destructive sins

The consuming of an orphan's property stands among the gravest sins in Islam. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record Abū Hurayrah's report that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Avoid the seven great destructive sins." The people asked what they were. He named them:

> To join others in worship along with Allah, magic, to kill the life which Allah has forbidden except for a just cause, to consume interest, to consume an orphan's property, to turn your back to the enemy and flee from the battlefield at the time of fighting, and to accuse chaste women, who never even think of anything harmful to their chastity, of wrongdoing.

And Abū Hurairah narrates that the Prophet ﷺ said: "I warn you to abstain from the property of the two weak ones, the woman and the orphan."

### Where it happens in ordinary homes

The warning is not for a vanished age. When a man dies, the right of every inheritor attaches to everything he owns, every part, big or small, and his minor children become orphans in that same hour. Whoever then assumes control, an uncle, an elder brother, the mother, a guardian or trustee, stands exactly where this section warns him. The pattern is familiar. The distribution is postponed for years while the household spends a little here and there on the children's food and clothes. Then the spending turns liberal, and the jointly held property goes on religiously unacceptable customs and wasteful heads of expenditure, on the guardian's own person, and at the limit into manipulated documents that enter the guardian's own children in place of the orphans. Hardly a home is untouched. Donations made for orphans in religious schools and orphanages must reach the orphans. Not spending them on the orphans is itself a form of eating up the orphan's property.

### Rules for what the dead leave

The verse yields concrete rulings for the estate before distribution.

Inheritance includes everything the deceased owned, down to the clothes on the body. People give these out in charity without realizing they belong to the estate, and in some places copper utensils are handed to the poor before the property is formally divided, though minors and absentees hold rights in all of it. The proper method is to distribute first, according to the shares fixed by Islamic law. After ownership has passed, the sharers may, if they willingly wish, give away part on behalf of the deceased. If they do it jointly, all must be adults, for a minor's permission is not valid, and nothing may be taken from the share of an absent inheritor without his permission.

The sheet spread over the bier on the way to the graveyard is not part of the required shroud, so it may not be bought from the estate, which is jointly held. Someone may cover its cost himself. In some places a prayer mat is cut from the shroud cloth for the imam who leads the funeral prayer and given to him afterward. That expense is extra to the needed shroud and may not come from the undivided inheritance.

In some areas new utensils are bought for bathing the deceased and broken after use. There is no need to buy new ones at all, since the bath can be given with what is in the house, and if they must be bought, breaking them is not permissible. It wastes property and causes loss to the orphans and absent inheritors whose rights run through the whole estate.

Expenses before distribution, such as entertaining guests or giving charity and alms, are impermissible. Such giving brings the deceased no merit. Done in the belief that it brings good returns for the departed soul, it is a far greater sin, because giving charity from a combined property that includes the orphan's share is like stealing from someone's property and giving it away on the deceased's behalf. Even the inheritors' permission does not make it right: an orphan among them cannot give valid permission in the first place, and an adult's yes may come with a heavy heart, only to ward off shame. The right order is: distribute first, then let each inheritor give from his own share for the good of the deceased, if he wishes.

A story of a pious elder seals the point. He went to visit a sick Muslim and had hardly sat down when the man died. The elder at once put out the lamp burning there and gave someone money to buy oil and relight it. Asked why, he said the lamp had belonged to the deceased while he lived, and its light was lawful to use. Now that he had died, his inheritors held the right over everything he owned, and since they were not all present to give permission, the lamp would be lit at his own cost.

### In short

- Whatever is taken from an orphan's property without right is, in reality, fire in the belly, revealed as fire on the Day of Doom, when flames are seen coming from the mouths, nostrils, ears and eyes of those who devoured it.
- Consuming an orphan's property is one of the seven great destructive sins, and the Prophet ﷺ warned against the wealth of the two weak ones, the woman and the orphan.
- Every use of an orphan's property without right, eating, drinking or utilizing, is unlawful, and the ordinary household patterns of postponing division and spending from the joint estate fall under the same warning.
- Before distribution, the estate is untouchable: no charity, no guest meals, no shroud extras, no broken utensils, nothing from the shares of minors or the absent. First distribute, then let each sharer give from his own share.
- Behind the warning stands Allah as the deputy of the helpless, who loves the servant who comes to Him with empty hands, and asks to be excused.

11.text:
This is the verse of inheritance, one of the three passages of this surah from which the whole science is derived: "Allah commands you regarding your children: the share of the male will be twice that of the female". In one sentence the verse gives the general rule for children, then works through the cases: daughters alone, a single daughter, parents with and without grandchildren, the mother's share when siblings exist, and the order of payment that governs every estate. Its closing words, "˹This is˺ an obligation from Allah. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise", fix the whole distribution as His decision, not ours.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah commands you regarding your children"** opens the law. The word translated "commands" is a waṣiyyah, a charge, and it means a plain command. The shares that follow are not counsel to be weighed. They are the ruling.

**"the share of the male will be twice that of the female"** is the universal rule for children. Where a man leaves sons and daughters together, the estate splits so that each boy receives twice each girl's portion. One boy and two girls, for example, divide the property into four parts: two for the boy, one for each girl. The rule entitles boys and girls both, against the practice of the Jāhiliyyah, which gave the males and nothing to the females. The doubled share is not a grading of worth. Men carry the financial duties of the family, the dependants, the commercial transactions, the work and the obligations, and so they carry the double portion.

**"If you leave only two ˹or more˺ females, their share is two-thirds of the estate"** handles the family of daughters. Where there is no son and the daughters are two or more, they share two-thirds of what is left equally among them, and the remaining third goes to the other rightful heirs, the parents of the deceased, or the wife or husband. The words "or more" were weighed word by word. Some said the verse means two daughters only and the "more" is padding, which is not so. Nothing in the Qur'an is useless or redundant. Had the verse been about two women alone, the wording would have been that both of them together share two-thirds. Two daughters follow the same rule as more than two, and this is proven twice over: in the Book, where two sisters are given two-thirds in the verse about the final case of inheritance (4:176), and in the sunnah, in the Prophet's ﷺ command that two-thirds go to the two daughters of Saʿd ibn ar-Rabīʿ. The argument runs by precedence: if a female is entitled to a third when she stands with a male, she is all the more entitled to the same share standing with another female. One grammarian note says the word "more than" simply introduces a relative clause. Another says it guards against a wrong impression, lest people think that the more females there are, the larger their total share grows beyond the fixed two-thirds.

**"But if there is only one female, her share will be one-half"** gives the only daughter half the estate when there is no other child, the rest passing to the other inheritors. A detail of the wording was read two ways, wāḥidatan and wāḥidatun, one making the construction complete and one leaving it suspended, both meaning the same.

**"Each parent is entitled to one-sixth if you leave offspring"** moves to the parents. Where the deceased leaves a child, male or female, the father and mother receive a sixth each. The phrasing "to each one of the two" was pointed: the parents do not share one sixth between them, they receive one sixth apiece. The word for child covers a grandchild as well, and the word for parent covers a grandparent. Where the deceased leaves one daughter only, she takes her half, the parents their sixth each, and the sixth that remains returns to the father. In the terminology of the science of inheritance this is the entitlement of taʿṣīb, agnatic kinship, by which the residue reverts to the nearest male relative.

**"But if you are childless and your parents are the only heirs, then your mother will receive one-third"** gives the second case. No children, no brothers or sisters, and the parents alone inherit: the mother receives a third and the father the remaining two-thirds, so that the father's share stays twice the mother's. If the deceased also leaves a spouse, the spouse's share comes out first, half for a husband or a fourth for a wife, and from what remains the mother takes her third and the father two-thirds, for the remainder is treated just as the whole estate would be for the parents' shares.

**"But if you leave siblings, then your mother will receive one-sixth"** is the third case. Where the deceased leaves no child but leaves two or more siblings, whether full brothers and sisters or half siblings from either side, the mother's share falls from a third to a sixth, and, absent other heirs, the remaining five-sixths go to the father. The siblings themselves inherit nothing here, because the father is nearer than they are. In the terminology of the science this is called ḥajb an-nuqṣān, the blocking that reduces. Qatādah commented on this part of the verse: their presence reduces the share of the mother, but they will not inherit. A single surviving brother does not reduce the mother's share. It stays a third unless the siblings are two or more. The people of knowledge explain the reduction this way: the father is the one who helps the deceased's brothers and sisters to marry, spending from his own money for the purpose, while the mother does not spend from hers, so her sixth leaves room for duties that will fall on him. That is a sound opinion.

**"after the fulfilment of bequests and debts"** sets the order of every estate. The scholars of the salaf, the early generations, and the khalaf, the later ones, agree that debts are paid before the will is executed, and this is apparent to anyone who reads the verse carefully. The full order under the sharīʿah: first the shrouding and burial of the deceased, done without extravagance or stinginess. Then the debts. If the debts equal or exceed the property, nothing is distributed and no will is applied. Then the will, up to a third of what remains, and a will for the entire property takes effect only to the extent of a third. Leaving more than a third is not appropriate, and where it is done with the intention of cutting out the inheritors, it becomes a sin. What remains after debts and the applied will is distributed among the heirs, and where there is no will at all, the whole of what remains after the debts is distributed as inheritance.

**"˹Be fair to˺ your parents and children, as you do not ˹fully˺ know who is more beneficial to you"** gives the reason for fixing the shares rather than leaving them to judgement. One may draw benefit in this life or the next from one's parents that one could never draw from one's children, and the opposite equally. The verse removes the guesswork: since benefit could come from either, a fixed share is appointed to each. One reading takes the benefit as the benefit of the Hereafter, in rank. Another takes it as benefit in this world with regard to inheritance. Read inwardly, children benefit a person with their service and parents with their compassion: parents stand by in the weakness at the beginning of one's life, children in the weakness at its end.

**"˹This is˺ an obligation from Allah. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise"** closes with authority. These appointed shares, some larger and some smaller, are a commandment Allah has decided and ordained. He places everything in its rightful place and gives each one his rightful due.

### Half of all knowledge

The knowledge of al-Farāʾiḍ, the shares of inheritance, is derived from this verse, the verses after it, and the last verse of this surah, together with the hadiths that explain them. Ibn ʿUyaynah said that the knowledge of al-Farāʾiḍ was called half of knowledge, because it touches all people. Muslim jurists collected and codified every rule of it from the Qur'an and the hadith, and gave it the standing of a permanent science, known in Islamic terminology as ʿIlm al-Farāʾiḍ, the science of the laws of inheritance.

### The occasions of the verse

Two reports carry the verse's revelation. Al-Bukhārī recorded that Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came visiting me on foot with Abū Bakr at the dwellings of Banū Salmah, and found me unconscious. He asked for water, performed the ablution, and poured some of it on me, and I came to. I said: "O Messenger of Allah, what do you command me to do with my money?" And this verse was revealed. Muslim and an-Nasāʾī recorded it the same way, and the rest of the six compilers collected the hadith as well. It is apparent, though, that this incident belongs to the last verse of the surah (4:176), for at that time Jābir had sisters, and no daughters, parents or offspring to inherit from him. It is mentioned here just as al-Bukhārī mentioned it.

The second report fits the verse itself. Aḥmad recorded from Jābir that the wife of Saʿd ibn ar-Rabīʿ came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and complained that her husband had fallen as a martyr at Uḥud, and his daughters' uncle had seized their money and left them nothing, though no one would marry them without some assets. He said: "Allah will decide on this matter." Then the verses of inheritance came down, and the Prophet ﷺ sent word to the uncle commanding him: "Give two-thirds of Saʿd's money to his two daughters, one eighth to their mother, and whatever is left is yours." Abū Dāwūd, at-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah collected this hadith. In another version of the same event, the woman is the widow of Thābit ibn Qays, who fell as a martyr at Uḥud, and she came with her two girls to complain that their uncle had taken possession of the whole fortune. The Prophet ﷺ told her Allah would judge for her, the surah was revealed, and he then sent for the woman and the uncle and delivered the same division: two-thirds for the girls, an eighth for the mother, the remainder for the uncle.

### What the rule replaced

Ibn ʿAbbās described the old world the verse entered. The custom in the early days was that the property of the deceased was inherited by his offspring, while the parents inherited only if the will named them. Allah cancelled from that custom whatever He willed, and ordained instead that the male receive twice the portion of the female, that each parent take a sixth, that the wife take an eighth or a fourth, and the husband a half or a fourth. The share of parents was thus moved from the uncertainty of wills to the certainty of law.

The doubling of the male's share is not a licence to favour sons. The verse itself testifies that Allah is more merciful to children than their own parents are, since He commands the parents to observe justice with their own children. Al-Bukhārī records the hadith of the captured woman who was searching for her child. On finding him she clasped him to her, put him to her breast and nursed him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked his Companions whether they thought she would willingly throw her child into the fire. They said no. He said: "By Allah, Allah is more merciful with His servants than this woman is with her own child."

### Why the shares are fixed and not chosen

Every human law of inheritance leans somewhere. In the ancient tribal age the boy was the strength of the tribe, so he took the sole right of inheritance and the girl was left nothing. That is now resented, and the modern answer declares boy and girl equal in share. But if the ancient principle was unjustified, the modern one is unrealistic. A law free of every bias can be expected only from God, to whom infinite knowledge and wisdom belong.

The verse says as much in its own words. If the distribution were left to opinion, usefulness would become the criterion, and who will deliver the real benefit, from a parent or a child, in this life or the next, is exactly what a person cannot know with any certainty. Left to personal judgement, a person might think well of someone and leave everything to him, or think badly and leave nothing, and be wrong both times. So Allah, in His exalted majesty, took the responsibility into His own hands, that justice and equity reign over the estate and the capital of the deceased circulates among competent inheritors in a manner that is just. His determination needs no justification. It is not built on analogy. Indeed, if the matter were decided by qiyās on the pattern of the verses around it, where the weak are given preference, the female would be favored, for her weakness and her inability to move about freely. The ruling stands on the wisdom of the Wise, and the shares are settled injunctions to be accepted wholeheartedly, with no one entitled to enforce opinion on them, increase them or decrease them.

### The Qur'an's care for daughters

Look at how the verse words the rule. It could have framed the rule the other way round, naming the females' portion as a fraction of the male's. Instead it says the male receives the equivalent of two females, making the daughters' share the stated basis from which the sons' share is derived. The Qur'an shows visible concern that girls be given their share. That concern indicts a practice still alive: brothers who keep the whole estate and say the sisters forgave their shares. Usually they forgave nothing. They waived reluctantly, knowing they would never be paid anyway and asking themselves why create bad blood between brothers and sisters. Such a waiver is not valid under Islamic law. The sisters' claim remains due against the brothers, and those who usurp inheritance are terrible sinners. Where the heirs include minor girls, the sin doubles: usurping the share of a legal heir and devouring the property of an orphan in one act.

### The two principles of the law

The whole law rests on two principles, the farḍ, the fixed obligatory portions, and the taʿṣīb, the inheritance by the group of agnate relatives. The taʿṣīb is the stronger of the two, for it can draw the entire estate to itself, while the fixed portions together never exceed two-thirds of it. The division therefore begins with the holders of the fixed portions, whose entitlement is weaker, and then proceeds to the ʿaṣaba, whose right is stronger. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whatever remains of the portions goes to the nearest male relative." That is His way, a sunna forever. It is the same order of generosity seen in the Book itself, for of the servants who inherited the Book, "Then We bequeathed the Book to those of Our servants whom We chose" (35:32), He began with the wrongdoer, who has the weaker claim, because the wrongdoer is broken-hearted and unable to withstand a prolonged deferral.

### In short

- A son's share is twice a daughter's. Daughters alone, two or more, share two-thirds. A single daughter takes half. These are fixed obligations from Allah, derived from this verse, the following verses, and the last verse of the surah, the science called al-Farāʾiḡ, half of all knowledge because it touches everyone.
- Parents take a sixth each when there are children, with the residue reverting to the father by taʿṣīb. With no children, the mother takes a third and the father the rest. Two or more siblings reduce the mother to a sixth without inheriting themselves, a reduction called ḥajb an-nuqṣān, explained by the father's duty of marrying off the deceased's siblings.
- Debts come before bequests, and bequests take effect only up to a third. Burial comes first of all.
- The shares are fixed because no one can know who will prove more beneficial, parent or child, in this life or the next. Human laws lean toward the strong tribe or the fashionable principle. Only God's law leans nowhere.
- The verse words the rule so the daughter's share is the basis of the son's, and the forced waiver of a sister's share is no waiver at all.

12.text:
The law of shares now widens from blood to marriage and then to the strangest corner of the system, the heir with no parent and no child: "You will inherit half of what your wives leave if they are childless. But if they have children, then ˹your share is˺ one-fourth of the estate—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts. And your wives will inherit one-fourth of what you leave if you are childless. But if you have children, then your wives will receive one-eighth of your estate—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts. And if a man or a woman leaves neither parents nor children but only a brother or a sister ˹from their mother's side˺, they will each inherit one-sixth, but if they are more than one, they ˹all˺ will share one-third of the estate—after the fulfilment of bequests and debts without harm ˹to the heirs˺. ˹This is˺ a commandment from Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing".

### Phrase by phrase

**"You will inherit half of what your wives leave if they are childless"** gives the husband his share. Where the wife dies leaving no child, her husband takes half of her property, after her debts are paid and her will executed, and the remaining half passes to her other heirs, her parents or her brothers and sisters.

**"But if they have children, then ˹your share is˺ one-fourth"** lowers the husband's share when children exist. The child may be one or more, male or female, born of this husband or of a previous one. The rest, three-fourths, goes to the other heirs.

**"And your wives will inherit one-fourth of what you leave if you are childless"** gives the wife her share when the husband dies childless, and **"your wives will receive one-eighth of your estate"** lowers it when he leaves a child, whether from the present wife or from another. The rule reaches to the grandchildren as much as the children, even to great-grandchildren and further, on which there is consensus among the scholars. If the deceased had more than one wife, all alive at his death, the prescribed fourth or eighth is divided equally between them. Each woman does not receive a fourth or an eighth of her own. They share the single portion.

**"And if a man or a woman leaves neither parents nor children but only a brother or a sister ˹from their mother's side˺"** opens the case of the kalālah, and **"they will each inherit one-sixth"** gives the single maternal sibling a sixth. **"But if they are more than one, they ˹all˺ will share one-third of the estate"** caps the group: whether one brother with one sister, or two of each, or any number more, they share a third equally, and here the male does not receive twice the female.

**"after the fulfilment of bequests and debts without harm ˹to the heirs˺"** repeats the order of every estate and adds a guard: the will must be fair and free of every kind of harm, neither depriving rightful heirs of all or part of their shares, nor adding to the fixed portion Allah ordained for anyone. Whoever does that has disputed with Allah concerning His decision and His division.

**"˹This is˺ a commandment from Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing"** closes with the same authority as the verse before it. He apportioned these shares knowing every heir's true state, He knows who obeys and who contravenes, and though He may hold back the punishment in this world, the one who disobeys should not deceive himself that he escaped.

### The husband's share first

The verse names the husband's share before the wife's, and there is a likely reason in the world it entered. After the death of the wife, the husband becomes attached to some other family. If the wife dies in her parents' home, with her assets there, her people may be tempted to avoid giving the husband his due. Naming his right first shuts the door on that practice.

One ruling completes the picture of the marriage bond. Before any distribution of inheritance, it must be confirmed that the wife's mahr (dower) has been settled. Should the deceased have left it unpaid, the mahr counts as a debt and is settled first from the total property, like every other debt, and only then is the inheritance distributed. Having received her mahr, the woman still receives her fixed share as a competent inheritor. If the estate is worth no more than the dower, the entire property goes to her against the debt of the mahr, and no heir receives anything from it.

### What a kalālah is

The word was debated from the earliest day. Lexically it is a derivative of iklīl, the crown that surrounds the head, and the sense here is that the heirs of such a person stand outside the first degree of relation. Ash-Shaʿbī reported that when Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq was asked the meaning of kalālah, he said:

> I will say my own opinion about it. If it is correct, the correctness is from Allah. If it is wrong, it is my error and the evil effort of Shayṭān, and Allah and His Messenger have nothing to do with it. Kalālah refers to the man who has neither descendants nor ascendants.

When ʿUmar became the khalīfah, he said: "I hesitate to contradict an opinion of Abū Bakr." Ibn Jarīr and others recorded it. And on his deathbed, among the last to see ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was Ibn ʿAbbās, to whom he said: "What you said was the correct opinion." Asked what he had said, he explained: that kalālah is the person who has no child and no parent.

The same view is held by Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, by Zayd ibn Thābit and Ibn Masʿūd, by an-Nakhaʿī and ash-Shaʿbī, by Qatādah and Jābir ibn Zayd, by al-Ḥakam and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, and by the people of al-Madīnah, Kūfah and Baṣrah, the Seven jurists of Madīnah, the Four Imams, and the majority of the scholars of the past and present, so that some scholars declared a consensus on it. Al-Qurṭubī gathers the definitions, and al-Ālūsī, in his Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, adds the root: kalālah is really a verbal noun from kalal, to become exhausted, denoting weakness. The name reaches every tie of kinship that is not the bond of father and son, since each such tie is weak beside that one. It came to describe the deceased survived by neither son nor father, and equally the heir who is neither the deceased's son nor his father, the word dhu, possessor, understood though unspoken: one having a weak relation. It even came to be applied to the property left by such a deceased.

### Brothers and sisters of the mother

The siblings in this verse are the akhyaḳī brothers and sisters, from the same mother and different fathers. The restriction is not spelled out in the verse, but consensus holds it. Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās, among the salaf, read the verse as "a brother or sister from his mother", a rendition reported by al-Qurṭubī, al-Ālūsī and al-Jaṣṣāṣ. It did not come through tawātur, a mass transmission, but the agreement of the entire Muslim ummah makes it the reading to practice by. The clear proof is at the end of this surah, where the inheritance of the kalālah appears again. There a single sister takes half, a single brother takes the whole, two sisters take two-thirds, and several brothers and sisters divide with the male taking twice the female. That ruling concerns the full siblings and the siblings of the same father. Were they included in our verse as well, the two injunctions would contradict each other.

Maternal siblings stand apart in four ways. First, they inherit on account of their mother. Second, their males and females take exactly the same share. Third, they inherit only in the kalālah estate, for they have no share where the deceased leaves a father, grandfather, child or grandchild. Fourth, they never take more than a third, however many they are.

### Why the will is named before the debt

In all three places where this section mentions the will, the word comes before the debt, though the practice of the Prophet ﷺ, as the scholars of the early generations settled it, was that debt is settled before the will is executed, and there is consensus on this among the scholars. One of the leading figures of the first generation removed the misunderstanding plainly: you recite the verse as "settling the will they might have made, or debt", but in practice the Prophet ﷺ settled the debt before the will.

Why, then, does the wording put the will first? Because the beneficiary of a will deserves it without paying any price, often without even a kinship to the testator, and the inheritors, seeing property they hoped for going elsewhere, might ignore the will or delay it. Not every person incurs a debt, and a debt, once due, is claimed by creditors whom the inheritors cannot refuse. The will has no such claimant once the deceased is gone, and it was the deceased's earnest hope, a running charity on his behalf. The verse puts the will first to protect it.

### No will for an inheritor

Making a will in favour of an heir is not lawful. A will for a son, a daughter, a husband or a wife, or anyone else who will already receive a share, is not enforceable. They receive their fixed shares and nothing beyond. In his famous address during his last ḥajj, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Surely, Allah has given every person his or her right. So there is no will for an inheritor." It is recorded in the Mishkāt with reference to Abū Dāwūd. One exception is allowed: where the other inheritors permit, the will in favour of a particular inheritor may be executed, and the rest distributed by the sharīʿah, with the inheritor still taking his fixed share. The hadith narrations carry the exception "unless the inheritors wish", as given in al-Hidāyah.

### Without harm to anyone

The words "without harm" guard the whole order of debts and wills against misuse. There are many ways to wound heirs through them. A man may lie about being in debt so the amount goes to a friend. He may declare what he owns personally to be a trust held for someone else, to keep it out of the estate. He may will more than a third. He may lie that a loan he gave was repaid, so it never reaches the inheritors. He may, in his final illness, gift away more than a third of his property. Every one of these is causing harm, strictly forbidden and a major sin. Though the words appear only with the kalālah rules, the rule they lay down is general, and is read at the two earlier mentions of debt and will as well. Every person about to leave this world should stay far from all of it in the last moments of life.

### The inner reading

Inheritance and worthiness to receive it are established in two ways: by a cause or by a lineage. The cause is marriage, and marriage is the cause of love, as Allah says: "He placed between you love and mercy" (30:21). Lineage is assistance and strength, as the report says: a man is many through his brothers. When a relative by lineage or a near one by cause dies, the wound lands on the heart and the pain on the spirit, and the Lord of the Worlds places balm on the pain. After the suffering, He commands consolation through the wealth of the one who passed. As the pain came from his going, the balm comes from what he left. This is His custom with His friends: if He places suffering on them through the prescribed Law, He makes a treasure appear afterward with the attribute of relief. Shaykh al-Islām Anṣārī said:

> How should I have known that suffering is the mother of happiness, and that beneath one disappointment lie a thousand treasures? How should I have known that hope is the courier of union, and that beneath the cloud of munificence despair is impossible? How should I have known that the Lovingly Kind is so forbearing that His gentleness to the sinner is beyond reckoning? How should I have known how servant-caressing is the Possessor of Majesty, and how much joy His friends have in Him?

He added that once, in the last stretch of night before dawn, the image of that consolation of the spirit appeared to him and asked: "How are you, wounded one?" He answered: "In my passion for You, that is the first opening."

### In short

- A husband takes half of his wife's estate if she died childless, a fourth if she left a child. A wife takes a fourth of her husband's estate if he died childless, an eighth if he left a child. Co-wives share the single portion equally, and grandchildren count as children.
- An unpaid mahr is a debt, paid before any distribution, and the wife then takes her fixed share on top of it.
- The kalālah is the deceased who leaves neither parent nor child, as Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq defined it and ʿUmar confirmed on his deathbed. In such an estate, maternal siblings take a sixth each, or share a third equally, male and female alike, never more.
- Debts are settled before wills in practice, though the wording names the will first to protect it, and no will may be made for an inheritor or stretched past a third.
- The words "without harm" forbid every trick that empties the estate before the heirs: false debts, invented trusts, exaggerated wills, disguised gifts in the final illness.
- Read inwardly, the verse is balm: where death wounds the heart, the inheritance the Law assigns is the relief placed beside the wound.

13.text:
The shares end and the warning begins: "These ˹entitlements˺ are the limits set by Allah. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger will be admitted into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there forever. That is the ultimate triumph". It is the consistent style of the Qur'an: once the beliefs and injunctions are laid down, promises of reward and warnings of punishment follow, pressing the believers to obey.

### Phrase by phrase

**"These ˝entitlements˺ are the limits set by Allah"** names the farāʾiḍ for what they are, His ḥudūd, His bounds: the commands and prohibitions by which His servants ʿibād show their devotion, and what He has allotted each heir according to the degree of relation and the degree of dependence. Bounds are not to be infringed. The root of servanthood, ʿubūdiyya, is preserving the ḥudūd and maintaining the promises, the ʿuhūd. Whoever keeps within His limit, nothing bad or harmful reaches him. The root of every affliction is going beyond the bounds.

**"Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger"** means obeying regarding the inheritance: adding nothing to the fixed shares by tricks and plots, subtracting nothing from them, giving each heir the appointed share as Allah commanded and decided.

**"will be admitted into Gardens under which rivers flow"** is the reward, read in one rendering as "He will admit him" and in another as "We will admit him". The rivers run beneath the habitations and trees, rivers of wine, water, honey and milk.

**"to stay there forever. That is the ultimate triumph"** is the dwelling that never ends and never breaks, the greatest salvation there is, which no other success comes near.

### Further limits the sunnah sets

Around the fixed shares stand further rules, settled in the sunnah and the books of fiqh, that guard who may inherit at all.

A Muslim does not inherit from a disbeliever, and a disbeliever does not inherit from a Muslim, whatever the lineage between them. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The Muslim does not inherit the kafir, nor does the kafir inherit the Muslim." This applies where the two religions are fixed from birth. A person who was Muslim and turned apostate is different: whatever he earned while Muslim goes to his Muslim inheritors, and whatever he earned after apostasy is deposited in the Bayt al-Māl, the public treasury. For a woman who apostatizes, all her property, from her days of Islam or of apostasy, goes to her Muslim inheritors. An apostate, man or woman, inherits from no one at all.

The killer does not inherit. Whoever kills a person from whose property he was entitled to a share is cut out of that inheritance, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "The killer shall not inherit." Some forms of accidental killing are excepted, the details of which stand in the books of fiqh.

The unborn child inherits. If a man leaves children and his wife is pregnant, the child in the womb is counted among the inheritors, and since its sex and number cannot be known, the distribution should be postponed until the birth. If it must be made at once, two situations are supposed, a boy or a girl, the inheritors are given the lesser portion of the two, and the remainder is held for the child.

The woman in her ʿiddah, the waiting period, may still inherit. If a man divorces his wife revocably and dies before the divorce takes effect and before her waiting period expires, she inherits, for the marriage was still in force. If he divorces her during the sickness that ends in his death, even irrevocably or with the three pronouncements, and dies before her waiting period expires, she still inherits, and the longer of the two waiting periods is applied for her: the three menstrual periods of divorce, or the four months and ten days of widowhood, whichever lasts longer, so that she receives the share as far as possible. But if he divorced her irrevocably or thrice before any death-illness, and he died a few days later while she was still waiting, she does not inherit, unless the divorce was revocable. And if the wife secures separation by khulʿ, at her own instance, during the sickness that kills him, she does not inherit, even if he dies within her waiting period.

### The residue and its people

Twelve heirs hold shares fixed by the sharīʿah, the aṣhāb al-furūḍ, the possessors of obligatory portions, as explained in the verses of this section. Where there is no such heir, or where property remains after they are paid, the residue goes to the ʿaṣaba, the agnatic residuaries. A person can inherit in both capacities at once. The children of the deceased and his father become ʿaṣaba, and so do the offspring of the father, the brother. An example shows the whole machine: Zayd dies leaving a wife, a daughter, a mother and an uncle. His property is divided into twenty-four shares. Twelve go to the daughter, her half. Three go to the wife, her eighth. Four go to the mother, her sixth. The residue of five goes to the uncle as the nearest male agnate. Where there are no ʿaṣaba at all, the residue returns to the fixed-share heirs in proportion to their shares, the principle of radd, the return. The husband and the wife are the exception: they never receive more than their specified shares.

### In short

- The fixed shares are Allah's bounds, and obeying them, exactly, without additions or subtractions, admits a person to Gardens beneath which rivers flow, forever.
- Bounds in inheritance include who may inherit: no cross-religion inheritance, no inheritance for the killer, full rights for the unborn child, and the protection of the divorced wife still within her waiting period.
- After the fixed-share heirs are paid, the residue goes to the agnatic residuaries, and where there are none, it returns proportionally to the fixed-share heirs, except the spouse.

14.text:
The counterpart of the promise: "But whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and exceeds their limits will be cast into Hell, to stay there forever. And they will suffer a humiliating punishment". To change what Allah has ordained is to dispute His judgement, and that is the behaviour of people who do not accept what Allah has decided and divided. So He punishes them with humiliation in an eternal, painful torment.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger"** means disobeying regarding the division of estates, contravening the legal rulings through deviation and refusal.

**"and exceeds their limits"** is to step over the bounds He set for His servants so they would act within them, not against them.

**"will be cast into Hell, to stay there forever"** is the counterpart dwelling, read with the same two renderings as the promise of Paradise, "He will admit" and "We will admit", and the abiding has no end, as long as Allah wills.

**"And they will suffer a humiliating punishment"** is the sharpest edge of the sentence. There are two punishments, one immediate and one postponed, and ignominy joins them both. If created beings tried to humiliate the disobedient as their disobedience has already humiliated them, they could not manage it. The saying is put plainly: whoever spends the night committing a sin wakes with his degradation upon him, wa-ʿalayhi madhallatuhu, and whoever wakes and passes the day in pious acts has his dignity upon him, wa-ʿalayhi mahābatuhu. One reading of the closing words takes them as a shameful doom, another as a severe torment.

### The seventy-year warnings

Two hadiths fix the seriousness of a will. Imam Aḥmad recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> A man might perform the actions of righteous people for seventy years, but when it is time to compile his will, he commits injustice. So his final work will be his worst, and he thus enters the Fire. A man might perform the deeds of evil people for seventy years, yet he is fair in his will. So his final work will be his best, and he thus enters Paradise.

Abū Hurayrah then said: read, if you will, from "These are the limits set by Allah" to "a humiliating punishment". Abū Dāwūd, in the chapter of his Sunan on injustice in wills, recorded with Abū Hurayrah again the parallel report:

> A man or a woman might perform actions in obedience to Allah for sixty years. Yet, when they are near death, they leave an unfair will and thus acquire the Fire.

At-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah also recorded it, and at-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan gharīb. The math of the verses is terrible and simple: a lifetime can be spent in obedience and undone by the document signed at the end, or spent in sin and redeemed by one fair division.

### In short

- Transgressing the limits of inheritance, changing the shares, loading the will against the heirs, is disobedience to Allah and His Messenger with Hell as its stated end.
- The punishment is humiliating: sin degrades a person immediately, and the disgrace continues into the Hereafter.
- The last act weighs enormously. Seventy years of righteousness can be lost to an unjust will, and seventy years of evil redeemed by a fair one.

15.text:
The verses that protected orphans and widows now turn to the women of the community themselves, and to the gravest charge that can be laid against one of them: "˹As for˺ those of your women who commit illegal intercourse—call four witnesses from among yourselves. If they testify, confine the offenders to their homes until they die or Allah ordains a ˹different˺ way for them". The ruling of this verse belonged to the first period of Islam and was later replaced. What remains permanently is its lesson about proof, protection and the veiling of sins.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹As for˺ those of your women who commit illegal intercourse"** speaks of zinā, unlawful intercourse. One reading limits the verse to free, married women, another includes the unmarried as well. The case goes before the executive authority, and it is that authority, not a mob of relatives, which acts on it.

**"call four witnesses from among yourselves"** sets the bar of proof. The witnesses must be four, they must be men, and the testimony of women is not valid in this matter. Islam took a deliberately strict attitude because the guilt is grave: it violates honour and modesty and brings a bad name on a whole family. Testimony from fewer than four renders the evidence invalid, and the complainant and witnesses may all be charged as liars, with the ḥadd of qadhf, the punishment for false accusation, falling on them for falsely accusing a Muslim. Sūrat an-Nūr says plainly that those who cannot produce four witnesses are liars (24:2). The severity is a shield. It stands so that a husband, a mother-in-law, a co-wife or a sister cannot level accusations out of personal spite, and no ill-wisher gets a channel for private hostility. Some revered elders gave another reason for the number four: the case involves two individuals, the man and the woman, so one case carries the purview of two, and as each requires two witnesses, four are necessary.

**"If they testify, confine the offenders to their homes"** was the first ruling. At the beginning of Islam the woman whose guilt was proven by sufficient evidence was confined to her house, kept from leaving, prevented from mixing with people, and that until death. No release was foreseen except one: **"until they die or Allah ordains a ˹different˺ way for them"**. The way referred to is the abrogation that came later.
