> O people! I allowed you the mutʿah marriage with women before. Now, Allah has prohibited it until the Day of Resurrection. Therefore, anyone who has any women in mutʿah, let him let them go, and do not take anything from what you have given them.

At-Tirmidhī devoted a chapter to the question and reported the same two hadiths, the second from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said mutʿah was only in the early period of Islam, until this very verse came down and closed every private part but those of the legally wedded wife and the bondwoman one lawfully comes to own. It is true that Ibn ʿAbbās held mutʿah permissible up to a certain time. He revoked the position on the good counsel of ʿAlī, as recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, and under the chastening impact of the verse itself. Strange, then, that the sect which claims to love and obey ʿAlī elects to oppose him on precisely this issue. The author of the Hidayah attributed permission to Imam Mālik, but scholars who explained that book clarified that the attribution was inadvertent. The author of Rūḥ al-Maʿānī reports from Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ the settled timeline: mutʿah was lawful before Khaybar, made unlawful during it, declared lawful on the day of the Conquest of Makkah, and three days later prohibited forever. And where two interpretations are equally possible, the settled principle of Islamic jurisprudence prefers the one supporting prohibition. The Qur'an's own words are explicit besides: those who guard their private parts, save from their wives or their bondwomen, are not to be blamed, and everything beyond that is unlawful. By extension, the time-bound marriage, al-nikāh al-muwaqqat, a marriage contracted with a fixed term even under the ordinary word nikāḥ, is equally unlawful.

### Graciousness after the settlement

The fixed dower is not frozen. Once the obligation is settled, the husband may add to it on his own accord, and the wife, willingly and happily, may forgo part of it or all of it. She may also agree to defer a dower that was originally prompt. Ibn Jarīr recorded from al-Ḥaḍramī a case of the mercy in it: men would designate a certain dowry and then fall into financial difficulties, and the verse teaches there is no harm in the mutual agreement that follows the requirement, for if she gives up part, the husband may accept.

### All-Knowing, All-Wise

The closing names carry the verse's authority. Allah knows. He is aware of everything, and if someone acts against His injunctions and no judge, ruler or other human being ever finds out, Allah in His most exalted state of being knows it all, so keep fearing Him in every circumstance. And the injunctions He revealed are all based on ḥikmah, wisdom, too deep to be understood by everyone. The commands concerning the lawful and the unlawful, whether or not one grasps their cause or justification, must be believed, accepted and obeyed, for the Creator and Master of the Command certainly knows them. There are educated but ignorant people, spread through contemporary societies, who go about searching for the causes of divine injunctions, and when they fail to find any, set the injunction aside as contrary to the modern age. The verse silences such people forever. It tells them: ignorant one, your Creator is All-Knowing. You lack understanding, while Allah is All-Wise, so never set your own reason up as the touchstone of the Truth.

The verse's whole frame is the law of desire. Natural desires make themselves felt in human beings, sexuality among them, and the Islamic law fixes a limit for every emotion. Only the alliance established through the standard, solemn social agreement of marriage is valid, and the family it builds must carry an environment of chastity.

### The inner reading

Read inwardly, the verse's permission has a condition of the heart. When you stay mindful of the ḥudūd, the limits, respect the ʿuhūd, the agreements, and obtain mutual consent with women according to the law, then no enmity arises among people over it, and no punishment follows from the Real, for what is lawful carries no further reckoning.

### In short

- Married women are prohibited except those lawfully acquired in war, and only after pregnancy is ruled out, the scruple of the Companions at Awtas being the occasion of the ruling.
- All women beyond the prohibited degrees are lawful, sought with wealth in marriage and not in fornication, within the limit of four wives.
- No marriage stands without a dower, due in full upon consummation and halved by divorce before it, and gracious increase or willing forfeiture after the settlement is no sin.
- Mutʿah, the temporary marriage, is prohibited forever, by the verse's own words, by the two Ṣaḥīḥs from ʿAlī, and by the farewell prohibition at the Conquest of Makkah, and Ibn ʿAbbās's early leniency was retracted on ʿAlī's counsel.
- The verse ends where obedience begins: Allah knows what no court finds out, and His wisdom needs no one's permission.

25.text:
The marriage laws close with a concession for the man who has nothing: "But if any of you cannot afford to marry a free believing woman, then ˹let him marry˺ a believing bondwoman possessed by one of you. Allah knows best ˹the state of˺ your faith ˹and theirs˺. You are from one another. So marry them with the permission of their owners, giving them their dowry in fairness, if they are chaste, neither promiscuous nor having secret affairs. If they commit indecency after marriage, they receive half the punishment of free women. This is for those of you who fear falling into sin. But if you are patient, it is better for you. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful". The verse opens a door, sets its conditions, halves its penalty, and then, at the end, quietly suggests the door be left closed.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But if any of you cannot afford to marry a free believing woman"** sets the threshold. The word behind "afford" is ṭaul, power, capability and means. The sense is that one who lacks the capability or means to marry a free believing woman may marry a believing bondwoman, and this alone already indicates that, as far as possible, a man should marry a free woman and simply not marry a bondwoman.

**"then ˹let him marry˺ a believing bondwoman possessed by one of you"** is the permission, narrow by design: a bondwoman who believes, owned by a believer.

**"Allah knows best ˹the state of˺ your faith ˹and theirs˺"** removes the sneer from the permission. Allah knows the true reality and secrets of all things, while people know only the apparent. Many a bondwoman stands far ahead of free women on the scale of faith.

**"You are from one another"** makes the kinship plain. Human beings, free or in bondage, all come from one species, the children of Ādam (Adam), all born of one soul. One reading takes it as some of you following the religion of others, another as you being strengthened by one another. Whichever way it is read, the betterness of one over another hangs on ʾīmān (faith) and taqwā (righteous conduct in fear of Allah), nothing else.

**"So marry them with the permission of their owners, giving them their dowry in fairness"** gives the two conditions: the owner's consent and the dower paid properly.

**"if they are chaste, neither promiscuous nor having secret affairs"** requires the woman herself to be muḥṣanah, guarded in decency, not a musāfiḥah, an open fornicator, and not the keeper of secret lovers.

**"If they commit indecency after marriage, they receive half the punishment of free women"** halves the ḥadd for the married bondwoman, as unfolded below.

**"This is for those of you who fear falling into sin"** ties the permission to need, and **"But if you are patient, it is better for you"** ties it further, for patience, and the children born free, outweigh it.

**"And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"** closes the door gently. Marrying a bondwoman is makrūh, not desirable, yet should a man do it, Allah will forgive him, and He is Merciful in that He allowed it at all rather than prohibiting it outright.

### Free first, bondwoman by need

The jurists graded the permission. According to Imam Abū Ḥanīfah, marrying a bondwoman while having the means to marry a free woman is makrūh, not desirable, especially a bondwoman of the people of the Book. According to al-Shāfī and other Imams it is unlawful outright for the man who can afford a free woman, and a bondwoman of the people of the Book is absolutely impermissible. Al-Shāfīʿī's school reads the restriction hard. Under all conditions, avoiding the bondwoman is better for a free man. Two reasons press it. The offspring of a bondwoman becomes automatically bonded to her owner, and where the mother is not a Muslim, the child may follow her religion rather than Islam. To rescue the children from bondage and secure their faith, the mother should be free, and if she cannot be free, let her at least be a Muslim so the child's faith remains secure for future flowering. On the same principle, marrying a free woman of the Book is correct in itself, but staying away is better, and in an age when such women often marry Muslim men precisely to draw the husband and the children to their own religion, the point needs no emphasis.

The verse also closes the mutʿah argument a second time. Had temporary marriage been permissible, the man who could not afford a free wife held the cheapest exit already, gratifying desire at a fraction of the cost of a regular marriage. By offering him the bondwoman instead, and requiring of her chastity within wedlock, the verse proves that mutʿah is not on the table, for mutʿah is all ṣafḥ, spillage and rank whoredom, one woman used by several men in short spans, the offspring unattributable to anyone, and the unique reservoir of human strength sent down the drain to oblige the wanton pursuit of sex.

### Faith is the unseen scale

Matters of external glamour are not the scale of a person's honour. The real standard is the unseen faith in the heart, which lies in the knowledge of God alone, and whether someone is great or otherwise is beyond human comprehension. That hidden aspect God Himself will weigh and disclose in His own court. Realizing it takes away the superiority complex that breeds most social evils. The verse plants exactly that realization. Faith is the criterion of precedence, so the marriage with a believing bondwoman is not to be held contemptible, and, as at-Tafsīr al-Mazharī puts it, the two sentences about Allah knowing your faith and your being one from another are there so that people become accepting of such marriage and shed any attitude of contempt for it.

### Permission and dower

The owner is responsible for the bondwoman, and she cannot marry without his permission. The same holds for the male slave, who cannot wed without his master's leave. A hadith states: "Any male slave who marries without permission from his master, is a fornicator." Where the owner is herself a woman, whoever is authorized to give a free woman away in marriage, her consent included, also takes charge of giving her bondwoman away, and another hadith states: "The woman does not give away another woman, or herself in marriage, for only the adulteress gives herself away in marriage."

The dower is owed to the bondwoman as to any wife, paid with a good heart and in full, with nothing withheld in belittlement of her status. One who marries her should pay the mahr promptly, honestly and gracefully, without hedging or delaying, and without causing her trouble in the matter just because she is a bondwoman. Imam Mālik holds the mahr to be her own right, while other Imams hold that the master becomes owner of what is received as her dower.

### Chaste, not promiscuous, no lovers

The two closing descriptions of the permitted woman were drawn sharply. Ibn ʿAbbās said the promiscuous are the whores, who do not object to relations with whoever seeks them, while "having secret affairs" refers to taking boyfriends. A similar explanation is reported from Abū Hurayrah, from Mujāhid and ash-Shaʿbī, from ad-Daḥḥāk and as-Suddī, from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, from Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr, and from Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān: not the open fornicator, and not the keeper of clandestine paramours. The verse addresses the choice of a bondwoman, but it is much better, on the same logic, to stay away from marrying a fornicating free woman as well.

### Half the punishment

The indecency in question is zinā after marriage. The free unmarried woman's punishment is one hundred lashes, as Sūrat an-Nūr gives it: "The fornicator, woman or man, administer each one of them a hundred lashes" (24:2). The married free woman's punishment is rajm, death by stoning, and since stoning cannot be reduced to half, the punishment the verse halves must be the lashes. All four Imams agree: the punishment of zinā by a bondsman or bondwoman, married or unmarried, is fifty lashes, and the bondman's case follows by the obvious analogy of the text. One reading adds banishment for half a year. In not making wedlock the precondition of the prescribed punishment here, the verse quietly shows that stoning does not apply to the bondwoman at all.

### For whom the door stands open

The permission is addressed to the man who fears being harmed in his religion or his body, the one who apprehends falling into the sin of fornication and finds patience hard. For the man who does not fear that distress, and for the one with means enough to marry a free woman, the door is shut, and on al-Shāfīʿī's reading, unlawfully opened. For the eligible man, the verse still ends by holding up patience: to keep himself morally pure above the pull of desire is a better state than marrying the bondwoman, and the practical reason stands beside the spiritual one, for the child of the bondwoman becomes enslaved to her master.

### Who the bondmen and bondwomen are

The bondmen of this verse are the bondmen of the sharīʿah. Disbelievers taken prisoner in jihād were distributed to the mujāhidīn by the Amīr al-Muʾminīn, the Chief Executive of the Muslims, as part of the spoils, and they became the bondmen and bondwomen, whose offspring remained in bondage except for cases detailed in the books of fiqh. In later times Muslims forsook jihād in the manner the sharīʿah prescribes, entrusted the options of peace and war to the enemies of their religion, and chained themselves to principles and policies that have nothing to do with the sharīʿah, and from that point they were deprived of what was known as the bondman and bondwoman. Common domestic servants of the present day are not bondmen and bondwomen, because they are free. And in parts of the world where children are sold or enslaved, the act is absolutely and totally ḥarām (forbidden), and those children do not become bondmen by it.

### The inner reading

Read inwardly, the concession has a rank and the abstention has a higher one. To the weak, the concessions are given. To the strong, He issues a different bidding: serious endeavour, and the embrace of what is most comprehensive and restrictive in the law, for their task is holding up the right of the Real, the ḥaqq al-ḥaqq. When an external matter distracts from attention to the heart, so that a person takes what is easier and less, it draws him away from the innermost self, for it abandons the most important and sublime matters, and whoever descends from the strongest and most comprehensive to what is merely permissible descends into the state of indulgence. Notice, then, the softness of the verse's close. He did not say "Be patient." He said "it is better for you to be patient", a soothing way of speaking to the servant, leaving him the choice while showing him the height.

### In short

- A man without the means to marry a free believing woman may marry a believing bondwoman with her owner's permission and a fair, promptly paid dower. With means, the marriage is makrūh on the Ḥanafī reading and unlawful on al-Shāfīʿī's.
- Faith, not status, is the real scale of worth, for all are children of Ādam of one soul, and Allah alone sees the unseen faith in any heart.
- The woman must be chaste, not an open fornicator, not a keeper of secret lovers, and her punishment after marriage is half the free woman's, fifty lashes, since stoning cannot be halved.
- The concession serves the man who fears sin, and the verse proves mutʿah unlawful a second time, since the poor man's lawful exit would otherwise have been the cheapest one.
- Patience remains better, freeing the children from bondage and the heart for the most sublime matters, and the verse's last words forgive what it merely permitted.

26.text:
After the laws, the reason for them: "It is Allah's Will to make things clear to you, guide you to the ˹noble˺ ways of those before you, and turn to you in mercy. For Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise". The verses that follow a long run of injunctions now step back and say what the whole legislation is for.

### Phrase by phrase

**"It is Allah's Will to make things clear to you"** means He sets out for the believers what He has allowed and what He has forbidden, in this surah and in others, the laws of the religion together with what lies in their interest. He makes His sacred law explicit, and one should not think the obligation is a burden without purpose, even where the purpose cannot be traced in every detail.

**"guide you to the ˹noble˺ ways of those before you"** means their righteous ways, and how to adhere to the commandments He likes and is pleased with. The communities before were charged with injunctions like these, and those who acted on them were rewarded with Allah's favour. One reading keeps the focus narrow: the people of the Book before you were forbidden the captives, and patience is better for you too.

**"and turn to you in mercy"** is His acceptance of repentance from sin and error, bringing you back from the disobedience you practised to obedience to Him, and forgiving what ensued in pre-Islamic times.

**"For Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise"** means He knows His creatures, knows your dire need for marriage, and is Wise in what He has ordained for you, making the laws according to His servants' interests.

### Nothing new in the standards

There is nothing new about the moral standards the Qur'an lays down. In every age God proclaimed them through His messengers, and believing people followed them. The ancient heavenly books could not remain untampered with, so the divine modes of living were lost or obscured, and God revealed them again, in Arabic, through His final Messenger. Whoever follows them today joins the eternal caravan of righteous humanity that walked the divine path under grace. The verse puts the believers in the line of the prophets and the righteous who came earlier, and the guidance itself is described as the path of those prophets and friends.

### The inner reading

When the Prophet ﷺ and his community were told the stories of past communities, what those people did and how they were dealt with, the believers looked to what would be done with them, for among them were some who had also done the impermissible. Their question was: if only we knew how God will deal with us, whether by abasement, by metamorphosis, or by punishment. So God most high said: "And to guide you in the ways of those before you", informing them of what was done with them, "and to turn toward you." To you, I turn. To those who came before you, destruction was already given in full. Other readings unfold the verse further: He desires to make clear to you by unveiling His secrets, so that what was hidden from others is manifest to you. He desires to make clear His singularity in bringing things into existence, in which no one else has any part. That guidance is self-entrustment to God, contentment of heart, and complete surrender before the decree and the judgement. And He turns toward you by accepting your repentance after having created it, then repaying you according to what He created for you in it.

### In short

- The laws were made clear so the believer knows the halāl from the ḥarām and walks the path of the righteous who came before.
- The moral standard is not new, only restored, and following it joins the company of the old caravan of the righteous.
- Read inwardly, the stories of the past are a mercy: their end was destruction, and yours is accepted repentance.

27.text:
The mercy named in the previous verse now meets its obstacle: "And it is Allah's Will to turn to you in grace, but those who follow their desires wish to see you deviate entirely ˹from Allah's Way˺". Two wills pull at the believer, the will of God to forgive, and the wish of the followers of desire to drag everyone down with them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And it is Allah's Will to turn to you in grace"** repeats the turning of the previous verse on purpose, expanding it. When God purposes to turn toward a servant, no enemy is allowed to gloat over him, and nothing bad reaches him in either abode.

**"but those who follow their desires wish to see you deviate entirely"** names the pull from the other side. The followers of Shayṭān among the Jews, the Christians and the adulterous wish that the believers would take the horrendous path of falsehood instead of the truth, transgressing what is right by committing what was forbidden them, so that they might become like them.

### The company that drags

The followers of desire include the fornicators and adulterers, and the nations and peoples of false creeds. For them the restrictions of halāl and ḥarām simply do not register, and no line is drawn between lawful and unlawful. There are creeds in which marrying women is permitted where marriage with them is not proper. There are many atheists who favour eliminating the institution of marriage itself as out of tune with the times. Not content with what they call living together, there are places where people talk of women as a shared item of enjoyment. One report of the verse's first audience names the Jews, who claimed that marrying the sisters of the father's side was lawful in their Scripture, and the Magians are named with the people of the Book in the same breath.

The verse is a guard for the weak. Some Muslims, subscribing to Islam yet weak in faith, keep company with disbelievers and atheists of such inclinations, fall prey to their lustful claims, and begin to think their own religion outdated and the enemy's position the very epitome of human progress. They have been framed into believing that people of such ideas are modern and forward-looking, and they start wishing their own religion had permitted what the enemy permits. Refuge with Allah from such spineless surrender. The best policy is the one the verse itself gives: take Allah's warning and stay away from owning and practising the ideas and ways of people with dispositions so wicked.

### The inner reading

The followers of passion are measured against the Real, and the measure is desire itself. Their desire, their irāda, becomes weak, enfeebled and held back before the desire of the Real. And the closing word of the passage, that man was created weak, describes the servants' need and affliction, their ḍurr, but does not accept it as their ʿudhr, their excuse. The will that turns toward them is stronger than the wish that pulls them away, and the lightening the Real desires for His servants runs through the whole of the law.

### In short

- God's will is to turn to you in grace, and no enemy gloats over the one He turns toward.
- The followers of desire, the adulterous and the creedless, wish the believers a tremendous deviation, so that they may be like them.
- Weak Muslims in their company begin to see the crooked way as progress. The verse's warning is to keep out of that company and those ideas.
- Read inwardly, the desire of the followers of passion is weak and held back before the desire of the Real, whose wish to forgive is the stronger pull.

28.text:
The passage's last word on the law is mercy: "And it is Allah's Will to lighten your burdens, for humankind was created weak". The legislation itself is shaped to the creature it addresses.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And it is Allah's Will to lighten your burdens"**, the first part of verse 28, means His legislation, His orders, His prohibitions and His decrees are made easy, prescribed so that everyone obligated with them can carry them. He does not burden a soul with more than it can do, for the sacred law is fitted to the strength of the creature. This is why the free man was allowed to marry a bondwoman under certain conditions, as Mujāhid and others stated, why the couple marrying could fix the dower by mutual consent, and why marrying more than one woman was allowed under circumstantial necessity, on condition that justice is not compromised.

**"for humankind was created weak"** is the reason. Man is weak by nature and constituted desire-prone. Had the demand been made of him to turn from women completely and forever, he would have proved a hopeless performer at keeping Allah's injunctions. In view of his weakness he was not only permitted to marry but induced to. Marriage is a smart mutual contract that removes the chances of the weakness afflicting men and women, for the life of the couple brings mutual self-realization, a sight untainted and a character unalloyed, and that purity makes both strong, self-reliant and happy.

### The weakness itself

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded that Ṭāwūs said the weakness is concerning women. Wakīʿ said: man's mind leaves when women are involved. One reading keeps it plain: man cannot do without women. Wherever the name of man appears in the Qur'an, a displeasing attribute is linked to it: "Surely man is a great wrongdoer, ungrateful" (14:34), "Surely man was created anxious" (70:19), "Surely man is rebellious" (96:6), "Surely man is ungrateful to his Lord" (100:6), "Surely man is in loss" (103:2). The reason lies in his origin: man comes of dust, and dust is the ground of density and the root of opacity.

The servant's hope rests on the day of his making: He saw the faults, and He bought along with the faults. The Pir of the Ṭarīqah prayed:

> O Lord, You called me ignorant. What comes from the ignorant other than disloyalty? You called me weak. What comes from the weak other than error? Take our inability to overcome ourselves as stemming from that weakness. Take our boldness and insolence as stemming from that ignorance. You lifted us up, and no one said "Lift up." Now that You have lifted up, don't put down. Keep us in the shadow of Your bounty. If You water, You Yourself planted. If You flatten the foundation, You Yourself raised it. I, the servant, am just what You fancied. Don't throw me down. You lifted me up.

Read inwardly, the verse gives both the diagnosis and its cure, and it does not let the weakness serve as a licence. By "man was created weak", He describes the servants' need and affliction, but He does not accept it as their excuse. The lightening is real and manifold: He lightens the weight of litanies through the intermittent incomings that visit the heart, the struggles of the seeker with the lights of witnessings that enter deeply, the burdens of service with the sweetness of acts of obedience, the difficulties of the trust He carries for you, and the hardships of seeking with the refreshment of arriving.

### In short

- The law is built light: bondwomen permitted under conditions, dowers settled by consent, plural marriage under necessity with justice.
- Man's weakness, Ṭāwūs's "concerning women" and Wakīʿ's departing mind, is the reason the law bends, and marriage is the smart contract that cures what it bends for.
- Wherever the Qur'an names man, it links a displeasing attribute, for he is dust upon dust, and his hope is that his Maker bought him with his faults.
- The weakness explains the law's ease but excuses nothing, and the lightening reaches from litanies to the refreshment of arrival.

29.text:
From marriage law to the two foundations of all social law, property and life: "O believers! Do not devour one another's wealth illegally, but rather trade by mutual consent. And do not kill ˹each other or˺ yourselves. Surely Allah is ever Merciful to you". The surah has guarded the orphan, the woman and the heir. Now it guards everyone.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do not devour one another's wealth illegally"** forbids every false means of taking property. The word is literally "do not eat", but in common usage it means do not usurp another's property by any false means at all, for the unauthorized use of what someone else owns is called eating, whether or not it is eatable. The word bāṭil, false means, covers in the view of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd and the majority of the Companions every impermissible form: theft, robbery, usurpation, breach of trust, bribery, interest and gambling, and all false transactions, as Abū Ḥayyān notes in his al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ. The same reading includes a man's own property spent on what is religiously sinful, or in straight extravagance, for that too is devouring in the verse's sense. The methods forbidden are often dressed as lawful, ribā and gambling and other wicked ways that appear legal, while Allah knows that those involved seek only the interest.

**"but rather trade by mutual consent"** is the one door left open, and the whole of the verse's economics stands in it, as the next section shows.

**"And do not kill ˹each other or˺ yourselves"** covers both the taking of another's life without right and suicide, and beyond both, the committing of Allah's prohibitions generally, falling into sin and eating up property unjustly, for that too is a killing of the self.

**"Surely Allah is ever Merciful to you"** closes the command. The injunctions come as mercy, so that you may guard against the punishment of the life to come and stay safe from punishments that could afflict you right here in the present life.

### The garment and the extra dirham

The earliest readers pressed the verse into corners. There is the buyer of a garment who declares that he will keep it if it pleases him, and otherwise return it with an extra dirham added. The comment on Ibn ʿAbbās's authority, in Ibn Jarīr's record, is that this is exactly what Allah meant by: "Eat not up your property among yourselves unjustly" (2:188). ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that when this verse came down, some Muslims said that Allah had forbidden them to eat each other's property unjustly, and food is the best property, so none of them might eat anyone else's food. Then Allah sent down: "There is no restriction on the blind" (24:61), to the end of the verse, and Qatādah said similarly.

### What counts as trade

Two conditions make a transaction lawful under this verse. It must be trade, an exchange of property for property, and it must be by mutual consent. Where there is no commodity on one side, there is no trade but deception. An interest-based loan pays the interest for the time allowed, and time is not a commodity. In speculation and gambling the commodity exists on one side but its counterpart is doubtful. In forward trading, the commodity does not exist and a promise stands in its place. Muslim jurists call these void sales, al-baiʿ al-bāṭil. And where both commodities exist but consent is missing, the sale is corrupt, al-baiʿ al-fāṣid, and equally forbidden. The second condition reaches further than it looks. Consent squeezed out by compulsion is not consent. The trader who corners the market's daily needs, stocks up, raises the price and leaves the customer no choice has taken a consent that is null and void. The husband who spins the terms of married life into thorns until his wife yields up her dower has taken nothing. The man ready to offer a bribe because his valid work will not move without one has not consented of his own free will either.

Trade itself is read generously. According to at-Tafsīr al-Mazharī, dealings of service, labour and tenancy are included, for in a sale one acquires property for property, and in hiring, property for service, and trade covers both. Mujāhid read the exception as selling and buying, or giving someone a gift. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The seller and the buyer retain the right to change their mind as long as they have not parted." Al-Bukhārī's wording reads: "When two men conduct a transaction, they retain their right to change their mind as long as they have not parted." The option before parting is part of the mutual consent the verse requires, and this one word of the Qur'an, trade by consent, is the key to the whole treasure of Muslim jurisprudence on sales and hiring. Every form the shariah forbids stands outside the approved core.

### The cleanest earning

The verse names trade for a reason: trade and labour are the best means of earning among all open to man. The Prophet ﷺ, asked by Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj which earning was the purest, said: "Man's work with his own hands, and all honest sale transactions." Al-Mundhirī carries it in his at-Targhīb. Abū Saʿīd al-Khudhrī narrates that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The truthful and trustworthy trader shall be with the prophets and the truthful and the martyrs", recorded by at-Tirmidhī. Anas narrates: "The truthful trader shall be under the shade of the Throne on the Day of Doom", reported by al-Iṣfahānī in his at-Targhīb. From Muʿādh ibn Jabal comes the price of cleanness: the trader who does not lie when he talks, commits no breach when trusted, does not pick faults in what he buys, does not over-praise what he sells, does not evade a debt he owes and does not harass a debtor who owes him. Otherwise the trade turns: "Traders will be raised on the Day of Doom as the sinners, except him who fears Allah, acts righteously and says what is true", as al-Ḥākim records from Rifāʿah ibn Rāfiʿ. Trading and the provision of services are the right way of earning. Theft, deceit, lies, bribery, usury and gambling are only different ways of plundering.

### The right to life

The verse places property before life, probably because injustice and negligence are far more common in matters of property, though unjust killing is graver. The right of life is guarded for all, related or unrelated, Muslim or non-Muslim bound by a pact of peace, as at-Tafsīr al-Mazharī notes. Whoever deprives a person of life outside the law of God commits an unlawful act, and the right to execute belongs to the established authority alone, after guilt is proved.

The prohibition of self-killing has its own reports. The story behind the mercy is ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ's. Sent by the Prophet ﷺ to the battle of Dhāt as-Salāsil, he had a wet dream on a night of severe cold, feared that a bath would end him, and performed tayammum with pure earth instead, leading his company in the Dawn prayer. Told of it, the Prophet ﷺ asked: "O ʿAmr, have you led your people in prayer while you were in a state of sexual impurity?" ʿAmr answered that he had recalled Allah's statement "And do not kill yourselves. Surely, Allah is Most Merciful to you", and feared to perish. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ smiled and said nothing. Abū Dāwūd carries the report. The mercy of the verse covered his case. Ibn Marduwyah then reported from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> Whoever kills himself with an iron tool, his tool will be in his hand and he will keep stabbing himself with it in the Fire of Jahannam, forever and ever. Whoever kills himself with poison, his poison will be in his hand and he will keep taking it in the Fire of Jahannam forever and ever. Whoever kills himself by throwing himself from a mountain will keep falling in the Fire of Jahannam forever and ever.

The two Ṣaḥīḥs collected it, and the Group collected from Thābit ibn ad-Daḥḥāk the word of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever kills himself with an instrument will be punished with it on the Day of Resurrection." And the Ṣaḥīḥ records the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying: "Cursing a Muslim is a sin and fighting him is kufr."

### Where the verse leads

Verse 29 closes one road and the next two open the accounting. Whoever takes or kills sinfully and unjustly, knowingly, will find the Fire, and that is easy for Allah. But the major sins named around these verses have their own catalogues, which the following verse recites: the seven destructive sins from Abū Hurayrah, the false testimony from Anas ibn Mālik, the greatest sins from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, from Abū Bakrah and from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, down to Salmān al-Farīsī's Friday, the day Allah brought together the creation of Ādam (Adam), on which the bath and the prayer and the quiet erase what lies between two Fridays.

### In short

- Every false means of taking property is devouring, including ribā, gambling, bribery and false contracts, and including the sinful or extravagant waste of one's own.
- The lawful door is trade by real mutual consent, with the option to withdraw before parting, and service and labour stand inside the same door.
- The truthful, trustworthy trader ranks with the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs, and the cleanest earning is the work of one's own hands.
- Life is guarded like property and above it: no self-killing, even to escape a cold bath, and no killing outside the proved judgement of law.
- The commands are mercy, closing the roads whose ends are fire.

30.text:
The sentence that follows the two prohibitions: "And whoever does this sinfully and unjustly, We will burn them in the Fire. That is easy for Allah". Verse 29 forbade the devouring and the killing. Verse 30 prices them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"whoever does this sinfully and unjustly"** carries two conditions, aggression and injustice, doing the forbidden thing deliberately, knowing it is forbidden and daring it still. The restriction matters: should the wrong come about through forgetfulness or mistake, it does not enter this warning. That is the reading of Islamic law on the passage.

**"We will burn them in the Fire. That is easy for Allah"** is a stern warning and a truthful promise, and every sane person who hears the speech with full comprehension should beware of it. The casting and the burning are an easy matter for Him, for He is powerful over everything.

### The place of the verse

The Fire here receives the deliberate taker and the deliberate killer, the ones who consumed the ribā and the false trade of verse 29, or destroyed a life or a self in the manner the reports of Abū Hurayrah and Thābit ibn ad-Daḥḥāk described. Against them stands the mercy the same verse promised, the mercy ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ leaned on at Dhāt as-Salāsil when he chose tayammum over death and the Prophet ﷺ smiled, a story Abū Dāwūd carries. Mujāhid and Qatādah read the warning as reaching every forbidden act committed knowingly, and Ibn ʿAbbās's garment bought with an extra dirham falling due shows how fine the line of injustice runs. The verse after this one opens the exit, the avoiding of the major sins, from shirk to false testimony to the killing of the child, which the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd and ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr catalogued, and ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr's own report, carried by al-Bukhārī, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī, closes the catalogue with the false oath.

### In short

- The deliberate wrong, in property or in life, is met with the Fire, and that is easy for Allah.
- Forgetfulness and mistake are excluded by the verse's own conditions.
- Between the mercy of verse 29 and the pardon of verse 31, this verse stands as the price list of persistence.

31.text:
After the warning, the offer: "If you avoid the major sins forbidden to you, We will absolve you of your ˹lesser˺ misdeeds and admit you into a place of honour". The Qur'an's habit is to follow a warning with a persuasion, and this verse is one of its greatest offers. Avoid the great sins, and the small ones are wiped out on arrival at a noble entrance.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If you avoid the major sins forbidden to you"** names the kabāʾir, the sins whose punishment has been threatened, murder, fornication, theft and their like. Avoiding them includes fulfilling every obligation, fard and wājib, for neglecting an obligation is itself a major sin.

**"We will absolve you of your ˹lesser˺ misdeeds"** is the promise of pardon for the ṣaghāʾir, written off and replaced with reward instead of punishment and Paradise instead of Hell.

**"and admit you into a place of honour"** is Paradise, entered through a noble gate.

### How the pardon works

Righteous deeds operate as kaffārah, expiation, for minor sins. In the authentic hadith, when a person makes wudu for ṣalāh, the washing of each limb expiates the sins of that limb: the face carries away the sins of the eye, the ear and the nose, the gargling the sins of the tongue, the washing of the feet the sins of the feet, and every step toward the masjid brings its own expiation. The intervals are named: the minor sins between one congregational prayer and the next, between one Friday and the next, between one Ramadan and the next.

Salmān al-Farīsī is the narrator, in Aḥmad's Musnad, of the hadith on the day of al-Jumuʿah:

> The Prophet ﷺ said to me, "Do you know what the day of al-Jumuʿah is?" I said, "It is the day during which Allah brought together the creation of your father, Adam." He said, "I know what the day of Jumuʿah is. Anyone who takes a bath and cleans himself as much as he can, then proceeds for the Friday prayer and remains quiet until the imam finishes the prayer, all his sins in between the present and the next Friday will be forgiven, as long as major sins were avoided."

Al-Bukhārī recorded similar wording from Salmān al-Farīsī.

The condition is strict. The expiation through wudu, ṣalāh and the rest concerns minor sins only, and only for the one who has stayed away from the major ones. Major sins are forgiven by taubah, repentance, alone. Whoever stays involved in the major sins while performing his wudu and ṣalāh will find that neither the minor nor the major is expiated, and when he appears on the Day of Resurrection carrying the heavy burden of both, he will find no helping hand to lighten it.

### Two kinds, and the truth about the smaller

The verse teaches that sins are of two kinds, kabīrah and ṣaghīrah, and the promise binds them together. But the technical "minor" sin is not minor in itself. In the absolute sense, sin is any act against the command and will of Allah, and to disobey Him is invariably a grave crime. A large number of scholars therefore ruled that every disobedience is a major sin, and the distinction is made only when the sins are compared with each other. Ibn ʿAbbās said it plainly: any act forbidden by the sharīʿah is a major sin.

A minor sin done with nerve or heedlessness does not remain minor. It becomes major. A sage compared the two to a small scorpion and a big one, or a large ember and a tiny spark, for a person cannot bear the pain of any of them. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī said no act of worship offered to Allah is greater than giving up sins, and that those who keep up prayers and the remembrance of Allah while still living in sins find no acceptance. Fudayl ibn ʿIyāḍ, the famous mystic, said: "The lighter you take a sin to be, the greater it will become with Allah as a crime." The most righteous elders used to say that every sin is a courier of kufr, inviting people to the manners of disbelievers. In the Musnad of Aḥmad, ʿĀʾishah wrote to Muʿāwiyah that a servant who disobeys Allah finds his admirers become fault-finders and his friends turn into enemies, and that heedlessness toward sins is the cause of permanent ruination.

The Qur'an gives the process its anatomy. In an authentic hadith, the Prophet ﷺ said that when a true believer falls into sin, a black dot appears on his heart. If he repents and seeks forgiveness, the dot disappears. If he does not, it keeps increasing until it covers the whole heart. The Qur'an names this dot rayn: "Their evil deeds have rusted their hearts" (83:14).

### What makes a sin major

The definition drawn from the Qur'an and the sunnah is: a sin on which a ḥadd punishment is prescribed for this present life, or on which words of curse have appeared, or on which a stern warning of Hell has been mentioned. Every sin whose evil outcome equals or exceeds a major sin counts as one, and so does a sin done in rebellious attitude or as a settled habit.

The number is not fixed. Someone said before Ibn ʿAbbās that the major sins were seven. He answered: "Not seven. Say seven hundred, which is better." In his book al-Zawājir, Imam Ibn Ḥajr al-Makkī listed them with full explanations, and the count reached four hundred and sixty seven. The Prophet ﷺ named them in threes and sixes and sevens as circumstances demanded, and the scholars concluded that no single number was meant as a universal count.

The lists themselves run long. In al-Bukhārī and Muslim: "I warn you against the top ones among the major sins. They are three: to associate a created being as a partner in the divinity of Allah, to disobey parents, and to give false witness or to lie." ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ what the greatest sin was. He said: "To make a rival for Allah while He alone created you." Then? "To kill your offspring for fear that he might share your food with you." Then? "To commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." He then recited from "And those who invoke not any other god along with Allah" (25:68) to "Except those who repent" (25:70). Abū Hurayrah's report in the two Ṣaḥīḥs counts the seven destructive sins: joining others in worship with Allah, killing the life Allah has forbidden except for a just cause, magic, consuming ribā, consuming an orphan's wealth, turning away from the enemy in battle, and accusing chaste women of unchastity. Anas ibn Mālik reported the mention of associating others with Allah, killing, and being undutiful to parents, then the words: "Should I tell you about the biggest of the major sins? The false statement, or the false testimony." ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakrah reported from his father the question "Should I inform you about the greatest of the great sins?", the answer naming the joining of partners and undutifulness to parents, and then the Prophet ﷺ, reclining, sat up and said: "And I warn you against false testimony and false speech", repeating it until they wished he would stop. ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr reported the greatest sins as joining others with Allah, being undutiful to parents or taking a life, and the false oath, recorded by al-Bukhārī, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī. Muslim carries his report on parents: one of the ugliest major sins is a man's cursing of his own parents, which comes about when he curses another man's father and the man retaliates upon his.

Al-Bukhārī's narration counts also the eating up of an orphan's property by false means, the devouring of interest, the deserting of the battlefield of jihād, the false accusation against chaste women, and the desecration of the Holy Kaʿbah. To migrate from the land of Islam back to the land of kufr is ruled a major sin in some narrations. So are the false oath, the withholding of surplus water from those who need it, and the learning and practising of magic. The Prophet ﷺ said drinking is the greatest of major sins and the mother of all shameful deeds, and that the gravest major sin is to impute to a Muslim brother a fault that stains his character. Bracketing two ṣalāhs into one time without an excuse the sharīʿah approves is a major sin, as are losing hope in the mercy of Allah and growing careless of His punishment, and making a will that injures an inheritor. From Abū Dharr, whom Abū Dāwūd's collection also serves on these catalogues, comes the triple cry, "Destitutes, losers, they are ruined", over six: the one who lets his garment hang below his ankles, the one who spends in the way of Allah then publicizes the favour, the old man who indulges in shameful deeds, the office-holder who tells lies, the family man who waxes proud, and the one who gives allegiance to a worthy imam for material gain. The backbiter will not be admitted into Paradise, as al-Bukhārī and Muslim proclaim, and an-Nasāʾī and the Musnad of Aḥmad add the drinker, the disobeyer of parents, the unjustified severer of kinsmen, the publicizer of favours, the diviner of the unseen through jinns and satans, and the dayyuth, so at ease with his shame that neither wife nor family is ever turned back from immodesty. From the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim: the curse of Allah is on whoever sacrifices an animal for anyone other than Allah.

### The great sins of the proximate

Read inwardly, the verse has a second register. The great sins of the folk of service on the path of the sharīʿah are the ones catalogued above. For the folk of companionship on the Ṭarīqah's street, the great sins are of another sort and carry another tasting, for the servers are hirelings of the wage, while the companions are the near ones. In the traditions: "The beautiful deeds of the pious are the ugly deeds of the proximate." To this belongs what the Pir of the Ṭarīqah said: "The hypocrisy of the recognizers is better than the self-purification of the desirers." The basis is the subtle point Muṣṭafā ﷺ reported about cloudiness: "My heart becomes clouded, so I ask forgiveness from God seventy times a day." Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq said: "Would that I could witness that for which God's Messenger asked forgiveness." The great sins of the recognizers are the lapses of lassitude in their travelling, when the innate disposition is overpowered by human attributes, and the realities of faith grow mixed with the contaminants of personal motive. Unless a messenger of sound discipline and truthful poverty comes out to seize them by the hand, they stay in the pit of selfhood. The great ones of the religion have said that a man must first reach that place of danger and leave the station of lassitude behind before he becomes a pir of the Ṭarīqah fit to take disciples. He must have lost the road a thousand times and returned to it, if he is to bring back someone who has lost the road. First comes the road to the road, and only then the road. Someone forever on the road knows the road, yet not the road to the road. This is the secret behind the slips of the prophets and their falls into lassitude, and God knows best.

### In short

- Avoid the major sins, fulfil the obligations, and the minor sins are expiated by the wudu, the ṣalāh, the steps to the masjid and the Fridays, as Salmān al-Farīsī was told on the day of Ādam's assembling.
- Major sins are forgiven by repentance alone, and no righteous deed expiates for the one who stays in them.
- In the absolute sense every disobedience is grave, the minor sin done heedlessly turns major, and the heart collects the rust the Qur'an names rayn.
- The major sins number not seven but seven hundred by Ibn ʿAbbās's count, four hundred and sixty seven by Ibn Ḥajr's book, and the hadiths name them from shirk to the sacrifice offered to other than Allah.
- Read inwardly, the proximate have their own great sins, the lassitude of the road, and only the one who has been lost can guide the lost home.

32.text:
A verse born from a woman's question: "And do not crave what Allah has given some of you over others. Men will be rewarded according to their deeds and women ˹equally˺ according to theirs. Rather, ask Allah for His bounties. Surely Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things". The halves and doubles of the inheritance law had raised it, and the answer governs every heart that has ever looked at another's portion.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And do not crave what Allah has given some of you over others"** forbids the wish itself, in worldly affairs or religion, for what Allah has preferred some with, because such wishing breeds mutual envy and hatred. A man should not covet the wealth, the mount or the wife of his brother, nor anything his brother possesses. The decree has come to pass, and wishing does not change it.

**"Men will be rewarded according to their deeds and women ˹equally˺ according to theirs"** means each person earns wages for works of their own, a reward if the deeds are good and punishment if they are evil, as Ibn Jarīr explains. No one is rewarded except through what they earn, and one reading ties the line back to the inheritance itself, each person receiving the due share, as al-Wālibī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās.

**"Rather, ask Allah for His bounties"** redirects the desire. The ideal conduct, on seeing someone excel in a grace of life, is not to wish oneself at par, but to pray to Allah for blessings from Him. The word for ask is read wa-s’alū, or wa-ṣalū. The instruction to the tongue is: "O Allah, provide us with the like of, or better than, what You have provided him with", and then to consign the matter to Allah.

**"Surely Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things"** closes the door. Allah knows who deserves this life and gives him riches, and whoever deserves poverty He makes poor. He knows who deserves the Hereafter and directs him to the deeds that make him successful in it, and whoever deserves failure, He prevents him from righteousness and what leads to it.

### The women's question

Imam Aḥmad recorded that Umm Salamah said: "O Messenger of Allah, men go to battle, but we do not go to battle, and we earn one-half of the inheritance that men get." At-Tirmidhī also recorded this hadith. Her purpose was not objection. She wished she were a man, to deserve the merits restricted to men, and other women wished the same: had they been men, they could have ridden out with the fighters and earned what the fighters earn in jihād. Another woman asked the Prophet ﷺ whether the double share of men in inheritance and the half weight of a woman's witness meant that women would receive half the reward for all their acts of worship. The verse came down carrying both answers: "do not crave" answered Umm Salamah, whose name appears in the reports as Umm Salama and Umm Salmah, and "men a share... women a share" answered the woman's arithmetic. The things in which men were preferred are named: praying in congregation, attending the Friday prayer, joining military expeditions, jihād, enjoining good and forbidding evil.

### The unacquirable

The verse forbids coveting precisely those things that cannot be acquired by effort. When a person finds themselves lacking in wealth, comfort, beauty, merit or knowledge, envy surges up and urges them to draw level or push ahead. But some excellences have nothing to do with effort. They are blessings of nature: being a man, being of a prophet's family, being born to rulers, being born beautiful. A woman cannot become a man. No one can choose a prophet's household, change a physique, or collect chosen features by any quantity of medicine and treatment. Finding themselves incapable of matching the other, the inner self begins to wish the blessings snatched away from the other too, so that both stand equal or the other lower. That is envy, a shameful and damaging trait, the cause of endless disputes, disturbances, killings and ravages.

The verse's counsel is rest, not resignation into sin. Whoever Allah elected to be a man should be grateful. Whoever He elected to be a woman should be pleased with being just that, for had she been a man she might have failed the responsibilities placed on men and ended a sinner. The beautiful should be grateful, and the lesser in looks should not grieve, for beauty does not guarantee good and might land its bearer in trial or corruption. The true descendant of the Prophet ﷺ should thank Allah for the connection, and whoever lacks it should neither worry nor pine, since it cannot be acquired and the coveting earns only a broken heart and an aching soul. The best policy is one's own doings. Let them be good and righteous, and a person so strengthened stands ahead of those with higher lineage.

### The open field of deeds

The verse does not close competition. Other verses and the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ exhort people to excel each other in good deeds, an open field where looking at another's trail of merit is right, because these are deeds within a person's control, acquirable by learning, training and working. Whoever is impressed by another's intellect, practical life or excellent morals may strive to acquire the same, and that is praiseworthy. The verse's own second half supports it: effort in acquiring merits does not go waste, and every man and woman will get a return, a share of what they worked for.

Two errors are removed on the way. Some ruin an otherwise peaceful life in devotion to merits that cannot be acquired, and if they go further into envy, wishing the blessing away from the other, the chances of salvation in the life to come stand destroyed by the grave sin. Others lack courage or shame and do not even try for acquirable merits, and when counselled they blame destiny and fate, camouflaging their own timidity and inertia. The verse's rule sorts them out. What man's effort cannot reach is resigned to fate, with contentment and gratitude. What effort can reach is pursued, with the promise that the share of the work will not be wasted.

### Sealing the crimes at the root

At-Tafsīr al-Baḥr points out, referring back to the prohibitions of verse 29, that this verse aims to seal the very root of those crimes. Theft, robbery and the other illegitimate ways of taking property, and the killing and destroying of people, all sprout from one emotional attitude: finding the other ahead in wealth and material things, feeling the pinch, wishing to draw level or rise above, and then being pushed by the intensity of that desire into the crime. The Qur'an blocks the crimes by blocking the desire for the unacquirables at its root.

### Ask for the grace, not for a fixed thing

The grace of Allah wears a different face on every person. For some, wealth is the blessing, for were they paupers they might fall into sin and disbelief. For others, the grace lies in their very straitened circumstances, for were they rich they might succumb to a thousand sins. For some the grace is power and influence, and for others, the unremembered and the unattended, the grace manifests in exactly that state, since a look at reality would show them that power might have caused their fall. So the instruction stands: do not ask Allah for some fixed quality of life, ask for His grace, and He in His infinite wisdom opens the doors of His blessings. The arrangement He has made is the quintessence of wisdom and justice, and only He knows how suitable each condition is for the one kept in it.

### The inner reading

Abū Bakr Kattānī drew the verse onto the road of the seekers. The one convinced that arrival comes without expended effort is a wisher. The one convinced that arrival comes only through effort is a drudge. Whoever fancies he will reach the goal without toil is a wisher, and "the incapable are those who follow their own caprice and wish for God." Shaykh al-Islām Anṣārī said:

> He is not found by seeking, but the seeker finds. Until he finds Him, he will not seek. Whatever can be found by seeking is of little worth. The servant finds the Real before the seeking, but for him seeking is the earliest step. The recognizer finds seeking from finding, not finding from seeking. O God, since finding You is before the seeking and the seeker, I am seeking because unsettledness has overpowered me. The seeker is seeking and the Sought is obtained before the seeking. This is a most marvelous business.

Another reading of the verse takes the wishers to task: they want the station of the masters without traveling the masters' path or clinging to their conduct. They want the state of the great ones, but they have not gone on the great ones' road. They search for the Kaʿbah of union with eyes that have not undertaken struggle, and they see the great good fortune of the friends without seeing their tribulation. Their trouble is wishing to be like those who have taken trouble. The lovers seeking God are full of longing like Alexander seeking the water of life. Not just anyone is suited for His wounds, and the chevaliers who made their spirits the target of His trial's arrow hum in the midst of it that their spirits must be worthy of His pain, for that share of passion's good fortune suffices. The wound of each is measured by his faith, and the burden of each by his strength. The stronger the strength, the heavier the burden carried.

### In short

- The wish for what others were given is forbidden because it changes nothing and ripens into envy.
- Each is rewarded by their own earning, and the field of acquirable merit stays open to every man and woman.
- What cannot be acquired, sex, lineage, looks, is resigned to destiny with gratitude, and the pain spared by each state is known only to Allah.
- Coveting is the root of the property crimes and killings of verse 29, and the verse cuts it there.
- Ask not for a fixed thing but for His grace, which wears a different face for every person.
- On the inward road, wishing without toiling is the mark of the wisher, and the wound of the friends is bought with tribulation, never with wishing.

33.text:
The inheritance law set down, the verse seals its wisdom and remembers a brotherhood that once inherited: "And We have appointed heirs to what has been left by parents and next of kin. As for those you have made a pledge to, give them their share. Surely Allah is a Witness over all things".

### Phrase by phrase

**"And We have appointed heirs to what has been left by parents and next of kin"** states that for everyone there are appointed heirs of what parents and relatives leave. From Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān down through Ad-Daḥḥāk, as-Suddī, Zayd ibn Aslam, Qatādah, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Mujāhid, the appointed ones, the mawālī, are read as heirs. Ibn ʿAbbās said the same, and was also reported to give mawālī the sense of relatives. Ibn Jarīr noted that the Arabs call the cousin a mawla. To all people, then, Allah appointed relatives who will later inherit what they themselves inherited from their own parents and family.

**"As for those you have made a pledge to, give them their share"** concerned the allies with whom covenants of mutual assistance and inheritance were made before Islam, and in the first years of the faith.

**"Surely Allah is a Witness over all things"** includes the pledges themselves. Allah witnessed everyone when the promises were given.

### The brotherhood that inherited

When the emigrants came to Al-Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ established bonds of brotherhood between them and the Anṣār, and the emigrant inherited from his Anṣārī brother, while the latter's own relatives did not, because of the pledge. The emigrant and his ally even stood together in jihād. Al-Bukhārī recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that when this verse was revealed, it cancelled the pledge of brotherhood regarding inheritance. What survived of "give them their due portion" was the duty of cooperation and mutual advice, with inheritance excluded, while leaving a bequest to the person who had held the right before stayed open. In the pre-Islamic era people used to adopt men and youth and allocate them a portion of wealth as they would their own children, and Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, the reporting authority for the occasion, said the verse was revealed about those adopters. Their due was apportioned in the bequest alone. The division of the estate went specifically to the immediate family and close relatives. The allies' share in that first period was a sixth, and the whole ruling of the pledge-inheritance was later abrogated by the verse on the womb-relatives (33:6). If other heirs exist, a pledge or mutual contract no longer affects the inheritance in any manner, though a gift to a former ally from a third of the wealth remains open.

So the shares stand on wisdom, as the previous verse insisted to Umm Salmah and the women who asked. Human reason cannot encompass the totality of factors holding the order of the universe together, and so cannot compute the wisdom inside the shares Allah determined. Whoever has been allotted whatsoever share should be pleased with it and grateful.

Read inwardly, the verse honours the covenant itself. At the faith's beginning He had ranked relationships of mutual commitment as equals of kinship ties in inheritance. That ruling passed away, but the rule of respect between the parties stayed. If that is the manner of commitments between men, what of the mutual covenant with God, of whom His servants say with the words of the Qur'an that they are men true to the covenant they made with Him (33:23)? Those who have died to the religion of whims, it has been said, find the decree of death a sweet watering place.

### In short

- Heirs are appointed for everyone from parents and near kin, and the shares rest on a wisdom reason cannot audit.
- The pledge-brotherhood of the emigrants and the Anṣār once carried inheritance, and the verse ended that, keeping cooperation, advice and bequests.
- Adopted men and allies receive from the bequest, not the fixed shares of the estate.
- Allah witnessed every pledge, and the covenant made with Him outlasts the ruling that passed away.

34.text:
The most closely argued verse of the surah's family law: "Men are the caretakers of women, as men have been provisioned by Allah over women and tasked with supporting them financially. And righteous women are devoutly obedient and, when alone, protective of what Allah has entrusted them with. And if you sense ill-conduct from your women, advise them ˹first˺, ˹if they persist,˺ do not share their beds, ˹but if they still persist,˺ then discipline them ˹gently˺. But if they change their ways, do not be unjust to them. Surely Allah is Most High, All-Great". It opens with a principle, draws a portrait, and then builds a ladder of correction that never leaves the house.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Men are the caretakers of women"** is the working rule. The word qawwām, from qayyām, names the person charged with a duty. It is the one who must manage a job or run a system, taking care of what has to be done about something, with the related factors under control. The man is responsible for the woman, her maintainer, caretaker and leader, who disciplines her if she deviates. Other renderings used are guardians, custodians, overseers and protectors. Read as a functional head, and not a ruler or dictator, the word rests on common experience. Any group-living, big or small, and any organized system rationally and customarily needs some head to arbitrate differences and run affairs. Countries and states accept this, and the older tribal organizations accepted it in their chiefs. A family, a micro-sample of the larger organizations, needs it no less. Allah in His wisdom elected men for the responsibility, because their natural capabilities are more pronounced. This is an open fact of human life. No sane person, man or woman, can deny it, and denial does not change reality.

**"as men have been provisioned by Allah over women"** gives the first reason: a God-given precedence in some qualities, like the sacred environs of Makkah where a particular House was declared Allah's House and Qiblah, and like the special honour given to the Bayt al-Maqdis in Jerusalem. Men did nothing to earn the precedence, and nothing is wrong with women for lacking it. It is a grace of creation, and prophethood and other great positions of leadership were made exclusive to men with it. The Prophet ﷺ said: "People who appoint a woman to be their leader will never achieve success", recorded by al-Bukhārī, and the same holds for appointing women as judges. Yet the verse does not say that Allah made men excel women. It says He made some of them excel the others, and the phrasing is the whole wisdom. Men and women are parts of each other, so the precedence of man over woman is like the precedence of the head over the hand, or the heart over the stomach. The head's precedence does not diminish the hand, and man's precedence lowers nothing in woman. If man is the head, woman is the body. The precedence is in terms of genus, and as for individuals, a woman may excel a man in qualities and accomplishments, even in the qualities of a caretaker.

**"and tasked with supporting them financially"** gives the second reason, and this one is earned: the dower, the expenditures and the various expenses laid on men for women by Allah's Book and by the sunnah His Messenger brought. This is why the degree spoken of elsewhere belongs to him: "But men have a degree of responsibility over them" (2:228). A comment of Ibn Ḥibbān, noted in al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, is worth attention: these two reasons prove that the right of authority is not established by force but deserved on competence and capability. The second reason also answers the inheritance arithmetic. All financial responsibilities rest with men. Before marriage the woman is her father's charge, after it her husband's. The twofold share is therefore not a gain that stays with men, for it zooms back to women after all. And the distribution is functional, not a value judgment. In her creation and nature, woman is not meant to go out and sweat for a livelihood. She has been made the means of human procreation. Motherhood and the holding of the house and family rest on her shoulders, and these are burdens man cannot carry. Authority here is hemmed with balancing factors: it is bound by the supreme law of the sharīʿah, must act on consultation and good counsel, and follows the command to treat women well. Consultation appears in the verse that bids husbands to act by mutual agreement with their wives in family affairs (2:233). Authority is thus hemmed with balancing factors throughout.

**"And righteous women are devoutly obedient"** describes the first of the two classes the principle produces. Qānitāt, obedient, as Ibn ʿAbbās and others stated: they accept the arrangement, devoted to their Lord and their husbands.

**"and, when alone, protective of what Allah has entrusted them with"** means she protects her honour and her husband's property when he is absent, as as-Suddī and others said. Abū Hurayrah is the narrator, in Ibn Jarīr's record, of the Messenger's ﷺ words: "The best woman is she who, when you look at her, pleases you, when you command her she obeys you, and when you are absent she protects her honour and your property", after which he recited this verse to its end. From ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, in the Musnad of Aḥmad, comes the word of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "If the woman prayed her five daily prayers, fasted her month, protected her chastity and obeyed her husband, she will be told, 'Enter Paradise from any of its doors you wish.'" The unseen is where the guarding happens. The duty is not restricted to his absence, for it applies during his presence too. Absence is named because that is when negligence threatens. What must be avoided is a show of alertness while men are in the house, and neglect once they are out of sight. The closing words credit the guarding to Allah's protection, for the temptations of self and satan surround every man and woman all the time. Women are weaker than men in some capabilities, yet in carrying these duties they tend to be much stronger. That is the taufīq of Allah, His help, and the reason women as a general rule are less involved in sinful immodesties than men.

**"And if you sense ill-conduct from your women, advise them ˹first˺"** turns to the second class. Ill-conduct is what appears from a woman towards her husband: acting as if she is above him, disobeying, ignoring, disliking him. The first step is to talk it over nicely and softly, reminding her of Allah's torment if she disobeys. Allah ordered the wife to obey her husband because of the enormity of his rights and all he does for her. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If I were to command anyone to prostrate before anyone, I would have commanded the wife to prostrate before her husband." And in al-Bukhārī from Abū Hurayrah: "If the man asks his wife to come to his bed and she declines, the angels will keep cursing her until the morning." Muslim's wording reads: "If the wife goes to sleep while ignoring her husband's bed, the angels will keep cursing her until the morning."

**"˹if they persist,˺ do not share their beds"** is the second step. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the abandonment means no intercourse with her, and lying on her bed with his back to her. As-Suddī, Ad-Daḥḥāk, ʿIkrimah and Ibn ʿAbbās in another narration added not speaking with her. The Qur'an says "in beds", and from here the jurists deduced that the separation is limited to beds and not the house itself. The woman is not to be left alone in the house, which would hurt her far more and strain relations further. The compilers of the Sunan and the Musnad recorded from Muʿāwiyah ibn Ḥaydah the question, "O Allah's Messenger, what right does the wife of one of us have on him?", and the answer: "To feed her when you eat, clothe her when you buy clothes for yourself, refrain from striking her face or cursing her, and not to abandon her except in the house."

**"˹but if they still persist,˺ then discipline them ˹gently˺"** is the third step, and the restraint in it is deliberate. Ibn ʿAbbās and several others said the verse means a beating that is not violent, and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said a beating that is not severe. It must not affect the body or reach the limits of hurt to skin or bones. As for slapping or hitting the face, it is absolutely forbidden. The first two steps, convincing and leaving apart in beds, are an exercise in nobility against arrogant intransigence. The prophets preached them and practised them. The third was permitted as a forced option, and alongside the permission stands the hadith that good men among you will never beat women. No such action is reported from the blessed prophets of Allah. Muslim recorded from Jābir that in the Farewell Ḥajj the Prophet ﷺ said:

> Fear Allah regarding women, for they are your assistants. You have the right on them that they do not allow any person whom you dislike to step on your mat. However, if they do that, you are allowed to discipline them lightly. They have a right on you that you provide them with their provision and clothes, in a reasonable manner.

The daughter of Abū Bakr is the narrator, in the records of Ibn Saʿd and al-Baihaqī, of a report that in the first days of Islam beating women was forbidden outright, then they grew far too oppressive, and the permission was reinstated.

**"But if they change their ways, do not be unjust to them"** closes the ladder. When the wife obeys in all that Allah has allowed, no means of annoyance are allowed against her. The husband has no right to beat her or shun her bed, and no right to go hair-splitting for faults on flimsy issues. The ending is a reminder aimed at him: if he transgresses without justification, Allah, the Ever Most High, Most Great, is her Protector, and He will exert revenge on those who deal with their wives unjustly.

### The occasion of the permission

The verse has a background. Zayd ibn Zuhayr had married his daughter Ḥabībah to Saʿd ibn al-Rabīʿ. During a dispute the husband slapped her. She complained to her father, who took her to the Prophet ﷺ. He declared that Ḥabībah had the right to hit Saʿd as hard as he had hit her, and they started back home to take their revenge. Then this verse was revealed, permitting the beating of women only as the very last option and allowing no retaliation against men. The Prophet ﷺ called both of them back, asked them to abide by the injunction from Allah, and set aside his first directive. One report of the occasion, given at the revelation of this pair of verses, names the woman as the daughter of Muḥammad ibn Salamah and says her husband, spelled Ibn al-Rabi there, slapped her because she refused to sleep with him, so that she came to the Prophet ﷺ seeking retaliation and Allah prohibited it.

### The inner reading

More was given to the men because the whole burden rides on them, theirs being the perfection of strength and the eminence of aspiration, and burdens come measured to strength or to aspiration. The folk of resoluteness are given resolutions in their measure. And in the matter of obedience itself a limit stands: her obedience in the body belongs to the husband, but love and inclination of the heart toward him belong to God's giving. He should not burden her with what God has not provided for her to give, for hearts are in the power of God, who causes love in them toward whom He will and hate toward whom He will. And when it is said "if they then obey you, do not seek a way against them", the warning reaches the past as well: do not forget her loyalty of the past because of a single incident of antipathy in the present, for perhaps the situation will become amicable again. Allah has not burdened man with what he cannot bear, so let him not burden women with what they cannot bear of affection.

### In short

- Men are caretakers by function, not by worth: headship in a family is as necessary as headship in any system, and it is bound by the sharīʿah, consultation and kindness.
- The precedence rests on a grace of creation no one earned and on maintenance men alone carry, and the twofold inheritance share circles back to women.
- The good wife guards herself and the house in the unseen, carried by Allah's help, and the birds of the air, the fish of the sea, the angels and the beasts pray for her.
- Correction climbs a ladder of three: counsel, the bed apart, a discipline that leaves no mark, and the face is never touched.
- When she returns, all means of annoyance are forbidden, for the Most High, All-Great is her protector.
- Love of the heart is God's to give, not the husband's to demand, and past loyalty is not erased by one present fault.

35.text:
When the ladder of the house runs out: "If you anticipate a split between them, appoint a mediator from his family and another from hers. If they desire reconciliation, Allah will restore harmony between them. Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware". The previous verse kept the correction inside the couple. This one keeps the fallout inside the family.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If you anticipate a split between them"** is said to the community around the couple. The genitive construction shiqāq baynihimā, a breach between the two, covers the long-drawn feud, whether the woman is temperamentally obstinate or the man unjustly oppressive. One thing is certain: it will not stay within four walls. Supporters of each party go about maligning the others, tempers rise, and the disagreement of two individuals becomes a confrontation between two families.

**"appoint a mediator from his family and another from hers"** names two arbiters, a ḥakam from each side. The pair of verses was revealed, one report relates, over the daughter of Muḥammad ibn Salamah, whose husband, spelled Ibn al-Rabi in that report, had slapped her when she refused to sleep with him, and who came to the Prophet ﷺ seeking retaliation until Allah prohibited it. The word itself fixes the qualification: the capability to decide the dispute, found in a person both knowledgeable and trustworthy. In the ordinary course the judge, when estrangement occurs, refers the couple to a trusted person who examines the case to stop the wrongs between them. If the matter continues or worsens, he sends a trustworthy person from her family and one from his to determine whether parting or staying is best.
