**"If they desire reconciliation, Allah will restore harmony between them"** carries the whole theology of the verse. If both arbitrators genuinely wish for peace, there will be unseen help from Allah, and through their efforts He creates love and harmony in the couple's hearts. Where rapport is not restored, it may be that one of the arbitrators lacks perfect sincerity in pursuing peace. Allah gives preference to staying together.

**"Surely Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware"** warns the arbitrators as much as the spouses. No injustice or crookedness from them will go unnoticed, for they appear before the One who knows all and is aware of the unseen in every heart.

### What the arbitrators may do

The Qur'an does not determine their rights, and the fuqahā', the scholars of fiqh, worked them out. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, in a report collected by Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr, that Allah commands a righteous man from the husband's side and one from the wife's side, and their task is to discover which of the spouses carries the wrong. A husband at fault is kept back from his wife and pays some restitution. A wife at fault stays with her husband, who pays nothing. Whatever the arbitrators decide, to keep the marriage intact or to dissolve it, is upheld. Should they decide it stays and one spouse dissents while the other consents, then at death the consenting one inherits, and the dissenting one does not.

An incident from before ʿAlī, narrated by ʿUbādah as-Salmānī in the Sunan of al-Baihaqī, sets the boundary. A man and a woman came to ʿAlī with groups of people on both sides, and he asked them to appoint an arbitrator from each family. To the two he said: do you know your responsibility? If you both agree to keep the husband and wife together and make peace, do it, and if you conclude matters cannot be set right and both concur that separation is the expedient course, do it. The woman accepted, leaving the decision to the arbitrators by Divine law whether it met her wishes or went against them. The husband said he would never accept separation, but authorized the arbitrators to impose whatever financial penalty they wished so his wife would return to him in peace. ʿAlī refused: he must authorize them exactly as she had done. From this, some mujtahid Imams deduced that the arbitrators have an inherent authority to divorce, while Imam Abū Ḥanīfah and Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, as the Rūḥ al-Maʿānī relates, took the opposite position: had the power been inherent, ʿAlī would have had no need to obtain the parties' authorization, and the very seeking of their agreement proves the arbitrators hold no such power. They become authorized only when the husband and wife delegate the authority, and then if both agree on divorce, divorce is effected, and if they decide release under khulʿ, the khulʿ takes effect and binds the parties.

Shaykh Abū ʿUmar ibn ʿAbdul-Barr summarized the agreed position: when the two arbitrators disagree, the opinion dissolving the marriage is not adopted, and their decision to keep the couple together is binding even if the spouses did not appoint them as agents. On separation the scholars differ, and the majority holds that it is binding all the same.

### Beyond the married couple

Muslim jurists apply the two arbitrators beyond marriage, profitably and especially where the parties are related, for a court decision is a short-term solution that leaves the germs of hatred in hearts, reappearing later in unpleasant forms. ʿUmar promulgated an order for his judges: "Send disputes between relatives back to them so that they make peace with the help of each other, as a court decision breeds heart burnings and hostility." The reason covers non-relatives too, and the jurists hold it appropriate for officials and judges, before hearing cases formally, to seek a conciliation between the disputing parties, as al-Tarablusī's Muʿīn al-ḥukkām and Ibn al-Shahnah's Lisān al-ḥukkām bear out. The two verses together present a comprehensive system of family life. Disputes are resolved in the house, method after method. When that fails, officials or kinsfolk settle them through two arbitrators, so the dispute leaves the house but not the family. Only then does the court investigate and decide justly, and a world that practised this would be spared the local dissensions that swell into tribal, racial, national and even international feuds.

### In short

- Two arbiters, one from each family, knowledgeable and trustworthy, take the feud before the families are pulled into it.
- Their ordinary task is peace, and their authority to part the couple exists only by the spouses' delegation, as ʿAlī's insistence on full authorization from both proved.
- Sincere desire for reconciliation draws unseen help from Allah, and its absence usually means an arbitrator's sincerity failed.
- The same arbitration serves relatives and strangers, for court victories breed hatreds, and ʿUmar ordered his judges to try peace first.
- The All-Knowing, All-Aware watches the arbiters as closely as the spouses.

36.text:
The great roster of rights, opened by the greatest right of all: "Worship Allah ˹alone˺ and associate none with Him. And be kind to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, near and distant neighbours, close friends, ˹needy˺ travellers, and those ˹bondspeople˺ in your possession. Surely Allah does not like whoever is arrogant, boastful—". One sentence holds the whole of Islamic social teaching: eight classes of people, and the one disposition that withholds from all eight.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Worship Allah ˹alone˺ and associate none with Him"** commands worship of Him with no partner joined to it, for He alone is the Creator and Sustainer, sending favours and bounties on His creation in every situation. To Muʿādh the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do you know what Allah's right on His servants is?" Muʿādh replied that Allah and His Messenger know better. He said: "That they should worship Him and should not worship any others with Him." Then he said: "Do you know what the right of the servants on Allah is if they do this? That He should not punish them."

**"And be kind to parents"** comes immediately after the worship of Allah. The word is iḥsān, doing beautiful good, far more comprehensive than mere fulfilment of rights. It includes spending to support the parents as needed, serving them physically when required, not talking in a voice too sharp or loud, saying nothing that breaks their heart, and treating their friends and well-wishers in a way that pleases them. Even where the parents fell short in their own duty to the children, the children may not take that as an excuse for ill-treatment.

**"relatives"** covers kind treatment of relatives after the parents, males and females. For the poor, a gift is ṣadaqah. For a relative, it is ṣadaqah and ṣilah together, charity and the keeping of the tie.

**"orphans"** names those who lost the caretakers who would spend on them, so they are to be treated with kindness and compassion.

**"the poor"**, al-masākīn, who have various needs and cannot find what sustains them, so they are to be helped in a sufficient manner that ends their inadequacy. The matter of the destitute is elaborated where the shares of ṣadaqah are set out (9:60).

**"near and distant neighbours"** names the two kinds of the Arabic al-jār, the neighbour. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah said that Ibn ʿAbbās read the near neighbour as the one who is also a relative, and the distant neighbour as the one who is not, with Qatādah, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, Zayd ibn Aslam, Ad-Daḥḥāk, Maymūn ibn Mihrān, Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah saying similarly. Mujāhid was also reported to read the distant neighbour as the companion during travel. Generally the near neighbour is the one next to the house and the distant one lives at some remove, and some read the near as the Muslim neighbour and the distant as the non-Muslim. The words of the Qur'an lend themselves to all of these, and it is agreed that every neighbour, whatever the distance, kinship or faith, holds the essential right of help and care to the best of one's ability, while an extra right gives its holder precedence.

**"close friends"**, the companion at your side, is the person sitting next to one in a meeting or a journey, and by extension everyone who works beside a person in some job or vocation, in industry or wage-earning or office work, as the Rūḥ al-Maʿānī notes.

**"˹needy˺ travellers"**, the son of the road, is the wayfarer who, having no relative or friend at hand, becomes a guest. Muslim or non-Muslim, his right of good treatment is obligatory as much as possible and convenient.

**"those ˹bondspeople˺ in your possession"** is an order of kindness to the owned, because they are weak, being held as captives by others, and by analogy and by the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ the same rules cover servants and employees.

**"Surely Allah does not like whoever is arrogant, boastful—"** closes the roster with the disposition that empties it: the one who thinks himself better than others, thinks high of himself while insignificant to Allah and hated by people.

### Why the worship of Allah opens the roster

The opening of the rights roster with the exhortation to worship Allah alone carries many wise considerations, and the basic one is fear. A person neglectful of Allah's right can hardly be expected to remain particular about anyone else's. He will find an excuse to satisfy his immediate circle, to keep his prestige in society, or to escape the law of the government. What forces a person to honour human rights, watched or unwatched, is the fear of Allah and the sense of responsibility before Him, and that taqwā is achieved through nothing but tawḥīd, the firm belief in the Oneness of Allah to the total exclusion of everything else. Muʿādh ibn Jabal said that of the ten things the Prophet ﷺ asked him to hold to, the first was to not associate anyone with Allah even if he were killed or burnt alive, and the second was to not disobey or hurt his parents even if they asked him to leave his children and family, in the Musnad of Aḥmad.

### The parents after tawḥīd

All blessings are really from Allah, yet in worldly means the favours closest after His are those from the parents. They are the fountain-head of one's being, and they carry a child through every stage of trial from birth to youth. This is why the command to worship Allah is supplemented with the parents' rights across the Qur'an: "Give thanks to Me and to your parents" (31:14), and "Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be dutiful to your parents" (17:23), and the covenant of the Children of Israel to worship none but Allah and do good to parents (2:83). The rewards are countless. In al-Bukhārī and Muslim: one who wishes his earnings and life increased by Allah's blessing should fulfil the rights of his relatives. In at-Tirmidhī: Allah's pleasure rests in the father's pleasure, and His displeasure in the father's displeasure. Al-Baihaqī reports in the Shuʿab al-ʾĪmān that when an obedient son looks at his parents with love and regard, every glance brings him the reward of an accepted Ḥajj, and by another narration that Allah forgives most sins, but the one who disobeys and hurts his parents is condemned to unforeseen troubles right here in this world, long before the reckoning of the Hereafter.

### Relatives and the verse recited every Friday

The relative's right goes beyond the general command. The verse still recited in the khuṭbah during Friday prayers all over the world reads: "Allah commands you to do justice and be good to all and to fulfil the rights of the relatives" (16:90). That includes serving relatives to the best of one's ability and keeping in touch with them. Recalling the orphans and the needy under the general head of relatives hints that helping orphaned children and the helpless should be felt as necessary as helping one's own kin.

### The neighbour's right

Jibrīl kept reminding the Prophet ﷺ of the neighbour's right, until he thought he was going to give him a share of the inheritance, as ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar narrated in a hadith the two Ṣaḥīḥs carry. Imam Aḥmad recorded the like from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, in a report Abu Dāwūd and at-Tirmidhī also carry, which at-Tirmidhī called fair though odd through its route. The degrees of the right were set out by the Prophet ﷺ himself: neighbours hold one, two or three rights by rank. A non-Muslim neighbour with no kinship holds one. A neighbour who is also a Muslim holds two. A neighbour who is a Muslim and a relative holds all three. From ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ comes the ranking: the best companions in Allah's sight are the best to their friends, and the best neighbours are the best to their neighbours, carried by at-Tirmidhī. And the Musnad of Aḥmad carries the rule that no neighbour may eat his fill while the next door goes hungry.

The weight of the wronged neighbour is heavier in the scale. Al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad narrated that the Prophet ﷺ asked his Companions what they said of adultery, and they said it was forbidden until the Day of Resurrection. He said that for a man to commit adultery with his neighbour's wife is worse than committing it with ten women. Asked the like about theft, he said that stealing from a neighbour is worse than stealing from ten homes, and only Aḥmad recorded this hadith. The two Ṣaḥīḥs carry the companion report from Ibn Masʿūd, who asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ what the greatest sin was. He said: "To make a rival for Allah while He alone created you." He said: "Then?" He said: "To kill your offspring for fear that he might share your food with you." He said: "Then?" He said: "To commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." On the practical side, ʿĀʾishah asked the Messenger of Allah which of her two neighbours should receive her gift, and he said: "The one whose door is closest to you", in a narration al-Bukhārī carries.

### The companion, the wayfarer, the owned

The companion by one's side, even for a single meeting or ride, holds a right made as obligatory as the regular neighbour's. Its lowest degree is to cause no pain by word or deed: nothing that hurts, embarrasses, annoys or troubles. Not a puff of cigarette smoke blown toward a face. Not things chewed spat at someone's side. Not a style of sitting that leaves the other person no room. If people followed this, the common disputes between passengers on trains, especially in overcrowded countries, would end, for each person's right is about enough space to seat one person, and no more.

To the wayfarer belongs honour as a guest. Honouring a guest for three days is the guest's right, and what is bestowed after the third day counts as charity from the host. One reading of the companion at your side even includes one's wife at home, with kindness to her commanded in the same breath.

For those in one's possession the instruction turns tender. In the illness before his death, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ kept advising his ummah about the prayer, the prayer, and those slaves whom the hands possess, repeating it until his tongue was still. From al-Miqdam ibn Maʿdykarib: what you feed yourself is ṣadaqah for you, what you feed your children is ṣadaqah, what you feed your wife is ṣadaqah, and what you feed your servant is ṣadaqah, carried by an-Nasāʾī with an authentic chain. Ibn ʿAmr said to a caretaker who had not yet fed his slaves to go and feed them, for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had said: "It is enough sin for someone to prevent whomever he is responsible for from getting their food", as Muslim records. Abū Hurayrah narrated that the slave has the right to food, clothing, and work only within what he can bear, which Muslim also carries. And in al-Bukhārī's wording: when a servant brings a meal, let him sit and share it, or at least receive a mouthful or two of it, for he prepared it. For hired servants and employees the same rules run by analogy. There is to be no niggardliness or delay in the due salary and meals, and no burdening beyond ability.

### The arrogance that withholds

The verse's last sentence is the unifying complement of the whole roster. Whoever falls short in the rights of these eight kinds must be none other than the arrogant and the proud, whose sense of superiority is offensively heightened and who love lording over others to exact esteem. Mujāhid said the proud one is the arrogant, and the boastful one boasts of what he has while giving no thanks to Allah, boasting before people of a bounty he is actually ungrateful for. Ibn Jarīr recorded from ʿAbdullāh ibn Wāqid Abū Rajāʾ al-Harawī that the mean are also proud and boasting, and that he who is undutiful to parents is also arrogant, deprived, reciting "dutiful to my mother, and made me not arrogant, deprived" (19:32). A man asked the Prophet ﷺ for advice and was told: avoid lengthening the dress below the ankles, for that practice is from arrogance, and Allah does not like arrogance. Ibn Masʿūd narrated the two-sided warning: faith the weight of a mustard seed keeps a heart out of the Fire, and arrogance the weight of a mustard seed keeps a heart out of Paradise. Asked about people who like good clothes and good shoes, he said: "Allah is beautiful, He likes beauty. Arrogance is wanton disregard of the other person's right and the holding of people in contempt." May Allah keep all Muslims safe from it.

### The inner reading

The verse begins with tawḥīd, root of the sciences and secret of the recognitions, the religion's basis and the Muslim's foundation, the partition between enemy and friend. Obedience without tawḥīd carries no value or weight, and its outcome is darkness and captivity. Disobedience along with tawḥīd yields familiarity and brightness. Tawḥīd is twofold: to say that God is one, and to be single for Him. Saying one is the submitter's tawḥīd, which drives away the devil, washes away sin and opens the heart. Being one is the recognizer's tawḥīd, which cuts away attachments, washes away the creatures and brings forth the realities, effacing the customs of human nature and burning the veil of mortality so that the breeze of familiarity blows and the friend gazes upon the Friend. Shaykh al-Islām Anṣārī said:

> The tawḥīd of the Muslims amounts to three words: affirmation of attributes without excess, negation of similarity without declaring ineffectuality, and going forward according to the outwardness without mixing.

Its reality is to acknowledge God's own explanation and what Muṣṭafā stated plainly about Him, surrendering to it without likenesses and without interpretation, for God comes into knowledge but not imagination. His are the creation and the command, and blessed is God, the Lord of the Worlds (7:54). Whoever is held back from this transmitted tawḥīd stays in the great associationism, far from forgiveness. The other tawḥīd belongs to the recognizers and the sincerely truthful. Water and clay cannot do this work, nor can tongue and heart serve as its place. With what tongue shall the tawḥīd-voicer speak it, when his state is itself a tongue? The unity of the One remains unvoiced, for every voicing is a denial, and every description a deviation. The Pir of the Ṭarīqah prayed:

> O God, the recognizer knows You through Your light and cannot express the radiance of finding. The tawḥīd-voicer recognizes You through the light of proximity and burns in the fire of love without turning away from joy.

That tawḥīd arrives amid heedlessness, unasked, and busies the servant with itself. Lit by the contemplation of the Near, the servant reaps beginningless love and forfeits the two worlds, saying: if seeing You brings loss to the spirit, I will buy the spirit's loss with the spirit.

### In short

- The worship of Allah alone opens the roster because the fear of Him is the only enforcer of rights that works watched or unwatched.
- The parents stand first after Allah, and iḥsān to them is a comprehensive beauty of word, service and support, repaid in lengthened earnings, accepted-Ḥajj glances and forgiveness.
- The neighbour's right was pressed by Jibrīl until inheritance seemed next, and its betrayal weighs ten times the ordinary wrong.
- Every companion at the side, every wayfarer, and every bondsman, servant and employee holds a right of kindness, food, clothing and fit work, with the deathbed advice still repeating it.
- The withholding disposition is arrogance, and a mustard seed of it keeps a person out of Paradise, for arrogance is contempt of people and disregard of their rights.
- Within, tawḥīd is both the saying that God is one and the being one for Him, and the recognizer loses the two worlds in exchange for the Friend's gaze.

37.text:
The portrait of the withholding disposition, now in full colour: "those who are stingy, promote stinginess among people, and withhold Allah's bounties. We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment". The previous verse ended by naming the arrogant and the boastful. This one shows what they hoard and how they recruit.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who are stingy"** describes those who refuse to spend their money on what Allah ordered: kindness to parents and compassion to relatives, orphans, the poor, the relative who is also a neighbour, the companion during travel, the needy wayfarer, the slaves and servants. They do not give Allah's right from their wealth. The word bukhl, niggardliness, is generally used for shortcoming in financial rights, but the background of the revelation gives it its general sense, covering close-fistedness in money and in knowledge both.

**"promote stinginess among people"** adds the negative extreme: through word and deed they persuade others to take up the habit. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Zayd said the verse was revealed about a group of Jews who used to mix with certain men of the Helpers and advise them not to spend their wealth, saying they feared poverty for them. Most exegetes said the verse came about the Jews who concealed the description of Muḥammad ﷺ written in their Scriptures, and al-Kalbī said the like, while one report names Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, and Mujāhid read the three verses together as revealed about the Jews. The general meaning includes all of it, for the miserly conduct with knowledge is as real as the miserly conduct with money.

**"and withhold Allah's bounties"** means the miser covers the favours Allah blessed him with and does not spread them, so their effect does not appear on him, in his food, his clothes or what he gives. Kufr means to cover something, and so the miser is described by the term kāfir regarding the favours granted him, ungrateful for them, as the Qur'an says of man that he is ungrateful to his Lord and bears witness to it by his manners and conduct (100:6-7), and violent in the love of wealth (100:8). A hadith states: "When Allah grants a servant a favour, He likes that its effect appears on him." Some of the Salaf held the whole of this reading.

**"We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment"** is the threatened end, disgraceful torment for the arrogance and the hiding both.

### The disease and its company

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked: "What disease is more serious than being stingy?" And he said: "Beware of being stingy, for it destroyed those who were before you, as it encouraged them to cut their relations and they did, and it encouraged them to commit sin and they did." Every morning two angels descend, one saying, "O Allah, bless him who spends in the way of good", and the other, "O Allah, send destruction on the wealth of the miser", in a report al-Bukhārī and Muslim carry from Abū Hurairah. From Sayyidah Asmāʾ comes the command: "Give, and do not calculate, for Allah will then calculate in your case. Do not withhold, for Allah will then withhold in your case, and give whatever you can." Abū Hurairah narrates that the generous sit near Allah, near Paradise and near people, while the miser keeps his distance from Allah, from Paradise and from people and sits near the Fire. The generous ignoramus, he adds, is dearer to Allah than a devotee grown miserly. Abū Saʿīd narrates the pair that cannot combine in a true believer: miserliness and bad morals.

### The inner reading

Read inwardly, the passage turns the two verses into one scale of hiddenness. Shirk has an open face and a hidden one. Openly it is belief in objects of worship other than God, what the masters call iʿtiqād of a maʿbūdin siwāhi. Hiddenly it is the glance that slides toward any existing thing besides Him, the mulāḥaẓa of a mawjūdin siwāhi. Under the hidden face gather the fine disguises of showing off and guile, the secret lairs of pride, performance staged for created eyes, the craving of their praise and the wilting under their censure. All of it is concealed idolatry. No atom, splinter or particle belongs to any but Him with power to originate anything. And iḥsān follows degrees of association: the parents' rights come first because they are the kin who raised a person to maturity, and when companionship has become sound with the near kindred, the poor, the needy and the orphans, a person is raised up from that to become worthy of His companionship. Among the neighbours are the two angels, who must not be annoyed with disobedience, and whose right observed in acts of kindness is what they are given to record.

### In short

- The stingy withhold both money and knowledge, and recruit others to the habit, as the Jews of Madinah withheld the description of the Prophet ﷺ and counselled the Helpers against spending.
- The miser is a coverer of favours, which is the literal sense of kufr, and the effect of Allah's favour never shows on him.
- The destruction stingy conduct brought on earlier peoples is held up as the disease more serious than any other.
- Read inwardly, the hidden shirk of showing off and pride stands behind the open hoarding, and kindness begun at home rises toward the companionship of God.

38.text:
The second face of the arrogant spender: "Likewise for those who spend their wealth to show off and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. And whoever takes Satan as an associate—what an evil associate they have". Not the miser, but his twin, who gives everything for the eye of the onlooker. The verse repeats the fate of verse 37's ending for them, for they are of the conceited and boastful the verse before (4:36) had already named.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Likewise for those who spend their wealth to show off"** announces the same humiliating punishment for them. They spend only when wishing to show off before people, to gain the reputation of generosity and not for the Face of Allah. One reading of the first audience names the Jewish leaders who gave so people would say they followed the practice of Abraham, and the hypocrites and the Meccans are named in the same breath.

**"and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day"** adds their creed to the charge. With no faith in Allah or in resurrection, the question of spending for His pleasure and the reward of the life to come simply does not arise.

**"whoever takes Satan as an associate"** names the prompter. It was Shayṭān who lured them into the evil act instead of performing the good deed as it should be performed, encouraging and exciting them by making the evil appear good. The end of it all will be no different from the end of their comrade.

### The minor shirk of the eye

A good deed aimed at drawing applause is not acceptable in the sight of Allah, and in hadith it is declared shirk, the associating of others with Allah's divinity. Allah Almighty says: "I am absolutely free of any need to have partners. Whoever does a good deed and associates in it someone else with Me, I leave him with this deed of his." Shaddād ibn Aws heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "Whoever performed ṣalāh to show off, committed shirk. Whoever fasted to show off, committed shirk. And whoever gave in charity to show off, committed shirk." Maḥmūd ibn Labīd narrates: "What fills me with grave apprehensions about you is the minor shirk." The Companions asked what that was, and he said: riyāʿ, doing a good deed just to show off. A narration of al-Baihaqī adds the settlement of the Day of Doom, when Allah will say to those who did good for applause: "Go to those you wanted to see you doing good deeds in the mortal world, and find out for yourself if they have the reward for your deeds." A hadith tells of the first three persons on whom the Fire will feed: a scholar, a fighter and a spender who showed off with their actions. In the report of the two angels that descends every morning, the one praying for the spender and the other for the miser's ruin is carried from Abū Hurairah. The wealthy will say he did not leave any area Allah likes to be spent on but spent on it, and Allah will answer: "You lie. You only did that so that it would be said, 'He is generous.' And it was said." The reward was collected in the life, and nothing else is owed.

### The she-camel

In the camel flock, the fakhūr is the she-camel with blocked teats, so that milk gathers in the udder beyond her real state. The buyer reads the swelling as her plenty, and is deceived. So too the one whose eye rests on himself and his present standing: his claim is false, and God does not love him. Conceit is the eye turned on oneself, and showing off the eye turned on others, and hidden idolatry brands them both, for God loves not the associaters. Their immediate punishment is that they stand outside the company of those whom He loves, and that alone is tribulation enough.

### In short

- Spending for the eye of people is the twin of hoarding, and its reward is paid out in full in this world.
- Riyāʿ is the minor shirk, and the ṣalāh, the fast and the charity done for show all fall under it.
- On the Day of Doom the show-offs are sent to collect their wage from those they impressed.
- The fakhūr she-camel, swollen with withheld milk, is the image of the one full of false claims.

39.text:
The question that closes the trap: "What harm could have come to them if they had believed in Allah and the Last Day and donated from what Allah has provided for them? And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of them". What, in fact, would it have cost them?

### Phrase by phrase

**"What harm could have come to them"** is the interrogative of disavowal: there is no harm in it at all. Nothing about believing in Allah, going on the righteous path and replacing showing off with sincerity is tough, difficult or frightening. Taking to these does not hurt, harm or inconvenience anyone. The harm lies in what they follow instead.

**"if they had believed in Allah and the Last Day and donated from what Allah has provided for them"** holds the two acts. Belief and spending, the two things the misers withheld and the show-offs counterfeited, are as easy as they come, and had they done them they would have received everything that is good, attaining glorious honour in this world and the hereafter.

**"And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of them"** reaches the intentions, good or evil. He knows who deserves success, and grants success and guidance, and who deserves expulsion from His great mercy, which is to fail in both lives.

### The nothing they were guarding

The verse exposes the arithmetic. The kāfir, as the earlier verse established, is a coverer, for kufr means covering, and what these people covered was the favour of the One who provided for them, as the Salaf read in the hadith that when Allah grants a favour He likes its effect to appear. Man stands witness against himself by his manners and conduct, ungrateful to his Lord (100:6-7) and violent in the love of wealth (100:8). Nothing prompts the turn away from God but a lack of commitment and respect, and the certain outcome of that disobedience is nothing but disaster in the Akhirah. Had they held the belief and made the donation, the loss would have been nothing, and the gain would have been the doubled reward the next verse holds out.

### In short

- Belief and spending cost nothing and inconvenience no one, and the question hangs the refusal on nothing but pride.
- What they guarded was not theirs, and covering the Giver's favour is the literal sense of kufr.
- The verse's close rests on Allah's perfect knowledge of intentions, the successful and the failed alike.

40.text:
The justice that makes the wish for dust comprehensible: "Indeed, Allah never wrongs ˹anyone˺—even by an atom's weight. And if it is a good deed, He will multiply it many times over and will give a great reward out of His grace". After the hoarders and the show-offs, the scale itself is described.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah never wrongs ˹anyone˺—even by an atom's weight"** states that on the Day of Resurrection no servant receives injustice from Him, not the weight of a mustard seed nor a speck of dust. The wrongdoer transgresses a limit ordained for him, but the creation is His creation and the kingdom His kingdom. Wrongdoing cannot enter the description of what He decrees.

**"And if it is a good deed, He will multiply it many times over"** gives the scale of increase. With Allah the least measure is one good deed recorded as ten, and the multiplication runs up to seven hundred times and beyond. He is first with His bounty for His servants, before any of them has deserved anything.

**"and will give a great reward out of His grace"** refers, in the reading of Abū Hurayrah, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and Ad-Daḥḥāk, the great reward means Paradise itself.

### The balances of the Book

The verse stands with the whole company of the reckoning. "We shall set up balances of justice" (21:47), Luqman's counsel to his son that a mustard seed's weight, though it hide in rock or heavens or earth, is brought forth by Allah (31:16), and the Day mankind walks in scattered groups to be shown its deeds, where a speck of dust's worth of good or evil is seen (99:6-8). The two Ṣaḥīḥs recorded the long intercession hadith narrated by Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī. In it Allah says: "Go back, and take out of the Fire everyone in whose heart you find the weight of a mustard seed of faith", and in another narration: "Whoever had the least, least, least speck of faith, take him out of the Fire", and many people are taken out. Abū Saʿīd closed the telling with the invitation to read, if one wills, the verse of Allah wronging not even the weight of a speck of dust.

### The least of the disbeliever's ease

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr commented on the doubling that the disbeliever's punishment is eased on the Day of Resurrection, yet the Fire never releases him. His evidence is the authentic hadith of al-ʿAbbās, who asked whether the Prophet's ﷺ uncle Abū Ṭālib, who used to protect and support him, had been of any benefit to him. The answer came: "Yes. He is in a shallow area in Hell-fire, and were it not for me, he would have been in the deepest depths of the Fire." The lessening applies to Abū Ṭālib alone, not to the rest of the disbelievers. Supporting this, the Musnad of Abu Dāwūd at-Tayālisī carries from Anas the word of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

> Allah does not wrong the faithful even concerning one good action, for he will be rewarded for it by provision in this life and awarded for it in the Hereafter. As for the disbeliever, he will be provided provision in this life for his good action, and on the Day of Resurrection he will not have any good deed.

### The million and the two million

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded Abū ʿUthmān an-Nahdī's pursuit of this report. No one, he said, had kept Abū Hurayrah's company longer than he. One year the older man went on Ḥajj before him, and at al-Baṣrah he found people claiming Abū Hurayrah narrated that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, "Allah rewards the good deed with a million deeds." He protested that he had never once heard it from him. Setting out to meet Abū Hurayrah, he learned he had left for another Ḥajj, and followed him there to ask. In Ibn Abī Ḥātim's second chain, Abū ʿUthmān put the Baṣrah claim to Abū Hurayrah's face, and the answer came back sworn: by Allah, what he heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was a reward of two million deeds for a single good one. He then recited: "But little is the enjoyment of the life of this world as compared to the Hereafter" (9:38). In truth Allah is al-Karīm, the most-noble and most-generous. He magnifies the blessing past all count and human measure. As for the dharrah of the verse, rendered here as particle, some commentators say it names the smallest of red ants, which the Arabs cited as the very type of the light and the little.

### In short

- No soul is wronged by so much as a speck, and the balances, the mustard seed and the scattered groups all carry the same guarantee.
- A speck of faith pulls a person out of the Fire, and the least of the disbeliever's easing, like Abū Ṭālib's shallow place, is exceptional, not a general hope.
- The faithful are repaid twice, here and hereafter, while the disbeliever's good is paid out in this life only.
- The good deed starts at tenfold, rises through seven hundred to the two million Abū Hurayrah swore to, and ends in Paradise, for the Giver is al-Karīm.

41.text:
The scene of the witnesses: "So how will it be when We bring a witness from every faith-community and bring you ˹O Prophet˺ as a witness against yours". The question is addressed to imagination: picture it, and then measure what your disobedience will feel like.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So how will it be"** invites visualization of the gravity of the Last Day's site. How shall the predicament of the disbelievers be once every community's witness is brought forward?

**"when We bring a witness from every faith-community"** means the prophets, each testifying that he delivered the message to his people, as the Qur'an says: "The earth will shine with the light of its Lord, and the Book will be placed open, and the Prophets and the witnesses will be brought forward" (39:69), and "the Day when We shall raise up from every nation a witness against them from amongst themselves" (16:89).

**"and bring you ˹O Prophet˺ as a witness against yours"** sets Muḥammad ﷺ, the last of the prophets, as witness over his community. In the Divine Court he declares that these people saw open signs and miracles, yet belied and rejected them. They refused to believe in the Divinity and his prophethood. The admonition lands first on the disbelievers of the tribe of Quraysh. It is also said the witness is in favour of his community, vouching for its reliability and uprightness, for that community is itself scheduled to testify for the other prophets against nations denying ever receiving a message.

### The recital and the tears

ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd is the narrator, in al-Bukhārī's record, of the recital. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked him to recite to him, and he marvelled: recite it to you, when it was revealed to you? The Prophet ﷺ said yes, for he liked to hear it from other people. So he recited Surat an-Nisāʾ until he reached this verse. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Stop now", and Ibn Masʿūd found his eyes tearful. Allāma al-Qastalanī writes that the verse set the whole Akhirah before his eyes, and his community with it, short on good deeds, and that is why the tears started flowing.

Some commentators hold the "yours" of the verse to be the disbelievers and hypocrites present during the age of prophethood, and others the entire community right through the Day of Doom, since, as hadith narrations indicate, the deeds of his community are continuously presented before him. Either way, the prophets of past communities appear as witnesses over their communities, and the Prophet ﷺ testifies over his own. No prophet comes after him to witness over a community of his, or the Qur'an would have mentioned him. Read from this angle, the verse is a proof of the finality of prophethood as well.

### The company of the verses

The whole run of reports around this passage stands behind the Day it describes. The balances of justice are set (21:47), Luqman's mustard seed is brought from rock or heavens or earth (31:16), and the scattered groups are shown their deeds (99:6-8). The earth shines and the witnesses come forward (39:69). Man sees what his hands have sent forth (78:40), the associaters plead innocence (6:23), and the little enjoyment of this world is weighed against the Hereafter (9:38). The intercession hadith of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī stands in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, with al-ʿAbbās's question about Abū Ṭālib beside it. Anas speaks in the Musnad of at-Tayālisī, and Abū Hurayrah's two-million reward was traced by Abū ʿUthmān through the Ḥajj and the people of al-Baṣrah, in the records of Ibn Abī Ḥātim. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr's readings with Ad-Daḥḥāk join them, all gathering around the ummah's standing before its witness.

### In short

- Every prophet is brought forward as a witness over his own community, and Muḥammad ﷺ over his, which is a proof that no prophet follows him.
- He wept when Ibn Masʿūd recited this verse to him, seeing his community short on good deeds.
- The community he witnesses against also stands as witness for the other prophets against their deniers.
- The Day gathers every balance and every record the Book has named, from the mustard seed to the scattered groups.

42.text:
The wish of the cornered: "On that Day, those who denied ˹Allah˺ and disobeyed the Messenger will wish they were reduced to dust. And they will never be able to hide anything from Allah". The verse before showed the witness. This one shows what the witnessed feel.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who denied ˹Allah˺ and disobeyed the Messenger"** are the disbelievers of the gathering place, the same who rejected the ordinary man devoid of outward splendour. It never struck them that God might choose him to carry His message.

**"will wish they were reduced to dust"** gives the shape of the wish. They will want the earth to open and swallow them, or to level itself with them so that they become dust with the beasts, because of the horror of the gathering place and the disgrace, dishonour and humiliation they suffer. This is like the Day man will see the deeds his hands have sent forth (78:40), and like the disbeliever's cry "O would that I were dust!" On the plains of Resurrection they will see the animals turned into dust after exchanging the retribution of each other's excesses, and they too will pine for an end like that, wishing to have become all dust.

**"And they will never be able to hide anything from Allah"** means they will admit everything they did and hide none of it. Their own hands and feet confess, the prophets testify, and everything is present in the Books of Deeds.

### The sealed mouths

The apparent puzzle of the Qur'an was put to Ibn ʿAbbās: at one place the Holy Qur'an says they shall not conceal anything from Allah (4:42), and at another they say "By Allah, our Lord, we were not those who joined others in worship with Allah" (6:23). His answer, in the record ʿAbdur-Razzāq carries from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, unfolds in stages. When the disbelievers see that none but true Muslims are admitted to Paradise, and that Allah forgives the sins, no matter how big, except shirk, they will lie, hoping for salvation. Then Allah seals their mouths, and the hands and feet speak out what their owners used to do, frustrating every plan of concealment, and at that they confess everything. The whole apparatus of the Day surrounds them. The balances of justice are set (21:47), and Luqman's mustard seed comes forth from rock or heavens or earth (31:16). The scattered groups are shown their deeds (99:6-8), the earth shines and the witnesses come forward (39:69), a witness stands raised from every nation (16:89), and the little enjoyment of this world is weighed against the Hereafter (9:38). Around it stand the records of the passage: the intercession of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Anas in the Musnad of at-Tayālisī, the two-million reward that Abū Hurayrah confirmed to Abū ʿUthmān across the Ḥajj from al-Baṣrah in Ibn Abī Ḥātim's record. Al-ʿAbbās asked after Abū Ṭālib, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr with Ad-Daḥḥāk read the great reward as Paradise.

Read inwardly, the day closes on them with its own sequence. Remorse comes, and does not benefit them. They bite their fingertips, and the anguish does not subside. Ignominy is wound about them like a veil. Then they are carried off to the homesteads of tribulation and adversity. Since the Messenger ﷺ is the witness against his community as well as their intercessor, he bears witness only to what can be the object of his intercession, and what remains outside it is the part the disbelievers keep for themselves: the record of their speech, actions and thoughts, showing that their rejection of truth came not from ignorance but from pride, and that the acceptance of reality looked to them like setting their own greatness at naught.

### In short

- The terror of the gathering turns the denial into a wish to be dust with the beasts.
- Nothing can be hidden: mouths are sealed, limbs speak, prophets testify, and the Books of Deeds stand open.
- The associaters' false oath of innocence is answered by the confession of their own bodies, and that resolves the puzzle the questioner brought to Ibn ʿAbbās.
- The tears of the witness, the intercession, and the mustard seed of faith all stand on one side of the balance. The proud stand on the other.

43.text:
The verse of the two purities: "O believers! Do not approach prayer while intoxicated until you are aware of what you say, nor in a state of ˹full˺ impurity—unless you merely pass through ˹the mosque˺—until you have bathed. But if you are ill, on a journey, or have relieved yourselves, or been intimate with your wives and cannot find water, then purify yourselves with clean earth, wiping your faces and hands. And Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving". Before wine was forbidden outright, the prayer was fenced off from it, and the fence is where the verse begins.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do not approach prayer while intoxicated until you are aware of what you say"** forbids the drunk from approaching the ṣalāh, for in that state one does not know the meaning of what one says. The drunk makes obvious mistakes in the recitation and cannot be humble in the prayer. It is the best description of intoxication itself: not knowing what one is saying.

**"nor in a state of ˹full˺ impurity—unless you merely pass through ˹the mosque˺—until you have bathed"** forbids the junūb, the one in major impurity from intercourse or ejaculation, from entering the masjid except as a passer-by, until the full bath, the ghusl, is taken. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the record of Ibn Abī Ḥātim, read it as: do not enter the masjid when junub unless just passing by, in which case pass through without sitting down. The same is reported from a wide company: ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, Anas, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, Mujāhid, Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, Ibn Shihāb, Qatādah and many others.

**"But if you are ill, on a journey, or have relieved yourselves, or been intimate with your wives and cannot find water"** opens the concession. The illness is one feared to be aggravated by water. The journey is known regardless of length. Relieving oneself is the minor impurity, which breaks the wudu, and the touching, "Lāmastum" women, was recited Lamastum and Lāmastum both, referring to intercourse in the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās, with Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, Qatādah, ash-Shaʿbī, Ṭāwūs, al-Ḥasan, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and ʿAlī saying similarly, as the Qur'an uses the word where it halves the dower of the untouched divorcee (2:237) and cancels her ʿiddah entirely (33:49). Another reading, that of Ibn ʿUmar and Imam al-Shāfī, takes the touching as the touch of the hand, extending to other parts of the skin.

**"then purify yourselves with clean earth, wiping your faces and hands"** is the tayammum, a substitute for the ablution rather than a cleaning of the same parts, so the wiping of face and hands with one strike on the earth is sufficient, as the consensus concurs. Linguistically tayammum is to intend, as the Arabs say, may Allah direct His care at you, and clean earth means dust.

**"And Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving"** makes the concession itself an act of pardon, allowing tayammum and the prayer after it when there is no water, to make things easy.

### The slow closing of the wine

This verse was revealed before alcohol was completely prohibited. Drinking was an old addiction in Arabia, a national habit and pastime involving everyone but a few naturally right-minded souls who felt a God-given distaste for it all along. One such was the Prophet ﷺ himself, who never touched liquor even before prophethood. Habit, any habit, is hard to leave, and none grips harder than drinking, to which farewell means a welcome to death. Had it been declared unlawful all at once, obedience would have been extremely hard. So the shift came gradually: first warnings of its evil effects, then this verse, which only kept the drunk away from the ṣalāh at its times, teaching that ṣalāh is fard and must rise to be offered as due. Many blessed souls made a spot decision to abandon the habit for good, and others began thinking seriously about its evils. Finally the verse of Sūrat al-Māʾidah came with the absolute command: "Intoxicants, gambling, al-Anṣāb and al-Azlam are an abomination of Shayṭān's handiwork, so avoid that in order that you may be successful" (5:90), to "So, will you not then abstain?" (5:91), and ʿUmar said: "We abstain, we abstain."

The stages show in ʿUmar himself. When the verse of the question in Sūrat al-Baqarah came, "They ask you about alcoholic drink and gambling" (2:219), the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited it to ʿUmar, who said: "O Allah, explain the ruling about al-Khamr for us in a plain manner." When this verse came down, the Prophet ﷺ recited it to him, and he still said the same. After that they would not drink close to the time of prayer. In another narration, when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would have someone proclaim at prayer time: "Let not any drunk approach the prayer", in the wording collected by Abu Dāwūd.

### The two occasions

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded the reports of the incident. Four verses, Saʿd said, were revealed concerning him. A certain Anṣārī had made food and called Muhājir and Anṣār guests to it, and they ate and drank to intoxication, and began boasting of their status. One man then took a camel's bone and gashed Saʿd's nose, leaving its scar, in the days before al-Khamr was prohibited. Muslim recorded this hadith, and the collectors of the Sunan with the exception of Ibn Mājah.

The second occasion belongs to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf made some food and served alcohol with it, and when the company grew intoxicated and the time for prayer came, someone was asked to lead. The leader recited Sūrat al-Kāfirūn (109) wrongly, saying "I do not worship that which you worship, but we worship that which you worship", the error of a tongue the drink had loosened. Then the verse came down. At-Tirmidhī collected this narration and called it ḥasan, ṣaḥīḥ. The same lesson reaches even the sleeper: if one feels sleepy while praying, let him sleep a while so that he knows the meaning of what he says, for he might want to ask forgiveness and instead curse himself, in the report of Aḥmad, al-Bukhārī and an-Nasāʾī from Anas, and of Qurṭubī's ruling that the prayer is not correct when sleepiness takes away control of speech.

### The mosque and the passer-by

The prohibition of the masjid for the junūb carried an exception with a history. Ibn Jarīr recorded that Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥabīb commented that some men of the Anṣār, whose doors literally opened into the masjid, would be junub without water, and their only way to reach water was to pass through the masjid, so Allah sent down the exception. Supporting this stands al-Bukhārī's report of the Messenger's ﷺ command: "Close all the small doors in this masjid, except that of Abū Bakr." It was given at the end of his life, knowing that Abū Bakr would be the khalīfah after him and would need to enter the masjid often to manage the Muslims' affairs. Some compilers of the Sunan recorded that only ʿAlī's door should remain open, but that reading is an error, and the Ṣaḥīḥ's version carries the weight. In his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim recorded that ʿĀʾishah said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me, 'Bring me the garment from the masjid.' I said, 'I am having my period.' He said, 'Your period is not in your hand.'" Muslim. He also collected a similar narration from Abū Hurayrah, indicating that a woman in menses or post-natal bleeding may still cross the masjid, and Allah knows best.

The exception itself divides the jurists. According to most commentators, including the Ḥanafī jurists, "traversing a way" refers to travel when water is unavailable, so the junūb cannot approach ṣalāh without the bath, unless he is on a journey without water, in which case he prays after tayammum. Imam al-Shāfī interprets it in a totally different manner: going near the ṣalāh means entering the mosque, prohibited for the junūb except as a passer-by heading elsewhere. The Ḥanafī jurists do not accept this, holding that the verse has no relevance to entering the mosque, as the background of its revelation shows, and that the prohibition of entering the mosque in impurity rests on other grounds.

### The dry ablution

ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn's report, carried in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, tells of Allah's Messenger noticing a person sitting apart from the people, not praying with them, and asking what prevented him. He replied that he was junub and there was no water. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Perform tayammum with clean earth, and that will be sufficient for you." Muslim recorded from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman the three preferences: the lines arranged in rows like the rows of the angels, the whole earth made a masjid, and its dust made clean when there is no water. Had any other substance replaced dust for tayammum, the Prophet ﷺ would have mentioned it. Aḥmad and the collectors of the Sunan, except Ibn Mājah, recorded from Abū Dharr: "Clean earth is pure for the Muslim, even if he does not find water for ten years. When he finds water, let him use it for his skin, for this is better", which at-Tirmidhī called ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.

The wiping was shown by the Prophet's ﷺ own hand. The demonstration comes through ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Abzā, in Aḥmad's record. A man came to ʿUmar junub and without water, and was told not to pray. ʿAmmār then spoke up with the memory: the two of them had once been on expedition together, grown junub, and found no water. ʿUmar had left the prayer, while ʿAmmār had rolled himself in the sand and prayed. When they told the Prophet ﷺ, he said to ʿAmmār that it would have been sufficient for him, and demonstrated: one stroke of the hand on the earth, a breath into it, and the wiping of face and hands. The Muslim ummah, above all other nations, was favoured with this allowance, and the shariah of Islam took the dry ablution as its symbol of purification where water fails. In the verses before this, the stress lay on acting with taqwā in mutual dealings, and the rules of worship here instil the fear of Allah that keeps those dealings right. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh narrated the five things given to no prophet before: victory by fright covering a month's distance, the earth as a place of prayer and an object of purification, the spoils made lawful, the right of intercession, and the sending to all mankind rather than one nation.

The occasion of the concession itself is ʿĀʾishah's. On one of the Messenger's ﷺ journeys, at al-Bayḍāʾ or Dhāt al-Jaysh, ʿĀʾishah's necklace was broken and lost. He stayed to search for it with all the people, in a place with no water. The people complained to Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq, who found his daughter detaining the Messenger and the people where there was no water, and admonished her and struck her flank with his hand while the Prophet ﷺ slept with his head on her thigh, which alone kept her from moving. At dawn the Prophet ﷺ rose with no water, and Allah revealed the verses of tayammum, and they all performed it. Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr said: "O the family of Abū Bakr, this is not the first blessing of yours." Then her camel was moved and the necklace was found beneath it.

Prayer, the whole verse insists, is too sacred to be performed in a deficient manner. It does not mean the mere repetition of words and motions with accuracy, for the mind must submit along with the body, and consciousness must inhere in the prayer. The purpose of ablution is to create the spirit of purity, and tayammum maintains that spirit when the usual means fail. Islamic law has granted exceptional relaxations under exceptional conditions, the three named being sickness, travel and the want of water.

### The inner reading

Drunkenness comes in many kinds, and its drunkards differ. The grape has its wine, and heedlessness has its own. This world's love intoxicates one sort, and the soul's frivolity and self-love another. Hardest of all is the last. Self-love grounds idol-worship, seeds estrangement, curtains ill fortune and roots every darkness. A person martyred a hundred times a day in the path of God is still an idol-worshipper if he sees himself in the midst. The wine-drunk who fears and shakes in dread of punishment may end in the fire, if He does not forgive him, and He may indeed forgive him, for He says: "Surely God forgives the sins altogether" (39:53). But the one drunk with the soul's arrogance, pride and self-worship, is in peril: his basis is loss, his deeds damage him.

As for the greater ablution, if the religion were based on reasoning, it would be incumbent after urination rather than after ejaculation, for urine is impure and semen pure. That the rule runs the other way teaches a lesson: religion stands on transmission, not on rational derivation, on the Book, not on reasoning, and on servanthood, not on self-exertion. The origin of the major ablution runs back to Adam. When he came from Paradise into this world and fell into companionship with Eve, Gabriel came and said: "O Adam, make a full ablution, for God commands you to do so." Adam obeyed and asked the reward, and Gabriel answered that for every hair on his body a year's reward would be written, and for every drop of water passing over his body God would create an angel to obey and worship until the Day of Resurrection, giving its reward to him, and that this was for him, the faithful, and his children until the resurrection. From Adam's era down to the Master of the World's, every prophetic shariah has carried this ablution for defilement as mandatory. One of the imams even said that the Trust Adam lifted up, concerning which God said "And man carried it" (33:72), was the trust of this ablution.

The closing names are the tenderest part of the verse. Sins are passed over, the defects of those who apologize are curtained, and the offenses of the sighers concealed. Before the commands and prohibitions came, He had taken away whatever was done up to that day. No one's sin can overcome His solicitude, and He says that whoever straightens his aim finds Him there in the road. The ruined life and the destitute days He buys. The poor man wounded by offenses, helpless before an adversary, finds in Him a Patron. The one weeping in shame, head bowed, burnt from having lost his heart, finds in Him the happiness of his spirit. And His word runs out to every place:

> Be wherever you will in the land and you will be near My remembrance.

### In short

- Wine was closed slowly: first the prayer was fenced from it, then the total prohibition of Sūrat al-Māʾidah answered ʿUmar's repeated plea.
- The two occasions were Saʿd's wounded nose and ʿAlī's misrecited Sūrat al-Kāfirūn, both at tables where drink was still lawful.
- The junūb keeps out of the masjid, passing through only, and the doors of the Anṣār that opened into it explain the exception.
- Sickness, travel and the want of water open the tayammum, one strike of clean earth for face and hands, a favour given to this ummah alone, and revealed over ʿĀʾishah's lost necklace.
- Prayer demands the mind's presence, and even sleep sends the worshipper back to bed.
- Read inwardly, the worst drunkenness is self-love, the ablution's logic is transmitted not reasoned, and the verse ends with the solicitude of the Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving.

44.text:
The turn from the family law to the old adversary: "Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who were given a portion of the Scriptures yet trade it for misguidance and wish to see you deviate from the ˹Right˺ Path". Those entrusted with revelation are shown buying the opposite of it, and wishing the same trade for the believers.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who were given a portion of the Scriptures"** are the Jews, who were given knowledge of the Torah. Receiving a portion of the Book, they could read its words, but could not mould their actions to them, defeating the Scripture's real purpose. They remained its bearers as far as words go, while in practice they adopted the ways of worldly communities, and then had the audacity to justify those ways by misquoting the Book itself.

**"yet trade it for misguidance"** means they purchased the wrong path instead of guidance, ignoring what Allah sent down to His Messenger ﷺ and the knowledge inherited from earlier prophets about his description, all for a small amount of the delights of this life. One report names the buyers as al-Yasaʿ and Rāfiʿ, the sons of Harmalah, two rabbis who pressed ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy and his friends to take up their religion and choose Judaism over Islam. Ibn Zayd's reading holds the like.

**"and wish to see you deviate from the ˹Right˺ Path"** makes the wish explicit: they would like the believers to disbelieve in what was sent down to them and abandon the guidance and beneficial knowledge they hold, straying from the path of truth and becoming like them.

### The exchange rate of error

The commands of God, in a community of declining bearers, become the subject of futile hair-splitting. In the name of theology, philosophies are concocted, and the divine book is altered to give wrongdoing a religious licence. God's words are detached from their context and read through the readers' own assumptions. That is the purchase this verse prices: the words of the divine Book recited to solicit blessings without any attempt to understand their meaning or apply them to life. The full story of their twisted courtesy toward the Prophet ﷺ, the Rā’inā affair, waits at the verse of the displaced words. There the warning already given to the believers, "Say not Rā’inā but say Unẓurnā" (2:104), is recalled against them. There too their little faith is weighed in the scale of "so little is that which they believe" (2:88).

### In short

- The people of the portion bought error with guidance, trading eternal gain for the small delights of this life.
- Their wish is company in ruin: that the believers leave the right path and become like them.
- Reading without practising, and justifying worldliness by misquoting the Book, is the essence of the trade.

45.text:
The answer to the wish: "Allah knows best who your enemies are! And Allah is sufficient as a Guardian, and He is sufficient as a Helper". The adversaries wish deviation on the believers, and the believers are told who actually holds them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah knows best who your enemies are"** means His knowledge of your enemies outruns yours, and He informs you of them so that you avoid them, from among the hypocrites and the Jews alike.

**"And Allah is sufficient as a Guardian"** names Him the wali, the Protector and Preserver of those who seek refuge with Him, keeping them safe from the enemies' harm.

**"and He is sufficient as a Helper"** completes the pair: a Sufficient Supporter for those who seek His help, defending them against the plotting.

### The two sufficiencies

The verse is placed between the enemy's wish and the enemy's methods, and it settles both. The wish to see the believers deviate from the path comes to nothing against a Guardian who cannot be circumvented, and the word-twisting that follows in the next verse, the mockery and the curse hidden in courtesy, cannot injure a community whose Helper is Allah. The path the enemies want abandoned is the very path the Guardian preserves. What the believers face here is the same adversary already warned of in the instruction not to say Rā’inā (2:104), and the same little faith measured by "so little is that which they believe" (2:88). Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Zayd read the enemies named here as the Jews and the hypocrites together, and the reading of the passage holds them both.

### In short

- Allah knows the enemies better than they can be known, and names them so they can be avoided.
- Guardianship and help are both sufficient in Him, and the enemies' wish runs against His protection.
- The verse stands as a wall between the adversary's wish and the community it was wished against.

46.text:
The methods itemized: "Some Jews take words out of context and say, 'We listen and we disobey,' 'Hear! May you never hear,' and 'Râ'ina!' [Herd us!]—playing with words and discrediting the faith. Had they said ˹courteously˺, 'We hear and obey,' 'Listen to us,' and 'Unẓurna,' [Tend to us!] it would have been better for them and more proper. Allah has condemned them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except for a few". Three phrases said with a twist, and three phrases they might have said instead.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Some Jews take words out of context"** means the meanings of Allah's words are deliberately and falsely altered, explained in a manner other than what Allah meant. One report names Mālik ibn al-Sayf and his friends, who changed the traits and description of Muḥammad ﷺ after they had been expounded in the Torah, wrenching the words from the contexts in which they were placed.

**"'We listen and we disobey'"** was said to the Prophet's face and behind his back, meaning: your words are heard, O Muḥammad, but your command is not obeyed, as Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd explained. The phrase exhibits their disbelief, stubbornness and disregard for Allah's Book after understanding it, sin and punishment fully in view.

**"'Hear! May you never hear'"** was their mocking jest: hear our words, and may you never hear anything, as Ad-Daḥḥāk reported from Ibn ʿAbbās.

**"'Râ'ina!' [Herd us!]"** is the sharpest of the twists of the tongue. They pretend to say "Hear us", which is what rā’inā means in Arabic, while in their own language it is an insult, and their true aim is to curse the Prophet ﷺ. The believers had already been told: "Say not Rā’inā but say Unẓurnā" (2:104), and the word is forbidden as an address to him for that reason. With tongues twisted and the religion slandered, they say one thing to his face and mean another.

**"Had they said ˹courteously˺, 'We hear and obey,' 'Listen to us,' and 'Unẓurna'"** sets the three courteous forms opposite the three twisted ones. They would have been better for them and more proper, worthier and more correct behaviour in the Prophet's presence.

**"so they do not believe except for a few"** closes with the curse. Their hearts are cast away from the path of righteousness, and no beneficial part of faith enters them, as with "so little is that which they believe" (2:88). The few who believed are ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions, who accepted Islam.

### The blessing they barred

They practised a deception and did not realize the way they were deceived in turn: given the book, they were deprived of the blessing of understanding, so that they distorted the words and persisted in unbelief. They acted shamelessly toward the Messenger ﷺ and refused him respect, and were punished with doubt concerning his affair. Their shamelessness raised a barrier between them and the blessing of his companionship and the bounties of serving him. Had they hastened instead to reject the envy they felt, and honoured him with veneration for his state, blessing would have met them on his road, and happiness in both abodes. But what had already been determined distanced them. They were kept back by fate from the carpet of service, and there is no manoeuvring that can help those held back by the divine decrees.

### In short

- Words were wrenched from their contexts, and three phrases of obedience were said as twists of mockery.
- Rā’inā wore the mask of courtesy while carrying a curse in another tongue, and the believers were already warned off it.
- The courteous forms stood ready, and would have carried blessing in both abodes.
- The curse removed them from mercy, and only a few, like ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, believed.
- Envy of the Messenger barred them from the blessing of his service, and no manoeuvring beats the decree that holds a person back.

47.text:
The call across the divide, with its warning attached: "O you who were given the Book! Believe in what We have revealed—confirming your own Scriptures—before We wipe out ˹your˺ faces, turning them backwards, or We condemn the defiant as We did to the Sabbath-breakers. And Allah's command is always executed". The People of the Book are commanded to believe in what was sent down to Muḥammad ﷺ, the Glorious Book conforming to the good news they already hold, and warned of a disfigurement should they refuse.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Believe in what We have revealed—confirming your own Scriptures"** addresses the Jews and Christians with knowledge of the Torah and the Gospel, asking them to recognize the Book that confirms what they possess of Allah's divine Oneness and the traits and description of Muḥammad ﷺ.

**"before We wipe out ˹your˺ faces, turning them backwards"** carries the threat. Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the effacing refers to blindness, and the turning means their faces are put on their backs, so that they walk backwards with their eyes behind them, as Qatādah and ʿĀṭiyah al-ʿAwfī said. The expression admits two probabilities: the features eliminated and the whole face turned around, or the face flattened like the nape of the neck, devoid of all features. It is a parable Allah set for ignoring the truth and turning from the plain path onto the paths of misguidance. Its likeness is the iron collars reaching to the chins, and the barrier before them and behind them (36:8-9).

**"or We condemn the defiant as We did to the Sabbath-breakers"** refers to those who breached the sanctity of the Sabbath by deceit in order to do more work, whom Allah changed into apes and swine, as the explanation of Sūrat al-Aʿrāf sets out. Whether the disfigurement and the transformation would come before the Day of Doom was argued by commentators, some holding it never came to pass because some of the Jews entered the Faith. On that view the verse suggests probability rather than certainty. Given their crime they deserve the punishment, and should He spare them, that is His mercy.

**"And Allah's command is always executed"** means that when He commands something, no one can dispute or resist His command.

### Kaʿb al-Aḥbār's Islam

The story reached the next generation through ʿĪsā ibn al-Mughīrah, in Ibn Jarīr's record, from a session with Ibrāhīm where Kaʿb's conversion came up. Kaʿb al-Aḥbār turned Muslim in ʿUmar's reign. Journeying to Jerusalem, he passed through al-Madīnah, where ʿUmar urged him to embrace Islam. His answer was to point to his Book: does it not say "The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Tawrāh..." (62:5), and he was among the entrusted? ʿUmar left him alone. On to Ḥimṣ in Syria he went, and there heard a resident reciting this very verse in sadness, and the fear of the threat struck him: I believe, O Lord, I have embraced Islam, O Lord. From there he returned to his family in Yemen and brought them back with him, all Muslims. After the verse was revealed, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions embraced Islam, and it was said the threat had been conditional, lifting when some of them believed. The passage then turns to the one sin that blocks every door of pardon, shirk, as the next verse states, and to the intercession reserved for the major sinners of the ummah, as hadith al-Bazzār relates in the Rūḥ al-Maʿānī's gathering of the reports.

### In short

- The People of the Book are called to confirm the revelation that matches their own, before a disfigurement they cannot answer.
- The effaced faces and the backward walk are a parable of choosing misguidance, and the Sabbath-breakers' transformation stands behind the warning.
- The threat reads as probability, and Kaʿb al-Aḥbār's Islam in Syria, and Ibn Salām's with his companions, show the mercy side of it.
- Allah's command, when it goes out, is executed without dispute.

48.text:
The one unforgivable, and everything else negotiable: "Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating others with Him ˹in worship˺, but forgives anything else of whoever He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has indeed committed a grave sin". The verse before called the People of the Book to faith. This one explains why some will not be forgiven: their kufr and their joining of partners.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah does not forgive associating others with Him"** means He does not forgive a servant who meets Him while associating partners with Him, if he dies in that state.

**"but forgives anything else of whoever He wills"** covers all other sins, to whom He wills of His servants, forgiving whom He wills by admitting him to Paradise without punishment, and punishing whom He wills of the believers for their sins and then admitting them.

**"has indeed committed a grave sin"** is the invention of a tremendous wrong, as Luqmān said to his son: joining others in worship with Allah is a great wrong indeed (31:13).

### The abundance behind the exception

Abū Dharr is the narrator of the two reports that open the verse's abundance. The first, whose chain Only Aḥmad carries, gives the divine word:

> O My servant, as long as you worship and beg Me, I will forgive you, no matter your shortcomings. O My servant, if you meet Me with the earth's fill of sin, yet you do not associate any partners with Me, I will meet you with its fill of forgiveness.

The second is the exchange Aḥmad recorded, on the servant who dies affirming that none deserves worship but Allah. Such a one enters Paradise, even if he committed adultery and theft. The allowance was pressed three times, and the fourth answer added the word about Abū Dharr's own nose being put in the dust. Abū Dharr departed pulling his izār and repeating it, and ever after told the hadith with that comment, and the two Ṣaḥīḥs carry it. The hadith of al-Bazzār then brings Ibn ʿUmar's report. The Companions used to hold back from begging forgiveness for the major sinners until they heard the Prophet ﷺ recite this verse. He added that his intercession on the Day of Resurrection was reserved for those among his ummah who commit major sins. And in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, Ibn Masʿūd asked which sin is greatest, and the answer came: to make a rival with Allah, while He alone created you.

Behind the verse stands the whole scene of its passage. Kaʿb al-Aḥbār won to Islam in Syria, in ʿUmar's reign at al-Madīnah, on the Jerusalem road, as ʿĪsā ibn al-Mughīrah told it in Ibrāhīm's circle. Ibn Salām and his companions believed after the revelation. With them stand al-ʿAwfī's report from Ibn ʿAbbās on the effaced faces, the Rūḥ al-Maʿānī's gathering, and the warning of Sūrat al-Aʿrāf's transformed Sabbath-breakers.

### What counts as shirk

The verse's articles are the sine qua non of religion: beliefs relating to the Being and Attributes of Allah, and holding the like of them for whatever He created is shirk. It has forms. Shirk in knowledge: believing that some pious person or spiritual master knows everything in the universe all the time, or asking an astrologer or fortune-teller about what is to come, for these belong to the unseen world, Allah's exclusive domain. It also covers taking omens from a pious man's writings, calling someone from a distance in the belief that the call has been received, and keeping a fast dedicated to other than Allah. Shirk in power: taking anyone besides Allah to have the authority to give gain or inflict loss. It includes asking anyone for sustenance or children. Shirk in worship: going down in prostration for anyone, releasing an animal dedicated in someone's name, making a vow or making tawāf of someone's grave or house. It covers bowing to anyone in the manner of the prayer's rukūʿ, slaughtering in someone's name, taking the world's affairs as ruled by the stars, and regarding a month as ill-omened.

### The inner reading

The associationism of the common people is the greater associationism: to say that the tremendous Enactor has an associate, or make Him similar to something of creation, which is to call upon an idol and be held back from the religion of guidance. The right belief holds the Creator pure of spouse, child and partner, free of new arrival and change. His attributes are pure, His artisanry fitting, His speech sweet and His love complete, a God outside imaginations whom no one knows how He is. The lesser associationism is of two sorts: for the faithful it is eye-service and the letting go of self-purification in deeds, which lessens faith, fissures certainty and closes the door of clarity, and for the recognizers it is the paying of regard to deeds and the seeking of deliverance thereby. Muṣṭafā ﷺ said: "I am very frightened of the ancient associationism for my community", and explained it as the mixing of eye-service into the doing of good deeds. Shaddād ibn Aws said he saw God's Messenger weeping over it.

### In short

- Shirk alone is closed to pardon for the one who dies in it, and every other sin is within Allah's will to forgive.
- The earth's fill of sin meets the earth's fill of forgiveness where no partner is joined, and the intercession is reserved for the major sinners of the ummah.
- Shirk wears many dressings, in knowledge, in power and in worship, from fortune-telling to the tawāf of graves.
- The lesser associationism, eye-service in deeds, is what the Prophet ﷺ feared for his community, and what made Shaddād see him weep.

49.text:
Self-certified holiness: "Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who ˹falsely˺ elevate themselves? It is Allah who elevates whoever He wills. And none will be wronged ˹even by the width of˺ the thread of a date stone". A strange lot, attributing sanctity to themselves and then broadcasting it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who ˹falsely˺ elevate themselves?"** was revealed, in the reading of al-Ḥasan and Qatādah, about the Jews and Christians who said: "We are Allah's children and His loved ones", the claim echoed in their appeal to their father's faith (5:18). Ibn Zayd connected it with their claim that Paradise admitted none but a Jew or a Christian (2:111). One report names Buhayr ibn ʿAmr and Marḥab ibn Zayd.

**"It is Allah who elevates whoever He wills"** means the decision belongs to Allah alone, whose knowledge covers the true reality and the secrets of all things, and who purifies whom He will through faith.
