**"none will be wronged even by the width of the thread of a date stone"** means no one's reward is reduced by the least injustice, for the fatīl is the scalish thread in the long slit of the date-stone, as Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid with ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah, among others of the Salaf, said.

### Why self-praise is forbidden

Claiming sanctity for oneself or others is forbidden on three counts. First, the cause of self-praise is mostly pride and arrogance, so what is really forbidden is pride. Second, only Allah knows how a person's end will come, whether in taqwā and purity, so the claim contradicts being God-fearing. Zaynab, daughter of Abi Salamah, is the narrator: the Prophet ﷺ asked her name, she said Barrah, pure from sins, and he said: "Do not claim sanctity for yourselves, for it is Allah alone who knows best who among you is righteous." He then named her Zaynab. Third, the claim plants the false idea that the claimant is nearer to Allah for being faultless, a lie, since no mortal is free of shortcoming. Where these impediments do not exist, a person may speak of a trait as gratitude for Allah's blessing.

### The inner reading

The instruction runs: no self-praise, no welcoming of others' praise, no eye on one's own good deeds, no weight given to one's own travelling, and the considering of oneself lower than everyone low. The group that has stolen reality's ball from the world's creatures never shows itself to itself for the sake of showing, never walks the edge of making claims, and their worthlessness and abasement makes them look like the riffraff in people's eyes. At the threshold of a generous man, the more abased a person makes himself, the more exalted he becomes, and the abasement is not despair of the Friend but testimony of truthfulness. The Pir of the Ṭarīqah prayed:

> O God, I lament at my abasement, for I have seen no one with misery like mine. I wept so many tears in longing that I sowed the seeds of pain with my eyes' water. If my eyes fall upon You once, I will not have seen myself with those eyes. When God's deeming pure reaches someone, its mark is release from the company of the scatter-hearted, as the next verses will show with the prostration before idols, the judgment of Ibn Abī Ḥātim's reports, the trench dug around al-Madīnah, and the alliance struck at Makkah.

### In short

- Sanctity is not self-declared: the Jews and Christians who called themselves Allah's children and loved ones are the verse's first exhibit.
- No soul's reward is trimmed by even the thread of a date stone.
- Self-praise is barred for pride, for the unknowability of one's end, and for the lie it plants in others, and the Prophet ﷺ renamed Barrah to make the point.
- On the inward road, self-regard is the greatest veil, and abasement at the threshold is exaltation.

50.text:
The audit of their forgeries: "See how they fabricate lies against Allah—this alone is a blatant sin". The claim of purity was one lie. Here the whole trade is inventoried.

### Phrase by phrase

**"See how they fabricate lies against Allah"** points at the whole list. They claimed purity for themselves, and claimed to be Allah's children and His loved ones. They said that Paradise belongs to none but a Jew or a Christian (2:111), and that the Fire will not touch them save for numbered days (3:24). And they leaned on the righteous deeds of the fathers before them, though Allah has decreed that those deeds do not help the children, every nation earning only its own reward.

**"this alone is a blatant sin"** means these lies and fabrications are sufficient, in themselves, as a manifest sin, enough to demonstrate their misguidance.

### The day-and-night forgiveness they invented

One of their fabrications was a standing licence: sins committed by day would be forgiven at night, and sins of the night forgiven by day. It was a clear lie told about Allah. Against this stands the verse's own logic, the same that measured the self-praisers by the thread of a date stone: no wrong is done to anyone, and no licence is invented for anyone, and the claim of inherited purity counts for nothing before the record each soul earns. The reports around the passage, from al-Ḥasan and Qatādah's reading to Ibn Zayd's, from the fatīl's measure to Buhayr ibn ʿAmr, from Ibn Abī Ḥātim's records to the trench of al-Madīnah and the alliance of Makkah, all gather against the fabricators, and the state of taqwā they claimed is the one thing their claims cannot produce.

### In short

- Their fabrications included inherited salvation, numbered days in the Fire, and a day-for-night forgiveness scheme.
- The verse counts the inventing itself as a blatant sin, sufficient without addition.
- The thread of a date stone measures what cannot be wronged, and the fathers' deeds do not cover the children.

51.text:
The scene of the great betrayal: "Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who were given a portion of the Scriptures yet believe in idols and false gods and reassure the disbelievers that they are better guided than the believers". Scripture-holders prostrating to idols, and grading the idolaters above the believers.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who were given a portion of the Scriptures"** names the Jews with knowledge of the Torah, one report naming Mālik ibn al-Sayf and some seventy friends.

**"yet believe in idols and false gods"** names al-Jibt and al-Ṭāghūt, two idols of the Quraysh. Jibt was originally the name of an idol, later used for every false god and for sorcery, and in Ethiopian, a magician. ʿUmar said Jibt is magic and Ṭāghūt is Satan. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr and Abū al-ʿĀliyah said Jibt is a magician and Ṭāghūt a soothsayer. Mujāhid said Ṭāghūt is a devil in the shape of a man to whom they refer for judgment, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from Jābir that they are the soothsayers on whom the devils descend. Imam Mālik's reading is the most inclusive: Ṭāghūt is every object worshipped instead of Allah. Al-Qurṭubī preferred it, supported by the Qur'an's command to worship Allah and avoid Ṭāghūt (16:36), and there is no real contradiction among the readings.

**"and reassure the disbelievers that they are better guided than the believers"** exposes their preference of the disbelievers over the Muslims, out of ignorance and disbelief in the Book before them.

### The bargain at Makkah

Ibn ʿAbbās narrates the occasion. After the battle of Uḥud, Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Kaʿb ibn Ashraf, chiefs of the Jews, came with a group to the Quraysh at Makkah, Kaʿb going to stir them to avenge their dead of Badr. The people of Makkah said: you are a people who cheat with false promises, so if you mean it, prostrate to these two idols. And he did, to reassure them. Then Kaʿb proposed that thirty of each side come forward and declare before the Lord of the Kaʿbah their resolve to fight Muḥammad ﷺ together. The Quraysh liked it, and that was the united front against the Muslims. Then Abū Sufyān asked the learned guests to judge between them and Muḥammad, and listed the ancestral credits: slaughtering camels for the ḥajj, offering milk to pilgrims, entertaining guests, keeping kinship ties, making tawāf of the House and performing ʿumrah. The other side was a man who had abandoned the ancestral religion, cut off his own people, and challenged the fathers with a new faith of his own. Kaʿb ibn Ashraf answered: "You are on the right path, and Muḥammad has gone astray." Thereupon Allah revealed these verses, exposing their lying and deceit, as the Rūḥ al-Maʿānī gathers the reports.

Kaʿb himself was a distinguished scholar among the Jews who worshipped none but Allah, yet the ghost of overweening desire overpowered him, and he swallowed the bitter pill of the prostration to achieve his end, showing no courage to part ways on a crucial issue. The Qur'an tells the like of Balʿam ibn Bāʿūr, a scholar with spiritual powers who launched his sinister plans against Mūsā (Moses), achieved nothing against him, and ended accursed and astray (7:175). Book-knowledge alone does not guarantee benefit without action, and action is impossible without abstaining from material greed. The alliance thus struck grew into the battle of al-Aḥzāb, where the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions dug a defensive trench around al-Madīnah. From it Allah saved the Muslims, driving the disbelievers back in their rage with no advantage gained, for He sufficed the believers in the fighting (33:25).

### The inner reading

Each person's Ṭāghūt is the lower self and its whim, the idol hunted among what is other than God. Heed paid to a person, a glance to a reason, a turn to a cause, obedience to a whim: that thing is his jibt and his Ṭāghūt. And whoever is at ease with the caprice of his own soul, remaining bound to what it desires, is a man of idols and a servant of demons, whatever his creed on paper.

### In short

- Jibt and Ṭāghūt are the idols of the Quraysh, and the names stretch to cover sorcery, soothsayers, Satan and every object of worship besides Allah.
- Kaʿb ibn Ashraf and Huyayy ibn Akhtab traded the Torah's judgment for a prostration and a verdict favouring Abū Sufyān's paganism.
- The bargain matured into the confederates' siege and the trench, where Allah sufficed the believers.
- Read inwardly, every soul's Ṭāghūt is its own whim, and whoever obeys it serves idols already.

52.text:
The verdict that ends the file: "It is they who have been condemned by Allah. And whoever is condemned by Allah will have no helper". The curse is pronounced, and the question the verse raises is who else ever stands under it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"It is they who have been condemned by Allah"** pronounces the curse, which means removal far from the mercy of Allah, with extreme debasement and disgrace, in this life and the next. For the Holy Qur'an says of the accursed that wherever they are found, they are to be seized and slain (33:61), and the disgrace of the Akhirah is far too grim to contemplate. In the reading of the passage, the immediate sense includes the humiliation put upon them, the capitation tax among its instruments.

**"And whoever is condemned by Allah will have no helper"** means no protector from His chastisement in this life or the Hereafter, for they sought the help of the idolaters and lured them with their verdict, and gathered the forces of al-Aḥzāb, and Allah drove them back.

### Who incurs the curse

The Prophet's ﷺ warnings reach a long list. He cursed the people of interest, the giver, the receiver, the consumer, the writer and the witness, all equally involved, in the report of Muslim. He said: "Cursed is he who does what the people of Lūṭ used to do", the reference being to the male act. He said Allah sends His curse on the thief who does not stop even at eggs and ropes, for which the hand is cut. He said: "Allah curses the eater of interest and its feeder, the woman who tattoos another and the woman who tattoos herself, and the picture-maker." He said Allah sends His curse on liquor, its consumer and server, its seller and purchaser, its squeezers, handlers, transporters and orderers, all of them. Abu Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah carry it. He said there are six types he had cursed and Allah had cursed them. They are the one who commits excess in the matter of Allah's Book, the one who rises to power by force and then honours whom Allah has disgraced and disgraces whom Allah has honoured, the denier of destiny, the one who takes as lawful what Allah made unlawful, the one of his progeny who rules as lawful what was forbidden, and the one who gives up his way, the sunnah. Al-Baihaqī records it in al-Mudkhal. He said Allah curses the ogler and the ogled at. The look at what is non-maḥram falls under the curse, and the looked-at likewise, where the look was deliberately invited. Abū Hurairah narrates his curse on men who take women's dress and women who take men's dress. ʿĀʾishah reported his curse on the woman who takes to masculine ways, in the report of Abu Dāwūd, and Ibn ʿAbbās his curse on the effeminate among men and the masculinized among women, with the command to expel them from the homes. From al-Bukhārī comes the report Ibn Masʿūd carries, and Abū ad-Dardāʾ the report of the curse's own journey:

The curse itself has rules, and the report of Abū ad-Dardāʾ, carried by Abu Dāwūd, shows its flight. When a servant curses something, the curse rises to the sky and its doors are shut against it. It comes down to the earth, and the earth's doors are shut. It takes a right and a left, finds no access anywhere, and returns to the one cursed. If he deserves it, it falls on him. Otherwise it returns to its pronouncer. The wind showed the same lesson, in the report of Tirmidhī: it swooped away a man's cloak, he cursed it, and the Prophet ﷺ told him not to, for it was under orders from Allah, and whoever curses what does not deserve it gets the curse back on himself. Unless it is known that a person died in a state of kufr, invoking the curse on him is not permissible, even if he was sinful. Ibn ʿĀbidin advised against cursing Yazid on that principle. A confirmed kāfir like Abū Jahl or Abū Lahab, however, may be cursed by name. Cursing without naming anyone is permissible, as in God's curse upon liars and tyrants. And in the terminology of the sharīʿah, the curse on disbelievers means their far removal from mercy, while on Muslims it means their falling from the level of the righteous.

### The inner reading

The companions of al-Jibt and al-Ṭāghūt deserve the curse that expels from the carpet of service, ʿubūdiyya, and veils from witnessing lordship. Read inwardly, then, the curse is the loss of service itself, and no helper can restore the servant who has walked out from under the Real's care to serve his own whim, for the Ṭāghūt he chose has nothing to give.

### In short

- The curse is removal from mercy, disgracing its bearer in both worlds, and no helper stands beside the one Allah has cursed.
- The Prophet's ﷺ curse reached interest in all its parties, the act of the people of Lūṭ, theft, tattoos, pictures, liquor in every role, and the six types al-Baihaqī's al-Mudkhal carries.
- The curse is not a loose word: the undeserving curse returns to its pronouncer, the unknown end bars it, and Abū Jahl and Abū Lahab stand among the confirmed names.
- Inwardly, the curse is expulsion from the carpet of ʿubūdiyya, and the whim that replaced Allah cannot help its server.

53.text:
The question that strips the claim: "Do they have control over shares of the kingdom? If so, they would not have given anyone so much as the speck on a date stone". The Jews projected their community as sacred, destined for deliverance by race alone, and the verse asks what, in fact, they hold.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do they have control over shares of the kingdom?"** is a statement of rebuke in the form of a question, for they have no share in the dominion whatever. What is the basis of the envy, the passage asks? If it is the belief that they are the real inheritors of the kingdom, and that what the Prophet ﷺ was blessed with is theirs, the belief is wrong twice over.

**"they would not have given anyone so much as the speck on a date stone"** exposes the first error. Even if they came to hold a share of the sovereignty, they are not the kind to give anything to anybody, especially not to Muḥammad ﷺ. Not even the naqīr would leave their hands, the speck on a date-stone's back, as Ibn ʿAbbās and the majority of the scholars read the word. The like stands elsewhere in the Qur'an: "Say: if you possessed the treasure of the mercy of my Lord, you would surely withhold it out of fear of spending it" (17:100), for fear that what they have might end, though there is no such possibility. Man is ever stingy, and this only demonstrates their greedy nature.

### Envy of the chosen

The second reason comes with the next verse: the kingdom did not pass from them onto him, and the question becomes why it had to go to him at all, seeing that the House of Abraham had already held the Book and wisdom. The envy of the Jews for the Prophet ﷺ was over the great prophethood entrusted to him, and their envy made them reject him and turn others from the path, his Arabness and his non-Israelite birth being the whole of their grievance. At-Ṭabarānī recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās read "do they envy men" as their claim to be the worthy ones above all other people. Mujāhid's reading of what follows, some who believed and some who rejected, takes the object as the Prophet ﷺ himself. Their rejection by disbelief is the more severe, the further from the truth they stand. The envy is unreasonable either way, and its rule is old: no one may have honour on the basis of race or community. Honour depends on the divine law of justice, and one who fails by his actions will never be honoured, whatever his community.

### In short

- They hold no share of the dominion, and even if they did, their niggardliness would keep the speck of a date-stone back from everyone.
- The envy behind their rejection is of an Arab prophethood, against their claim of being the worthy people.
- Community-based salvation is an invention, and honour follows the divine law of justice, not the bloodline.

54.text:
The ancestry they forgot: "Or do they envy the people for Allah's bounties? Indeed, We have given the descendants of Abraham the Book and wisdom, along with great authority". The kingdom they begrudge has been in the family of prophets all along.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Or do they envy the people for Allah's bounties?"** names their envy of Muḥammad ﷺ and his Companions, for the prophethood, the faith and the establishment in the land, and, in one reading, for the abundance of women given him, they wishing him deprived of such things, saying: were he truly a prophet, he would not be concerned with women.

**"We have given the descendants of Abraham the Book and wisdom"** means prophethood went to the tribes of the Children of Israel, the offspring of Ibrāhīm, with the Books sent down to them, the prophets ruling by the prophetic tradition and Al-Ḥikmah, the wisdom, given with the Scripture. The house of Abraham held the likes of Mūsā (Moses), Dāwūd (David) and Sulaymān (Solomon), and it was honoured with prophethood and al-Islām's way and sovereignty over the Children of Israel. David had 100 legitimate wives by one count, 99 by another, and Solomon 300 wives plus 700 concubines, or a thousand free women and slavegirls by the other count.

**"along with great authority"** is the mighty kingdom, and the envy of it forgets that the kingdom has not come to a stranger. He too comes from the family of prophets who ruled kingdoms before him.

### The rules of envy

ʿAllāmah an-Nawawī, the commentator on Muslim, defines envy, ḥasad, as the desire to see the other person's blessing disappear, and this is forbidden. The Prophet's ﷺ hadith on it runs:

> Do not hate and do not envy and do not turn your backs on each other. Instead, become servants of Allah, as brothers. And it is not lawful for a Muslim that he abandons his brother for more than three days.

Another hadith says: "Beware of envy, for envy eats up good deeds as the fire eats up wood." Zubayr narrates: "Stealthily creeping into you is the disease of earlier peoples, envy, and hatred, which is a shaver. I do not say that it shaves hair, but it does shave the religion off." Envy over worldly excellence or spiritual excellence is forbidden on both counts, for verse 53 pointed at the worldly and this verse's Book and wisdom point at the spiritual.

### The inner reading

The mighty kingdom is read four ways: true knowledge of the King, dominion over the lower self, standing above the secrets of the realm so that nothing is hidden, and the viewing of the secrets of creation from on high. Abū ʿUthmān al-Maghribī said that whoever responds to the Real finds the empire responding to him, so that whatever appears in it is brought to him as news. Ibn al-Barqī, one of the great shaykhs of Egypt, was once ill and refused his medicine, saying that some disaster had happened in the empire, and until he found out what, he would not drink it. Thirteen days passed before word came: the Qarmatians had struck the Sanctuary, slain many and worked great destruction. Shaykh al-Islām Anṣārī set the limit: servanthood cannot bear more than knowing some and not knowing some. God does not show His unseen to anyone except a messenger He approves (72:26-27), and of the unseen He informs no one (3:179). God knows all, and no one else. The Pir of the Ṭarīqah said: "O God, who is like me in becoming worthy for this work? Enough for me is that I have the worth of Your companionship. Tell them to call me nothing but lord, that's a name suited for Your serving boy."

### In short

- The bounty envied is old family property: prophethood, Book and wisdom ran through the house of Abraham before it reached an Arab prophet.
- David's and Solomon's households answer the sneer at the Prophet's marriages, with the counts of the wives given as the reports carry them.
- Envy, defined by an-Nawawī as wishing the blessing away, eats good deeds as fire eats wood and shaves the religion off.
- Read inwardly, the mighty kingdom is knowledge of the King, and its news reaches those who respond to the Real, within the limits God set on the unseen.

55.text:
The split down the family line: "Yet some believed in him while others turned away from him. Hell is sufficient as a torment". The bounty given to the house of Abraham divided its heirs as soon as it arrived.

### Phrase by phrase

**"some believed in him"** refers, in Mujāhid's reading, to Muḥammad ﷺ, and in another to the bounty itself, the prophets, the Books and the kingship, which some of the Children of Israel believed in.

**"while others turned away from him"** means disbelieving it, ignoring it, and barring the people from its path, though the bounty was from them and for them. They disputed with their own prophets, so what of Muḥammad ﷺ, who is not even of the Children of Israel? Their rejection of him is the more severe, and they are further from the truth he brought. One reading names the object of belief as the Scripture of David and Solomon, and the burned ones of the close as Kaʿb and his followers.

**"Hell is sufficient as a torment"** means the Fire is a just punishment for their disbelief, rebellion and defiance of Allah's Books and Messengers. It needs no addition.

### The old pattern

The verse is the family portrait of every prophet's people: some who believed in what was revealed to Abraham and the prophets among his descendants, and some who denied it and turned others away from it, and now do the same with what was revealed to Muḥammad ﷺ. At-Ṭabarānī's record from Ibn ʿAbbās and the whole scene of verses 53 and 54 stand behind the split, the envy an-Nawawī defined, the speck of a date stone withheld, and the Book and wisdom given to the house of Ibrāhīm, with David and Solomon its royal heirs. The believers inherited the path, and the deniers inherited the blaze, the old pattern the hadith records of every prophet's people.

### In short

- The bounty divided its heirs: some believed in the prophets and the Book, and some rejected and barred the path.
- Their own prophets were disputed with before Muḥammad ﷺ, so his rejection is the older habit renewed.
- Hell needs no helper as a torment, being a just punishment for the defiance of Books and Messengers.

56.text:
The anatomy of the punishment: "Surely those who reject Our signs, We will cast them into the Fire. Whenever their skin is burnt completely, We will replace it so they will ˹constantly˺ taste the punishment. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise". After the particular believers and disbelievers, the universal rule of the two ends.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who reject Our signs"** are those who disbelieved in the verses and hindered from the path of the Messengers.

**"We will cast them into the Fire"** names the Fire of Jahannam, which will encompass every part of their bodies, and the torment in it is everlasting.

**"Whenever their skin is burnt completely, We will replace it"** means fresh skins replace the burnt ones, returning the burned to their first state, that the punishment may keep its taste and its severity. Al-Aʿmash gives Ibn ʿUmar's word: at each burning a replacement skin arrives, and it comes white as paper, in a report Ibn Abī Ḥātim collected. Ibn Abī Ḥātim also recorded from al-Ḥasan the daily count: seventy thousand roastings through. Ḥusayn, with Fudayl adding from Hishām, recorded al-Ḥasan's other reading of verse 56: once the Fire has roasted them through and eaten their flesh, the command comes to go back as they were, and they do. Muʿādh explained verse 56's replacement as coming with such speed that the skin is changed a hundred times in one moment.

**"Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise"** means nothing is beyond His power, and He is Wise in His creation and His ruling that burnt skins be exchanged for fresh ones.

### The lightest of them

The scale of the torment is set by its least. The lightest in punishment among the people of the Fire will be the man with two smouldering embers in the soles of his feet. Their heat keeps his brain boiling like a cauldron to the brim, in the report al-Mundhirī carries in his at-Targhīb. Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said the fire will eat them every day seventy thousand times, and when it has eaten them up, they will be commanded: return, and they shall return to be as they were, as al-Baihaqī records, quoted by al-Mazharī.

Read inwardly, the verse alludes to those who deny the signs of the friends of God. He keeps them in a state of insignificance and leaves them to the estrangement of denial. Whenever something of this story appears to their hearts, rejection makes them abandon faith in it and dismiss its people with contempt, and so the punishment repeats.

### In short

- The Fire encompasses every part, and the skins are renewed at each burning so the taste never dulls.
- The replacement is instantaneous by Muʿādh's account, seventy thousand times a day by al-Ḥasan's, and the new skin comes white as paper.
- The lightest punishment boils a brain with two embers in the feet, and the rest rise from there.
- Inwardly, the renewed skin is the repeated denial that punishes the denier of the friends each time the truth appears.

57.text:
The other end of the rule: "As for those who believe and do good, We will admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there for ever and ever. There they will have pure spouses, and We will place them under a vast shade". After the burning skins, the gardens.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who believe and do good"** are the believers in Muḥammad ﷺ, in the Qur'an and in all the Scriptures and messengers, sincerely performing what lies between them and their Lord.

**"We will admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow"** describes the destination of the happy ones, the gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow in all their areas and corners, wherever they desire: rivers of wine, milk, honey and water.

**"to stay there for ever and ever"** means they reside for eternity, not transferred or removed, nor wanting to move.

**"they will have pure spouses"** describes the purified mates: no menstruation, no postnatal bleeding, no filth, no bad manners, no shortcomings. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are purified of filth and foul things, with as-Suddī, ʿĀṭiyah, Abū Ṣāliḥ, an-Nakhaʿī, Ad-Daḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan and ʿAṭāʾ saying similarly. Mujāhid's list adds urine, spit, mucous and pregnancies to the freedoms. According to al-Ḥākim's record from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, the women of Jannah will be pure from menstruation, defecation, urination and nasal mucus, and Mujāhid added freedom from procreation and seminal impurity, the answer to verse 56's renewing burn.

**"We will place them under a vast shade"** means wide, extensive, pure and elegant shade, everlasting, never replaced by any sun. Ibn Jarīr recorded that Abū Hurayrah said that the Prophet ﷺ said: "There is a tree in Paradise, that if a rider travels under its shade for a hundred years, he will not cross it. It is the Tree of Everlasting Life." Abū Hurairah narrates the like with the invitation: read, if you wish, the verse of the shade, ever-extended, ever-stretched. Rabīʿ ibn Anās read it as the Throne's shade, al-ʿarsh, that never declines.

### The shades of this world and the next

Read inwardly, the believers are in shade already: today in the shade of God's care, riʿāya, tomorrow in the shade of His protection, ḥimāya, and His sufficiency, kifāya. They are in the shade of His solicitude, ʿināya, in this world and the next, and the people of this group are of different types: those in the shade of His mercy, those in the shade of His care, those in the shade of His special generosity, those in the shade of His solicitude, and those in the shade of His nearness.

### In short

- The gardens hold rivers of wine, milk, honey and water in every corner, and their stay has no end.
- The purified spouses are free of every impurity the material lists, from menstruation to mucous, and Mujāhid adds freedom from childbearing.
- The vast shade is the Tree of Everlasting Life, a hundred years' ride across, or the shade of the Throne that never declines.
- Inwardly the shade begins now, as care, protection, sufficiency and solicitude, ending in the shade of nearness.

58.text:
A verse revealed inside the Kaʿbah, and large enough to hold a whole theory of the state: "Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners; and when you judge between people, judge with fairness. What a noble commandment from Allah to you! Surely Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing". Two commands, one about what is held in trust, one about how disputes are decided, and both addressed to everyone who holds anything at all.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners"** commands that the trusts be rendered back to those to whom they are due. The addressee is everyone who holds anything in trust, the masses and those in authority alike. The Holy Qur'an deliberately uses the plural, amānāt, and the plural is a hint that a trust is not simply cash or kind left for safe-keeping. The command covers all things one is expected to look after, Allah's rights on His servants, such as praying, zakāh, fasting, penalties for sins and vows, and the rights of the servants on each other, including the cases that are never recorded or documented.

**"and when you judge between people, judge with fairness"** commands justice between people, addressed primarily to those in authority who decide cases, and secondarily to all appointed to arbitrate, since among the common people the practice is to appoint a neutral arbitrator.

**"What a noble commandment from Allah to you!"** praises the whole instruction, the returning of trusts, the judging with justice, and all His complete, perfect and great commandments and laws.

**"Surely Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing"** means He hears the statements and knows the actions, even of the person with no ability to speak, no power or means to protest. That is why His principles are practice-worthy in every country, every age, always, while principles made by human minds stay within the parameters of their environment and must change when circumstances change.

### The key of the Kaʿbah

The verse was revealed in the background of the Kaʿbah's custodial service, an office of great honour even before Islam, with the areas of service distributed over different people. From the days of Jāhiliyyah, the providing of drinking water to pilgrims from the well of Zamzam during Ḥajj, the siqāyah, was entrusted to al-ʿAbbās, the revered uncle of the Prophet ﷺ, and similar services were in the charge of Abū Ṭālib, another uncle. The custodial duty of keeping the keys of the House and opening and closing it on fixed days belonged to ʿUthmān ibn Ṭalḥah al-Ḥajabī.

Before the Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ came with some Companions to enter the Kaʿbah. ʿUthmān ibn Ṭalḥah, then an unbeliever, stopped him rudely. The Prophet ﷺ showed great restraint, tolerated the harsh words, and said: "O ʿUthmān, a day will come when you would perhaps see this key in my hands, when I shall have the power and choice to give it to anyone I choose." ʿUthmān answered that then the Quraysh would be uprooted and disgraced, and the Prophet ﷺ said no, they would be established and very honourable. ʿUthmān's own account continues: the soul-searching convinced him it would happen, and he resolved to embrace Islam then and there, but his people vehemently opposed him, and he could not. At the conquest of Makkah the Prophet ﷺ called for the key, and ʿUthmān presented it. Some narrations say he had climbed over the Baytullāh with the key, and ʿAlī, in deference to the Prophet's order, took it forcibly from his hand.

So the Prophet ﷺ went in and prayed. Coming out, he returned the key, saying: "Here, take it. Now this key will always remain with your family right through the Last Day. Anyone who will take this key from you will be a tyrant." Al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ also instructed him to use whatever money or things came in return for this service in accordance with the rules set by the shariah of Islam. As ʿUthmān walked off delighted with the key, the Prophet ﷺ called him back: "Remember, ʿUthmān, did I not tell you something way back? Has it come to pass, or has it not?" And that was when ʿUthmān recited the Kalimah and entered Islam, as al-Mazharī relates from Ibn Saʿd. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb testified that the Prophet ﷺ came out of the Kaʿbah reciting this very verse, which he had never heard from him before. Ibn Jarīr recorded the report through Ibn Jurayj, that the verse was revealed concerning ʿUthmān ibn Ṭalḥah, and it is popular as the reason for its revelation, though the application is general, which is why Ibn ʿAbbās and Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah said this verse is for the righteous and the wicked alike. At his death, ʿUthmān passed the key to his brother Shayba, and it remained in his descendants' keep.

The returning itself was a judgment, for al-ʿAbbās and ʿAlī had both requested the office of the key, since the water supply and custodial services were already in their charge. The Qur'an directed the Prophet ﷺ, in verse 58 itself, to bypass their request and return the key to none but ʿUthmān, out of regard for the nature of the trust involved. One reading of the judgment places it between ʿUthmān ibn Ṭalḥah and al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd, of the house of al-Muttalib, giving the key back to ʿUthmān and the water to al-ʿAbbās. That the ruler's choice is bound by the command is the first lesson of the scene: the real command is from Allah, and all rulers of the mortal world are carriers of it.

### Trusts of every kind

Ḥasan al-Baṣrī narrated from Samurah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Return the trust to those who entrusted you, and do not betray those who betrayed you." Imam Ahmad and the collectors of the Sunan recorded this hadith. Those who do not implement the command in this life will have it extracted from them on the Day of Resurrection, qiyāmah, for it is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ: "The rights will be rendered back to those to whom they are due, and even the sheep that does not have horns will take revenge from the horned sheep."

Anas said it must have been a rare sermon in which the Prophet ﷺ did not say: "One who does not fulfil trust obligations has no faith, ʾīmān, with him, and one who does not stand by his word of promise has no religion with him", reported by al-Baihaqī in the Shuʿab al-ʾĪmān. And in narrations from Abū Hurairah and Ibn ʿUmar in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, among the signs of hypocrisy stands: give him a trust, amānah, and he will commit a breach, khiyānah.

The key of the Kaʿbah was not a financial asset, and that is precisely the verse's hint. Offices and ranks of government, whatever they may be, are handed over as trusts from Allah, and their holders are trustees. This covers everyone who wields the powers of appointment and dismissal. No office or job may be given to someone undeserving of it in practical expertise or intellectual capability. If the most perfect candidate cannot be found, preference goes to the one superior in capability and trustworthiness from among those available, the best of the lot. The Prophet's ﷺ warning is stark on the appointment of the undeserving. Whoever, charged with a responsibility relating to the general body of Muslims, gives an office away on friendship or connection alone, without weighing capability or merit, draws the curse of Allah on himself. No act of worship he was obligated with, fard, is accepted from him, nor any voluntary offering, nafl, all along until he enters the Fire. In some narrations, entrusting an office to one person while knowing another is more suited and deserving is itself a breach against Allah, His Messenger and all the Muslims. When affairs are put in the charge of the unfit, the instruction recorded in the Kitāb al-ʿIlm of the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī says: wait for the Day of Doom, for that chaos has no solution. The corruption seen in many systems of governance, with offices distributed on connections, recommendations and bribes, is the sad consequence of ignoring this teaching.

The kinds multiply in the hadith. Meetings are a kind of trust, so that reporting what transpired without the participants' permission is not permissible. The consultant is a trustee, bound to give the counsel he judges most beneficial, and if he gives advice he knows is not in the seeker's best interest, he has breached the trust right there. A secret confided becomes an article of trust, and disclosing it without permission is a breach. A trust is not to be doled out to a beggar out of pity, or to a relative or friend to fulfil their rights, for what is held in trust goes to its rightful owner, properly and duly, and to no one else.

### Judge with fairness

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, Zayd ibn Aslam and Shahr ibn Ḥawshab said the judging command came down about those in authority, the judges between people. A hadith states: "Allah is with the judge as long as he does not commit injustice, for when he does, Allah will make him reliant on himself", and a saying goes that one day of justice equals forty years of worship. The just person is loved by Allah and closest to Him, while the unjust is cast far from His mercy and grace, and the first to go under the shade of Allah will be those who hasten to accept truth when it appears, who spend their wealth when asked, and who judge between people as fairly as they would have done for themselves.

The verse says "between people", not between Muslims or between believers. All human beings are equal in the sight of the decider: Muslims or non-Muslims, friends or enemies, same country or another, same colour and language or different. The judge is duty-bound to cast all these connections aside and let the decision follow truth, right and justice. And the one who lacks the ability and power to maintain equity should not become a judge at all, for judging with fairness is itself a trust too heavy for the weak and incapable. When Abū Dharr requested the governorship of some place, the Prophet ﷺ answered:

> O Abū Dharr, you are weak and this is an office of trust, which may, on the Day of Doom, become the cause of disgrace and remorse, except for one who has fulfilled all his trust obligations, fully and duly.

### The state the verse sketches

Four principles emerge from the verse's opening. First, by beginning with "Surely, Allah commands you", the real command and rule are shown to be from Allah, and the supreme authority, the ultimate sovereignty, belongs to none but Him. Second, the offices of government are not the rights of a country's residents to be distributed by the ratio of population, which error has forced fixed quotas into many constitutions, so that a person from another province cannot be appointed no matter how deserving, while the local man may be an evil-doer. Offices are trusts, given only to those capable and deserving of them, whatever their province, though preferring a local appointee is sound where ability and trustworthiness are first verified. Third, man's rule on this earth is legitimate only as a deputy or trusteeship, bound and guided in lawmaking by the principles laid down by Allah, the Absolute Sovereign, given through revelation. Fourth, it is the standing duty of those in authority to judge with equity, without discrimination of race, country of origin, colour, language, even religion and creed.

Trust comes before justice in the verse's order, and the order is necessary. A system guaranteeing equity all over a country is just not possible unless those who hold power first fulfil their trust obligations. That means appointing the best of the lot to every job, with no back doors of friendship, connection, recommendation or bribe. Otherwise gangs of the undeserving entrench themselves, and even a ruler genuinely wishing to usher in an era of justice can do nothing about it, for these officials are the very functionaries through which the government acts. The command structure itself has layers, and verse 59 will spell them out. The direct commands, the rejection of shirk and kufr, the worship of the One and the ṣalāh He made fard, are His word outright. The open field, the mubāḥ, is what the Book and sunnah leave unrestricted, rated neither wājib nor ḥarām, and its rules are entrusted to rulers so that systems run.

### The inner reading

After the servant's faith and recognition, no attribute outranks holding in trust, and after unbelief none is uglier than betrayal. Obedience comes forth from holding in trust, disobedience from betrayal, the basis of corruption, the start of every misfortune, the foundation of disobedience. To hold in trust is the religion's pillar, tawḥīd's perfection, and the mark of prophets and angels. The revealed Book describes Gabriel as the one "brought down by the trustworthy spirit" (26:193), and elsewhere as "obeyed, and also trustworthy" (81:21). The daughter of Shuʿayb said of Mūsā (Moses), God's speaking companion, "hire him, surely the best one to hire is the one strong and trustworthy" (28:26), and the king of Egypt said of Yūsuf (Joseph) the sincerely truthful, "surely today with us you are emplaced, established, trusted" (12:54). The trusts of the Book and the sunnah are three. First, obedience and the religion, which the Lord of the Worlds calls the Trust He offered (33:72). Second, women, held as a trust by men, taken as a trust from God with their private parts made lawful by His word. Third, the property left with someone or the secret told to him: "let him who has been entrusted deliver the trust" (2:283). Deliver the trust back to the one who entrusted you. If a man relates some words, pay regard, for they are his trust. And sitting together is a trust: company must be kept on the condition of holding in trust.

### In short

- The verse was revealed over the key of the Kaʿbah, returned to ʿUthmān ibn Ṭalḥah against the requests of al-ʿAbbās and ʿAlī, and its rule is universal, for the righteous and the wicked alike.
- Every office is a trust, and connection-based appointment draws a curse that no fard or nafl worship lifts.
- Judgment is between people, all people, and the weak, like Abū Dharr, are warned off the bench before they are disgraced by it.
- The verse sketches the state: Allah's sovereignty, offices as trusts, rule as deputyship, justice without discrimination.
- Read inwardly, trustworthiness ranks right after faith, the attribute of Gabriel, Mūsā and Yūsuf, and its three trusts are the religion, the wife, and whatever is left or told to you.

59.text:
The community's chain of command: "O believers! Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. Should you disagree on anything, then refer it to Allah and His Messenger, if you ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and the Last Day. This is the best and fairest resolution" (4:59). Verse 58 addressed the holders of power. Verse 59 addresses everyone under it, and one reading of its first addressees names the new believers around ʿUthmān ibn Ṭalḥah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Obey Allah and obey the Messenger"** opens the chain. Command and obedience really belong to Allah alone, though the practical form of obeying His command divides into parts. The direct commands, the rejection of shirk and kufr, the worship of Allah the One, the belief in the Last Day and in Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ as the Last and True Messenger, and the practice of ṣalāh, fasting, ḥajj and zakāh as obligations, come as the Qur'an's own word. The commands needing explanation are obeyed through the Messenger's ﷺ own explanations, which are also a kind of revelation. His word and deed become the interpretation of the divine command, and obedience to him walks beside obedience to Allah throughout the Qur'an. The Prophet's ﷺ word in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, ties the pair to its root: whoever obeys him obeys Allah, and whoever disobeys him disobeys Allah.

**"and those in authority among you"** names the ulu'l-amr. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, among the earliest readers of the Book, applied the term to the scholars and jurists, the ʿulamāʾ and fuqahāʾ, the succeeding deputies of the Prophet ﷺ, in whose hands the proper regulation of religion lies. Another group, including Abū Hurairah's report, takes it to the officials and rulers holding the reins of government. At-Tafsīr al-Mazharī, with the leading commentary that transmits it, includes both categories, for the system of command is inevitably connected with these two.

**"Should you disagree on anything, then refer it to Allah and His Messenger"** commands that whatever areas the people dispute about, major or minor, go back to the Book of Allah and the sunnah of His Messenger, as Mujāhid and several others among the Salaf said, for "in whatsoever you differ, the decision thereof is with Allah" (42:10). Whatever the Book and sunnah testify to is the plain truth, and what is beyond truth save falsehood.

**"if you ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and the Last Day"** carries the verdict: whoever does not take the Book and sunnah as judge in disputes has no claim on belief in Allah or the Last Day.

**"This is the best and fairest resolution"** was read by as-Suddī and several others as having a better end and destination, and by Mujāhid as carrying a better reward.

### The occasions

Al-Bukhārī recorded, from Ṣadaqah ibn al-Faḍl, that Ibn ʿAbbās named the occasion. The verse was revealed about ʿAbdullāh ibn Ḥudhāfah ibn Qays ibn ʿAdī, whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent on a military expedition. The Group collected it with the exception of Ibn Mājah, and at-Tirmidhī called it ḥasan gharīb. Another narration through the chain of Ibn Jurayj, in the records that include ibn Zakariyyā's Ḥāfiẓ, tells of Khālid ibn al-Walīd sent against an Arab clan with ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir along. A Muslim of the clan came by night to ʿAmmār asking whether staying would benefit him, was told to stay, and so instructed his family. In the morning Khālid found no one but him, imprisoned him and seized his property, and ʿAmmār said: let him go, for he is a Muslim and I have given him amnesty. Khālid objected that ʿAmmār gave protection while he was the leader, and ʿAmmār's answer stood: protection is given from you to others even while you are the leader.

Imam Aḥmad recorded from ʿAlī the story that makes the verse's limit vivid. A troop sent under a man from the Anṣār provoked their commander, who called for wood, lit a fire and said: I command you to enter it. The people almost did, but a young man among them held them back: they had run away from the Fire to Allah's Messenger, so let them not rush until they returned to him, and if he commanded, then they could enter. When they told the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he said: "Had you entered it, you would never have departed from it. Obedience is only in righteousness", in the two Ṣaḥīḥs.

### The limits of obedience

The Muslim is required to hear and obey in what he likes and dislikes, unless commanded to sin, and then there is no hearing or obeying, as Abu Dāwūd recorded from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, a hadith the two Ṣaḥīḥs carry. ʿUbādah ibn aṣ-Ṣāmit told of the pledge given to Allah's Messenger to hear and obey in activity and rest, ease and difficulty, even if deprived of their due shares, and not to dispute the leadership with its rightful people, and the Prophet ﷺ added: "Except when you witness clear kufr about which you have clear proof from Allah." Another hadith from Anas runs: hear and obey, even if an Ethiopian slave with a head like a raisin is set over you as chief, recorded by al-Bukhārī. Umm al-Ḥusayn heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ during the Farewell Ḥajj give the ruling: a slave appointed over you who rules by Allah's Book is to be heard and obeyed, recorded by Muslim, whose other narration adds the mutilated nose. There is no obedience to anyone in disobedience to Allah, and whoever obeys the commander obeys the Messenger, and whoever disobeys the commander disobeys him.

The commands of the third kind, not explicit in Qur'an or hadith, belong to the mujtahid ʿulamāʾ. They delve into the established texts with the precedents and parallels of the problem, arriving at the rule of conduct within the parameters of the sacred imperatives. And where the Qur'an and sunnah leave a matter open, the mubāḥ, the making and enforcing of rules belongs to rulers and their officials, so that systems run: how many post offices a city needs, what transit serves it, how shelter is provided for a growing population. Obedience to jurists in matters of juristic research, and to officials in administration, is in reality the obedience to Allah's commands, which is why it stands third in the verse, with its own distinct identity. The reverting itself takes two forms, as the proof of ijtihād and qiyās shows: back to the code of commands mandated in the Book and the sunnah, or, where no textually-mandated rule exists, to analogical deduction from their precedents, for the word of the command is general and includes both.

### The inner reading

According to the explanation of deeper knowledge, the ʿārif holds authority over the beginner who is just setting out. The shaykh has authority over the aspirant, the murīd, and the leader of each group over its members. Of the aspirant it is said that his friend and guardian, the walī, serves his interest better than he serves it himself. Obedience to the Messenger ﷺ is set beside obedience to God, honouring his affair and elevating his status. And when the verse says to refer the quarrel to God and the Messenger, the scholarly language reads the Book and the sunna, but the explanation of God's unity, bayān al-tawḥīd, reads it as committing and entrusting knowledge of the matter to God. Two conflicting inclinations may arise in a believer's heart. Where the reasoning of the scholars is at hand, he weighs what he grasps of their understanding. The master of the heart goes another way: the matter is entrusted to the Real outright, and he attends to what is said within his innermost self, to what has been cast into the heart without any intermediary.

### In short

- Obedience runs to Allah, to His Messenger as the interpreter of His command, and to the scholars and rulers in their proper spheres, and all three are really one obedience.
- The occasion was a military command, and the fire-lit commander learned that obedience is only in righteousness.
- No hearing or obeying in sin, no obedience in clear kufr, and yet obedience even to the maimed slave who rules by the Book.
- Disputes go back to the Book and sunnah, or to the analogical deduction of the mujtahids, and the non-referrer's belief is in question.
- Inwardly, the ʿārif governs the beginner, and the master of the heart settles his quarrels by committing the matter to God.

60.text:
The claim measured against the courtroom: "Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who claim they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you? They seek the judgment of false judges, which they were commanded to reject. And Satan ˹only˺ desires to lead them farther away". The verses before commanded the reverting of all matters to Allah and the Messenger. These ones censure the reverting to anything else.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who claim they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you"** catches the pretenders. Their claim covers the Torah of the past and the Book now revealed to Muḥammad ﷺ. Some had been of the people of the Book and then entered Islam, or claimed to. The claim is a verbal camouflage for hypocrisy, with hearts stuffed with the old disbelief.

**"They seek the judgment of false judges, which they were commanded to reject"** is the exposure. In their disputes, judgment is sought from something other than Allah's Book and the sunnah of His Messenger. The word left untranslated is Ṭāghūt, one who exceeds the limits, and in usage the Satan, so that carrying a dispute to Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf is equated with carrying it to Satan: he was a satan personified, or bypassing a God-given decision can only come from Satan's teaching, and the follower of that course has taken his case straight to Satan's court.

**"And Satan ˹only˺ desires to lead them farther away"** warns that whoever follows Satan will be misled onto a remote wrong way.

### The two courts of Madinah

In the early period of Madinah, judgement on controversial issues could be sought at two courts. One pre-dated Islam, run by the leaders of the Jews. The other was set up by the Prophet ﷺ after the Migration. Muslims with flimsy cases, aware they could not win in the Prophet's court, used to approach the court of Kaʿb ibn Ashraf, a Jewish tribal chief and a sworn enemy of the Prophet and his followers.

The special incident behind the verses identifies a hypocrite by the name of Bishr, who got into a dispute with a Jew. The Jew proposed going to Muḥammad ﷺ, and Bishr countered with Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf. The secret on both sides was the same: both were certain the Prophet's ﷺ judgment would be true and just, free of any tilt or favour, so the Jew, being in the right, trusted him over his own chief, and Bishr, being in the wrong, knew the judgment would go against him. After cross-talk they did go to the Prophet ﷺ, whose investigation proved the Jew right, and he decided for him. Bishr then hit on a new plan: persuade the Jew to take the case to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, expecting that ʿUmar, usually hard on disbelievers, would decide for the Muslim claimant against the Jew. The Jew agreed, and before ʿUmar told the whole story, including the Prophet's ﷺ decision. ʿUmar asked Bishr whether this was really how it happened, and Bishr confessed. ʿUmar told him to wait, went into the house, and came out with a sword and finished the hypocrite off. The word that came with the stroke: this is the decision for him dissatisfied with the decision of the Holy Prophet ﷺ. The incident appears in the Rūḥ al-Maʿānī from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās, as narrated by Thaʿlabī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim. The heirs of the killed man then sued ʿUmar for killing a Muslim without legal authority, submitting interpretations of his kufr in words and deeds to prove he had been a believer, and the verse unfolded the reality: the person killed was a hypocrite, and ʿUmar stood absolved.

Other reports give other faces of the same disease. A man from the Anṣār had a dispute with a Jew, who urged going to the Prophet ﷺ because he knew he would not be wronged, while the Helper insisted on a soothsayer in Medina, and Allah rebuked them both. At-Ṭabarānī recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that Abū Barzah al-Aslamī was a soothsayer who judged between the Jews in their disputes, and when some Muslims came to him for judgment, the verses came down. The occasion reports come through several chains, naming Abū Burdah al-Aslamī the soothsayer, a property dispute involving one Qays, and, through Dāwūd from ash-Shaʿbī with Isḥāq in the chain, a hypocrite who steered a Jewish disputant to arbiters he knew took bribes, away from the Prophet who did not, with Abū Ṣāliḥ and Abū Ḥātim aṭ-Ṭamīmī among the transmitters. The verse's meaning is general regardless: it censures all who refrain from the Qur'an and sunnah and prefer whatever judgment of falsehood they choose. The contrast is drawn on both sides: the polytheists say, when told to follow what Allah has sent down, "No, we shall follow what we found our fathers following" (31:21), while the only saying of the faithful believers, called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, is: "We hear and we obey" (24:51).

### The inner reading

Outwardly they proclaimed sincerity while acting hypocritically in secret, He exposed them through the tongue of Gabriel, yakfurū bihi, reject him, the command they ignored. Whoever leaves the path and turns to anyone but his master, his ustādh, earns exclusion and condemnation.

### In short

- The claim to believe both revelations is refuted by the choice of judge, and the Ṭāghūt of the verse is the false judge, the Satan, and Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf in one.
- Bishr's route from the Prophet's true judgment to ʿUmar's sword is the occasion, and the verse absolved ʿUmar by naming the killed man a hypocrite.
- The soothsayer's court, the bribetaking arbiters and the flimsy case are all faces of the same refusal.
- The believers' answer to the call of judgment is "we hear and we obey", the polytheists' answer is the path of the fathers, and the pretenders stand between, claiming the first while walking the second.

61.text:
The flinch that gives them away: "When it is said to them, 'Come to Allah's revelations and to the Messenger,' you see the hypocrites turn away from you stubbornly". Called to the court of the Book, the munāfiq turns his back.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When it is said to them, 'Come to Allah's revelations and to the Messenger'"** is the call to the ruling Allah has revealed and to the judgment of the Messenger ﷺ in matters of mutual quarrels and disputes.

**"you see the hypocrites turn away from you stubbornly"** means they turn away in arrogance and aversion, to others. One report of the first occasion names Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿah, the pretender, in a dispute with az-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām, the Prophet's cousin, turning away from the judgment in complete rejection.

### What the flinch proves

No Muslim turns away from a decision given under the dictates of the sacred law. Whoever does it is a munāfiq by definition. When this hypocrite's disbelief was practically exposed through his dissatisfaction with the Prophet's ﷺ decision, his being killed by ʿUmar became all the more justified, for he no longer remained a concealing hypocrite and became an open kāfir, an apostate. The occasion stands with all the reports of the passage: the Anṣārī with the soothsayer, Abū Barzah al-Aslamī the soothsayer of the Jews, the property dispute, Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf's court, and the two courts of Madinah after the Migration, the one of the Jewish leaders and the one of the Prophet ﷺ.

Read inwardly, the hypocrites find easy listening in everything save the word of the Real, while God's unity is heard only by the sincere. The listless and the hostile miss what is true, since opposing personal whims is hard for the insincere. The bat's eye cannot face the sun, and the hypocrites could not stand firm before him ﷺ, which is why they turned away so vehemently.

### In short

- The call to the Book and the Messenger meets the hypocrite's back, and the flinch is itself the diagnosis.
- Dissatisfaction with the Prophet's judgment turned the concealer into an open apostate, justifying what ʿUmar did.
- Everything but the Real's word is easy listening for hypocrites, and the sun that the bat cannot face is the sincerity of the call.

62.text:
The oaths that arrive too late: "How ˹horrible˺ will it be if a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have done, then they come to you swearing by Allah, 'We intended nothing but goodwill and reconciliation.'". The disaster strikes, the accomplice is killed, and then the swearing begins.

### Phrase by phrase

**"if a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have done"** is the catastrophe befalling them for the unbelief and disobedience their hands sent before them. The question carries one answer: there is no turning away and escaping it.

**"then they come to you swearing by Allah"** shows them compelled by the disaster, in need of the Prophet ﷺ, apologizing and swearing.

**"'We intended nothing but goodwill and reconciliation'"** was their plea in gist: not any lack of belief in the truth of his station and mission, not a preference of others' decisions over his as the ultimate truth, but expedient considerations. A case going to the Messenger of Allah would have meant a decision strictly legal, true and just, devoid of options for mutual patch-up, so, they said deceptively, they took it elsewhere so that something good would show up for both parties through a mutual conciliation, an approximate judgment without regard for the painful truth.

### The timing of the oaths

They came up with these interpretations only when their secret was revealed, their wickedness and hypocrisy came into the open, and their man was killed at the hands of ʿUmar. The verse makes clear that they are liars in their oaths and interpretations, and that everything they did, they did because of their disbelief and hypocrisy. Their pattern of behaviour stands exposed. Called to the Book of Allah and His Messenger, they turn away, all averse, and that is no hallmark of a true Muslim. But once their own evil deeds bring trouble, the exposure of their breach or the killing of their man, they become all alert and come swearing by Allah that they meant nothing but good. The like of them appears elsewhere in the Book, those in whose hearts is a disease, hurrying to the friendship of disbelievers and saying: we fear a turn of fortune, until they become regretful for what they kept secret in themselves (5:52).

Read inwardly, the insincere beseech at misfortune's attacks without foundation, and their plea deserves no consideration, for it lasts only until the tribulation passes. Greater than the affliction is indifference to the affliction brought on by one's own hands. And part of the affliction is losing the blessing of the present moment to what is of no use.

### In short

- The disaster is homemade, and the oaths come only after the secret is out and the accomplice dead.
- Goodwill and reconciliation were the camouflage for preferring an approximate judgment to the painful truth, when doing good involves following the rulings of Allah's sacred law.
- The insincere plea expires with the tribulation, and the worst affliction is not to feel the affliction.

63.text:
The sentence on the whole affair: "˹Only˺ Allah knows what is in their hearts. So turn away from them, caution them, and give them advice that will shake their very souls". After the exposure and the oaths, the instruction to the Prophet ﷺ.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹Only˺ Allah knows what is in their hearts"** names what is rooted there: disbelief and hypocrisy, with all the mendacity of the excuses. Nothing escapes Allah's watch, and He will punish accordingly. Let Him be sufficient for His Messenger, whose knowledge covers their apparent and hidden affairs.

**"So turn away from them"** means do not punish them because of what is in their hearts, turning aside from them with forgiveness, and, in the case at hand, rejecting their charge of excess against ʿUmar, since the killed man's disbelief had become manifest.

**"caution them"** means advising them against the hypocrisy and evil residing in their hearts, making them fear God.

**"give them advice that will shake their very souls"** means speaking, between the Prophet ﷺ and them, effective words that might benefit them, penetrating words affecting the issue of their souls, a reprimand in plain terms, so that they repent.

### The counsel that remains

The end of the verse asks the Prophet ﷺ to give good counsel to the rest of the hypocrites in a way that touches their hearts: tell them to fear what lies beyond the present life, invite them to follow the path of Islam sincerely, and remind them of the likely worldly punishment if they cling to their hypocrisy, which might be exposed some day, and they might meet the same fate as Bishr. Another reading of the passage applies the verses to the builders of the counter mosque, Thaʿlabah and Ḥāṭib, who came swearing they intended nothing by the building except kindness to the believers and religious harmony, asking only that a man of knowledge be sent to teach them, while Allah knew the hypocrisy and antagonism in their hearts. The reports of the soothsayer's court in Madinah, the Anṣārī's insistence, Abū Barzah al-Aslamī and Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf stand behind the whole passage, in the records Ibn Abī Ḥātim shares, and the sunnah it defends.

Read inwardly, the instruction balances generosity with reserve: be generous with them in admonition as sympathy dictates, but hold the heart back from concern and from trust. None can help those whom God does not support, in any way.

### In short

- Allah's knowledge of the hearts settles the case, and ʿUmar's absolution comes with it.
- The pretenders are turned from, not punished for their hidden state, but cautioned and shaken with plain words that reach the soul.
- The counsel aims at repentance, from the fear of the beyond to the reminder of Bishr's fate.
- Generosity in admonition goes with reserve of trust, for none can help whom God does not support.

64.text:
The station of the Messenger stated as a universal principle: "We only sent messengers to be obeyed by Allah's Will. If only those ˹hypocrites˺ came to you ˹O Prophet˺—after wronging themselves—seeking Allah's forgiveness and the Messenger prayed for their forgiveness, they would have certainly found Allah ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful". A messenger is not sent to be praised and covered in glory, but to be obeyed.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We only sent messengers to be obeyed by Allah's Will"** means his obedience was ordained for those he is sent to, all of them to follow the rules he sets, by Allah's will and command. "By Allah's leave" means none shall obey except by His leave, as Mujāhid read, for the prophets are only obeyed by whomever Allah directs to obedience. The like appears where Allah says He fulfilled His promise to the believers when they were killing the enemy with His permission (3:152), by His command, decree, will, and the superiority He granted.

**"If only those ˹hypocrites˺ came to you ˹O Prophet˺—after wronging themselves—seeking Allah's forgiveness"** points the sinners and evildoers, in their errors and mistakes, toward the Messenger ﷺ. They are to seek Allah's forgiveness in his presence and ask his supplication for them.

**"and the Messenger prayed for their forgiveness"** adds the second of two conditions binding their repentance: presenting themselves before the Prophet ﷺ, and his prayer for them. The reason reaches back to the crime: they violated the great station of prophethood and caused him undue pain by disregarding his decision, so the repentance over that crime requires his presence and his prayer.

**"they would have certainly found Allah ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful"** is the outcome: forgiveness with mercy and pardon awarded. Rather than false oaths and interpretations, confession and presentation would have served them better, and Allah would certainly have accepted their repentance.

### The word that guards his path after him

Though revealed in the background of the hypocrites' incident, the verse's words yield a general ruling: anyone who presents himself before the Prophet ﷺ, with his prayer for forgiveness, is forgiven. And the presence before him holds the same effect today as it did in his blessed lifetime, for the visit to the sacred precincts of his Mosque and the presenting of oneself before the blessed resident of the sanctified mausoleum fall within the jurisdiction of the rule. ʿAlī tells of the villager who came three days after the burial, fell down close to the blessed grave weeping bitterly, and recalled this very verse: Allah has promised that a sinner presenting himself before the Rasul, with the Rasul's prayer for his forgiveness, is forgiven, so here I am, presenting myself. A voice rang out from the mausoleum in answer: you have been forgiven, as al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ relates.

The verse's judgment on the opponent is equally general. The one who stands against what the Messenger has set is dealt with as disbelievers are dealt with, which is why what ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb did turned out correct. Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Isḥāq Ibrāhīm ibn Duhaym, in his tafsīr, has the report from Damrah: two men took their dispute to the Prophet ﷺ, and he gave judgment to the benefit of whoever had the right. The loser said he did not agree, and proposed going to Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq, who answered that the decision was what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had issued. Still refusing, the man proposed ʿUmar, and when the winner recounted the story and the loser concurred, ʿUmar went into his house, emerged holding aloft his sword, and struck the head of the man who rejected the Prophet's ﷺ decision. Then the verse came down.

### The inner reading

From first to last the passage alludes to the greatness of Muṣṭafā's rank in God's sight, one of the robes of honour given him. God lifted away the intermediary and set the Messenger's decree beside His own. As approval of the Real's decision settles the certainty of the tawḥīd-voicers, approval of the Messenger's decree settles the faith of the faithful. Obeying the Messenger is obeying the Real, disobeying him is disobeying the Real, his words are the revelation of the Real, his explanations the road of the Real, his acts the argument of the Real, his shariah the creed of the Real, his decree the religion of the Real, and following him friendship with the Real. Thus He says: "Follow me, God will love you" (3:31). To the master of masters, the paragon of engendered beings, the centre where the circle of new arrivals turns, the word goes out: tell My servants that whoever wants God's friendship and the approval of his servanthood should travel in your tracks, bind the belt of following, receive your decrees in spirit and heart without resistance, put forth the body, put down the neck, and throw himself into the decree, giving narrowness and tightness no access.

### In short

- Messengers are sent to be obeyed, and obedience itself comes only by Allah's leave.
- The hypocrites' repentance had two conditions, presence before the Prophet ﷺ and his prayer, and the villager at the grave found both, and the word of forgiveness.
- The general ruling stands past his lifetime, and the visit to his sanctuary falls under it.
- ʿUmar's sword against the rejecter was confirmed by the verse, and the inner reading makes the Messenger's decree equal to the Real's own.

65.text:
The oath that measures belief: "But no! By your Lord, they will never be ˹true˺ believers until they accept you ˹O Prophet˺ as the judge in their disputes, and find no resistance within themselves against your decision and submit wholeheartedly". The ultimate oath, by His Glorious, Most Honourable Self, and a definition of faith sworn upon it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But no! By your Lord"** is the oath Allah swore by Himself, opening with the strongest negation the language holds.

**"they will never be ˹true˺ believers"** is the verdict on the claim: nobody becomes a believer unless the Prophet's ﷺ verdict is accepted willingly, calmly and fully, with not the slightest strain left in the heart over it. His judgment is the very criterion of belief and disbelief, the distinguishing feature between īmān and kufr, as the incident of Bishr showed.

**"until they accept you ˹O Prophet˺ as the judge in their disputes"** states his office. He is the exerciser of God-given authority over his community, responsible for adjudicating every dispute that arises, and his authority to decide does not depend on being made a judge by some litigant. People are generally more satisfied with an arbitrator they choose than with a judge appointed by government. But he is not only a ruler of state. He is a Messenger of Allah, protected against sins, sent as mercy for the worlds, and a loving father for his community. The instruction is therefore compassionate. In every conflict of social or religious matters, the contesting parties must make him arbitrator and judge, accept the verdict wholeheartedly, and act accordingly.

**"and find no resistance within themselves against your decision"** allows no hesitation, inhibition, constraint or doubt regarding what he decides.

**"and submit wholeheartedly"** demands total submission, inwardly and outwardly, without rejection, denial or dispute.

### The stream and the two authorities

Al-Bukhārī recorded that ʿUrwah said that az-Zubayr quarrelled with a man about a stream both used for irrigation. The Prophet ﷺ said: "O Zubayr, irrigate your garden first, and then let the water flow to your neighbour." The Anṣārī became angry and said: "O Allah's Messenger, is it because he is your cousin?" The face of the Messenger ﷺ changed colour, and he said: "Irrigate, O Zubayr, and withhold the water until it reaches the walls surrounding the palms, then release it to your neighbour." So he gave az-Zubayr his full right when the Anṣārī provoked him, having first given a generous judgment beneficial to both. Az-Zubayr said he thought the verse was revealed concerning that case.

The rule extends to all times. Acting on this command is not restricted to his blessed lifetime, for after him the verdict of the sacred Law he left is nothing but his own verdict, and turning to his shariah is, in all reality, a return to him. The disputes covered are not restricted to dealings and rights alone, as al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ notes: they cover articles of belief, ideas and theoretical problems, and when mutual differences in views go to undesirable limits, the duty is not continued disputation but reverting to him, and after him to his shariah.

The verse also settles the appeal that followed ʿUmar's stroke. The heirs of the killed man sued ʿUmar before the Prophet ﷺ for killing a Muslim without valid legal reason, and the words came spontaneously from his blessed lips: he never thought ʿUmar would ever dare kill a believing Muslim. The higher authority, approached against the decision of a lower one, should not side with his subordinate but decide by justice and fairness alone, as the Prophet's ﷺ displeasure over ʿUmar's decision illustrated, before the verse bore on the incident. Once the verse was revealed, the reality stood open: the person killed was not a believing Muslim.

### The self-assessment of the heart

To do with a heavy heart what the Prophet ﷺ provably said or did is a sign of weakness in faith. The shariah has allowed ṣalāh by tayammum in place of the regular wudu with water. Whoever feels uneasy with the symbolic tayammum, longing for the regular wudu, should not mistake the attitude for taqwā, for it is a spiritual sickness. Who can be more God-fearing than the Prophet ﷺ? If the form in which he allowed prayer while sitting, and himself prayed sitting, does not find favour with someone, and he insists on standing through unbearable hardship, there is sickness in his heart. Conversely, one whose need is not acute may decline the leave, rukhṣah, and take the path of high determination, ʿazīmah, which is correct by his very teaching. But feeling strain in using the granted leaves is no taqwā. The way Allah is pleased with what is done with high determination, He is pleased with what is done by using leaves. The same holds for worship generally. The best method of adhkār, the remembrance of Allah, the aurād and durūd and tasbīḥ, is what was the routine of the Prophet ﷺ himself and his Companions after him, and Muslims must find these out from the authentic narrations of hadith, the sunnah itself, and make them part of daily life.

Many places in the Qur'an make his obedience mandatory beside its own, with the formula of obeying Allah and the Messenger together (24:54, 64:12, 3:32, 5:92, 4:59, 47:33, 3:132), and the word that whoever obeys the Messenger really obeys Allah (4:80). He was sent the Law so that he could decide cases by it (4:105), and the whole radiant grandeur of his authority hangs on those verses.

### The inner reading

"Do you not know that all the work has been bound to my tracks, and both houses attached to my street?" What a rank and good fortune, what a nobility and excellence! From Ādam's (Adam) era until that day, none had such bounty, such well-arranged work, such exaltedness and such lustre. Some 500 years and more after him, the pillar of his shariah's good fortune flourished, branches blooming, wood yielding fruit, eminence high, decree predominant. His splendour is in this world, his fame in the next. From him each heart has a lamp, each tongue a burning brand, each head a call, each spirit a place. There is gentleness of God above what the fancies suppose, and the spirits of good men in their passion do have familiarity with the beauty of the dust of his feet, and when the lamp of the spheres shines, it shines from him.

### In short

- Faith is sworn upon submission to his judgment, with no residue of strain in the heart.
- The stream of az-Zubayr and the sword of ʿUmar are the verse's two occasions, and the appeal between authorities was decided by fairness, not favour.
- After him, his sacred Law is his own verdict, and reverting to it covers beliefs and ideas as much as property and rights.
- A heavy heart at his proven practice is sickness, not piety, and the leaves he granted carry Allah's pleasure as the high determination does.
- Inwardly, all the work is bound to his tracks, and both houses attached to his street.

66.text:
The counterfactual that answers the taunt: "If We had commanded them to sacrifice themselves or abandon their homes, none would have obeyed except for a few. Had they done what they were advised to do, it would have certainly been far better for them and more reassuring". The verses before it closed the file of Bishr, who first proposed Kaʿb ibn Ashraf and then refused the Prophet's ﷺ true decision. Verse 66 answers what the Jews said in the affair's wake.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If We had commanded them to sacrifice themselves or abandon their homes"** states what Allah knows of what has not occurred, and how it would be if it did: even if people were commanded to commit what they were prohibited from, most would not submit, for their nature is to dispute orders. The reference reaches back to the Children of Israel, Banī Isrāʾ in the Arabic, who were commanded to kill one another so their repentance would be accepted, a severe command they obeyed to the loss of seventy thousand, or to go forth from their dwellings empty-handed as was decreed for them.

**"none would have obeyed except for a few"** counts the doers: the innocent killing the guilty, or the leaving of homes, would have found few hands, one reading naming among them the leader Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, the Anṣārī.
