**"Had they done what they were advised to do"** means doing what they were commanded and refraining from what they were prohibited, the repentance and sincerity they were exhorted to.

**"it would have certainly been far better for them and more reassuring"** weighs the outcomes: better than disobedience, with a firmer conviction of faith, as as-Suddī read the strengthening, more real in this world and better in the Hereafter.

### The taunt and the answer

When the news of Bishr's affair got around the city of Madinah, the Jews chided the Muslims: what sort of people are you, believing in a Messenger of Allah yet not accepting his decisions? Look, they said, we were commanded to kill each other for our repentance, a severe command, and we obeyed it, seventy thousand of our people killed. Your lot, given such a charge, would have refused it. Then the verse came down with its conditional: had these hypocrites, or common people generally, been charged with something severe, the self-killing or the migration like the Banī Isrāʾ's, very few, being what they are, would have obeyed.

This is a stern warning for those who take the solutions of their disputes outside the Law and Way of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and at the same time an answer to the chiding, for the state of affairs fits the hypocrites and certainly not those firm in faith. When the verse was revealed, someone among the noble Companions said: Allah did not put us through this trial. The Prophet ﷺ answered: there are people in my community in whose hearts faith is entrenched firm like mountains. Ibn Wahab says the speaker was Abū Bakr. By another narration, when Abū Bakr heard the verse he said that had this command been prescribed, by God he would have been the first to sacrifice himself and his family to obey. And by some narrations the Prophet ﷺ said that had the command to self-kill or migrate come, Umm ʿAbd, ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, would have acted accordingly. As for migration itself, the Companions had already proven it, leaving homes, properties and businesses in Makkah for Madinah.

### In short

- The counterfactual exposes the disputing nature: a severe command would have found few doers among them.
- The Jews' boast of seventy thousand killed is answered: the trial fits the hypocrites, not the firm.
- Abū Bakr's pledge to be first, and Ibn Masʿūd's name, stand against the few, and the Companions' actual migration had already answered the leaving of homes.

67.text:
The reward held out: "and We would have granted them a great reward by Our grace". One line of promise, tied to the obedience the previous verse found so rare.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We would have granted them"** follows the ladder: had they confirmed themselves in what they were admonished to do, the giving would have followed.

**"a great reward by Our grace"** is from Us, as the verse's Arabic has it, and the great reward is Paradise, the abundant reward in the hereafter. In the reading by allusion, the great reward is the thawāb ʿaẓīm given from Us, with an enduring gift, ʿaṭāʾ muqīm, rendered besides.

### The giving behind the verse

The promise sits inside a passage whose reports run from the Anṣārī's sadness and Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammas to Rabīʿah ibn Kaʿb al-Aslamī's water for wudu at tahajjud hours, from Jibrīl's descents to the hadith only Aḥmad recorded, from ʿAmr ibn Murrah al-Juhanī's five prayers and zakah and fasting of Ramaḍān to the great commentary's chains through Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and ash-Shaʿbī and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas. All of it is gathered by al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū ʿAbdullāh al-Maqdisī in his book Ṣifat al-Jannah, and by Abū Bakr ibn Marduwyah before him, with Muslim and al-Bukhārī carrying the central reports. The reward itself needs no narrator: it is the great wage from Us, and verse 68 will show the road that reaches it.

### In short

- The great reward is Paradise, given from Us, not earned.
- Read inwardly, the ʿaẓīm reward comes with an enduring gift for the obedient.

68.text:
The road itself: "and guided them to the Straight Path". Better for them, then rewarded from Us, and now guided, in this life and the Hereafter.

### Phrase by phrase

**"guided them"** means that had they stood firm in the obedience they were admonished to, Allah would have made them firm in this world upon an established religion He is pleased with.

**"to the Straight Path"** is the ṣirāṭ mustaqīm, the path that leads to Him and to His Paradise, the straight path laid out in the Book of God and the sayings of the Prophet.

### The question the verse answers

The path was promised, and the question came at once. Some Companions asked the Prophet ﷺ how they would see him in Paradise when he would be in the highest stations and they lower than him, and the following verse came down in answer, with this one standing as its doorstep. The whole run of reports is behind it: the Jews' taunt of the killing command, the Anṣārī and Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, the migration from Makkah to Madinah that proved the leaving of homes, Jibrīl's descents, tahajjud and the water for wudu, the zakah and fasting of Ramaḍān in ʿAmr ibn Murrah al-Juhanī's report that only Aḥmad carries, and the chains of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ash-Shaʿbī, ar-Rabīʿ and as-Suddī, gathered in the Ṣifat al-Jannah of al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū ʿAbdullāh al-Maqdisī. Ibn Jarīr and al-Bukhārī hold the reports, and verse 69 carries the answer to the Companions' question.

### In short

- The guided path is an established religion in this world and the road to Paradise in the next.
- The Companions' question about seeing him ﷺ in the high stations is what the next verse answers.

69.text:
The answer to every longing heart in the passage: "And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger will be in the company of those blessed by Allah: the prophets, the people of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous—what honourable company". A universal promise after the special addressees of the verses before, and the most beloved hadith of the Companions standing under it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger"** means implementing what they commanded and avoiding what they prohibited, obeying Allah regarding the obligations and the Prophet ﷺ regarding the prophetic practices.

**"will be in the company of those blessed by Allah"** means Allah will grant him a dwelling in the Residence of Honour, placed in the company of the prophets and those lesser in grade.

**"the prophets"** enjoy the support of the Divine power, like someone seeing something from a close range, so that Allah says of such a one: "Do you argue with him over what he sees?" (53:12).

**"the people of truth"** are the ṣiddīqīn, lexically the very truthful, and in the Islamic terminology the Companions of a prophet who excel all others in submission, enjoying the highest status of piety after the prophets, like Abū Bakr, who believed in the very initial stage without hesitation or hostility. They are people close to the prophets in spiritual excellence, like someone seeing from a distance. Somebody asked ʿAlī whether he had seen Allah Almighty, and he said he could not worship something he had not seen, then added that though people have not seen Allah with their eyes, their hearts have seen Him through the realities of faith.

**"the martyrs"**, the shuhadāʾ, sacrificed their lives and wealth in the way of Allah, a word not translated by martyr, since martyr is also applied to those killed in ethnic or racial wars. In the stations of knowledge they recognize their objective through the chain of reasons and proofs, with no access to direct vision, like someone seeing something in a mirror from close range, very similar to Ḥārithah's word that he seemed to see the Throne of his most sublime Lord.

**"the righteous"** are the ṣāliḥīn, who hold themselves, outwardly and inwardly, to only the good and the right, their objective reached by following the precepts of the sharīʿah, like someone seeing something in a mirror from a distance, the level of "and if you cannot see Him, then He sees you anyway".

**"what honourable company"** promises the pleasures of Paradise: seeing them, visiting them, being in their presence, even with the difference of stations.

### The occasions of the promise

Ibn Jarīr recorded that Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said that an Anṣārī man came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ feeling sad, and being asked, told the whole of it: his days and nights were spent looking at the Prophet's ﷺ face and sitting by him, and tomorrow the Prophet would be raised with the prophets, out of their sight. He said nothing in answer, until Jibrīl came down with this verse, and he sent the good news to the man. The mursal narrations run from Masrūq, ʿIkrimah, ʿĀmir ash-Shaʿbī, Qatādah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas. Abū Bakr ibn Marduwyah recorded a different chain from ʿĀʾishah: a man told the Prophet ﷺ he was dearer to him than himself, his family and children, and that remembering him at home he could not wait to look at him, but contemplating his death, he knew the Prophet ﷺ would be housed with the prophets in Paradise's highest stations and feared he might never see him there. The Prophet ﷺ did not answer until the verse came down. Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū ʿAbdullāh al-Maqdisī collected it in his Ṣifat al-Jannah, commenting that he saw no problem with the chain.

Ibn ʿAbbās says the verse came down concerning Thawbān, whom the love of God's Messenger had wasted and weakened, bending his back and yellowing his face. Asked whether night-waking or discipline had done it, and then whether he was desiring, Thawbān wept: he did not know how the nights passed until day came and he saw him again. Wishing for him by day was the veil of his idleness, aching for him by night the chamber of his wakefulness, separation from him the adornment of his sorrow. The hardest sorrow was that in the next world the Messenger would be in the highest of the High Chambers, and he would be held back from seeing him. Mid-conversation arrived Gabriel, the Presence's messenger, the courier of mercy, with the verse, and God's Messenger recited it, gladdened his heart and laid the balm on his woundedness. Yes, it takes a pain like this for a balm like that to appear. Without burning, no way out opens. Without drowning in the ocean of remembrance, the shore of security is never reached by the hand of "Remember Me, I will remember you" (2:152). The pain of Ishmael calls for the burn of Abraham.

### The forms of the meeting

The meeting in Paradise takes forms. Paradise's inmates see the strata above them as stars are seen, by the Muʾatta's report from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī. The strata above come down to those below, to meet and sit with them, as Ibn Jarīr reported from ar-Rabīʿ. And those below may be permitted upward visits. And those below may be permitted to visit the higher strata, as the Prophet ﷺ gave many the glad tidings of being with him in Paradise. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Rabīʿah ibn Kaʿb al-Aslamī, who used to spend nights at the Prophet's house, brought his water for wudu and the miswak at the hour of tahajjud, and being told to ask, asked for his company in Paradise. Anything else, said the Prophet ﷺ, and being told no, he said: then help me fulfil this wish by performing many prostrations, the sujūd of plenty of voluntary prayers. By the Musnad of Aḥmad, from ʿAmr ibn Murrah al-Juhanī, a man testified to the unity of Allah and the messengership, prayed the five, gave the zakah and fasted Ramaḍān, and the Prophet ﷺ said the one dying in that state is with the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs on the Day of Resurrection, as long as, finger raised for the condition, his parents never met disobedience from him. Only Aḥmad recorded this hadith. And at-Tirmidhī adds the businessman who is truthful and trusty to the prophets', the ṣiddīqīn's and the shuhadāʾ's company.

Love is the way of nearness. On being asked about a person who loves a people without achieving their standards of deeds, the Prophet ﷺ said: one is with those whom he loves, in the mutawātir reports of al-Bukhārī from many Companions. Anas said Muslims were never happier than with this hadith, and in another narration named his loves, the Messenger of Allah, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, hoping to be resurrected with them though his actions fell short of theirs. The company is not restricted to any colour or race. In al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr, al-Ṭabarānī reported from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar that a man from Ethiopia came and asked whether, believing and doing as the Prophet ﷺ did, he could have the honour of being with him in Paradise. The answer: definitely yes, and by the Power whose hands held his life, the black race will become fair and beautiful in Paradise, radiating from a distance of a thousand years. Then the Ethiopian asked whether his eyes would see the blessing the Prophet's blessed eyes would witness, and hearing "definitely yes", he wept until he died in that state, and the Prophet ﷺ performed his last rites, bathing, shrouding, the funeral prayer and the burial, with his own blessed hands. The exchange with this brother from Ethiopia carried the recitation of the opening of Sūrat ad-Daḥr, spelled Ad-Daher in one report, that man has passed through a period of being nothing at all (76:1), and the report of the one hundred and twenty-four thousand virtues written for "Pure is Allah and praised is He", beside the mountain-crushing deeds that still leave man's virtues no match for Allah's blessings unless He elects to be generous.

### The ranks and their convergence

Some commentators say all four ranks can be found in one person, for the Qur'an itself names a prophet a siddīq, saying of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) "surely he was a man of truth, a prophet" (19:41), of Yaḥyā "a prophet from among the righteous" (3:39), and of ʿĪsā that he shall speak to the people in the cradle and in middle age and be one of the righteous (3:46). The attributes overlap as the scholar's attributions do, the commentator, the ḥadīth scholar, the jurist and the historian converging in one person. By common practice, a person is identified with the attribute dominating his life-work, so the ṣiddīqīn mean the most illustrious Companions, the shuhadāʾ the martyrs of Uḥud, and the ṣāliḥīn the general run of righteous Muslims. Imām Rāghib al-Isfahānī determined all four ranks different, a view the al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, the Rūḥ al-Maʿānī and the Mazharī carry: Allah classified true Muslims in four ranks, appointing stations of precedence, and inducing common Muslims not to lag behind in reaching for them. Prophethood itself can never be acquired by effort, but its company can, and the path to it runs through obedience and love.

### In short

- The obedient are promised the company of the four ranks, with seeing, visiting and presence despite the difference of stations.
- The occasions are the longing of the Anṣārī, of Thābit ibn Qays and of Thawbān, whose yellowed face drew Gabriel down with the verse.
- The sujūd of many prostrations, the five prayers with zakah and Ramaḍān fasting, and the truthful business all earn the company, and love is its shortest road.
- One is with those whom he loves, said the mutawātir hadith, and no Companions were ever happier with any word.
- The ranks may converge in one person, and their gradations are gradations of the knowledge of one's Lord.

70.text:
The closing attribution: "This is Allah's favour, and Allah fully knows ˹who deserves it˺". The company of verse 69 is not a wage earned but a bounty given, and the Giver knows His gifts.

### Phrase by phrase

**"This is Allah's favour"** names the whole gift's origin: from Allah by His mercy, for He it is who made them suitable for it, and not their good deeds. The being-with is bounty, favour unhooked from every cause, merit and reason, for what arrives to them and happens through them is the disbursement of His bounty and originates in His generosity.

**"and Allah fully knows"** means He knows who deserves guidance and success, and He suffices as Knower of the reward of the Hereafter. Trust what He has told you, for none can tell like One Who is aware.

### The key and the Giver

The verse closes a passage in which obedience to al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ was made the key to the stations of prophethood, truthfulness and martyrdom, in a manner suitable for the community and appropriate to his high rank. The key turns by favour, not by claim. The bounty stands over the whole ladder of the passage, from the severe command few would obey to the great reward and the straight path, from the Anṣārī's sadness and Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammas to Thawbān's yellowed face, from Rabīʿah ibn Kaʿb al-Aslamī's water for wudu at tahajjud to the sujūd he was told to multiply, from ʿAmr ibn Murrah al-Juhanī's five prayers, zakah and Ramaḍān fast to the man of Ethiopia whom al-Ṭabarānī's al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr carries, from the Ṣifat al-Jannah of al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū ʿAbdullāh al-Maqdisī to the chains of Abū Bakr ibin Marduwyah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ash-Shaʿbī and as-Suddī, from Ibn Jarīr's records to the hadith only Aḥmad carries, and the report of Abū Bakr's pledge in the Ibn Wahab attribution, with Muslim and al-Bukhārī holding the centre. None of the doers earned the company. The obedience was the key, the favour turned it, and the verse's close names the one who needs no auditor: Allah fully knows, of every heart in Madinah and Makkah and beyond, who deserves what He gives. The Qura'n's own commentary on the verse trusts Him outright, for none can tell like One Who is aware, and the Rūḥ al-Maʿānī's gathering of the reports ends at the same place, the bounty that detached their situation from every cause.

### In short

- The company is bounty, not wage, detached from merit and cause.
- Obedience to al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ is the key, and the favour turns it.
- The All-Knowing Giver needs no auditor of His gifts.

71.text:
From obedience to arms: "O believers! Take your precautions and go forth either in groups or together". After the command to obey Allah and His Messenger comes the prescription of jihād for the obedient and faithful, to vitalize their faith and raise the word of Allah high.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Take your precautions"** commands the faithful to guard against their enemies, preparing the necessary weapons and supplies, increasing the troops fighting in His cause, wary and vigilant. The command teaches two things at once. Gathering the means that work toward a good purpose does not contradict tawakkul, trust in God. And the text limits itself to the command of means. No guaranteed security is promised by their support, for means bring nothing but a certain peace of mind. The Qur'an says: "Nothing will befall us except what Allah has decreed for us" (9:51).

**"go forth either in groups"** means group after group, party after party, expedition after expedition. ʿAlī ibn Ṭalḥah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās read it as groups, expedition after expedition, with the like from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurrāsānī and Khusayf al-Jazarī, from Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, Ad-Daḥḥāk, Qatādah, as-Suddī, ʿIkrimah and Mujāhid. The thubat is the small group, the military company called a sariyyah in the campaigns of the Prophet ﷺ, for going alone in fighting is very likely to hurt.

**"or together"** means all of you, marching as one large army.

### The rule beyond the battlefield

Even in normal circumstances this is what the sharīʿah teaches: do not travel alone. In one hadith a lone traveler is called one satan, two of them two satans, and three a group. Another says: the best companions are four, the best military company four hundred, and the best army four thousand, from the Mishkāt as reported by al-Ṭabarānī. The instruction to be vigilant, organizing defence through peaceful policies and strategic preparations, guarding against enemies individually and collectively, runs through the believer's life, for this world is a place of trial where even miscreants may oppress without justification. The two Ṣaḥīḥs hold the guarantee that stands over all the marching: whoever goes forth in Allah's cause, He will either admit him into Paradise by death, or help him return safely home with whatever reward and booty he gained, as Ibn Jarīr's records of the verse's occasion confirm.

Read inwardly, fleeing toward God, firār ilā God, is among the attributes of those who seek, and fleeing with God among the attributes of those who arrive. Rest with God cannot be found except by those sincere in fleeing to Him, and fleeing from everything other than Him is the concern of anyone who declares His unity.

### In short

- Precautions and marching orders are commanded together, and means do not cancel tawakkul, for nothing befalls but what Allah has decreed.
- The march is in companies or as one army, and the lone traveler is called a satan.
- The mujāhid's guarantee covers both ends of the road, martyrdom and safe return with reward.
- Inwardly, the true march is the flight to God, and rest is found only by the sincere in flight.

72.text:
The lingerer described: "There will be some among you who will lag behind so that if you face a disaster, they will say, 'Allah has blessed us for not being there among them.'". The verse that follows the marching orders shows who stays home, and why.

### Phrase by phrase

**"There will be some among you who will lag behind"** was revealed about the hypocrites, as Mujāhid and others said, and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān read the lingering as staying behind and not joining jihād. It is also possible that the person lingers while luring others away from joining, as ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy, may Allah curse him, used to linger behind and lure others to refrain, as Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Jarīr stated. The one meant is Ibn Ubayy, but the description runs wider than one man. Al-Qurṭubī says the characteristics cannot be those of the believers, and signify the hypocrites, who claimed Islam outwardly and were therefore identified as a group from among the believers.

**"if you face a disaster"** means death, martyrdom, or, by Allah's wisdom, defeat by the enemy.

**"'Allah has blessed us for not being there among them'"** shows the reasoning: since he never joined them in battle, he counts his safety a favour, unaware of the reward he might have gained from enduring war or martyrdom.

### The two faces of the lingerer

Seen at the battle of Uḥud and after, these are people who want success in the Hereafter at no cost in this world. They show up enthusiastically where worldly gain is possible, and find excuses when a religious struggle brings worldly loss. They occupy the same materialistic ground as before Islam, lacking the conviction that the Hereafter is what truly matters. Read inwardly, their beliefs are not firmly established in one state. Tied to worldly concerns, they are grateful when something unpleasant nears the Muslims, saying praise be to God for protection from what afflicted them, and they incline toward the Muslims when a blessing comes. They lose in both worlds, neither complete disbelievers nor loyal believers, having dropped the commitment to protect the rest in lives, property and honour.

### In short

- The lingerer is the hypocrite, Ibn Ubayy chief among them, who stays back and holds others back.
- Disaster draws from him the sigh of relief, booty will draw the other sigh, and both reveal the same unbelief.
- The Uḥud pattern of wanting the Hereafter without risk is his signature, and his loss runs through both worlds.

73.text:
The other face of the same man: "But if you return with Allah's bounties, they will say—as if there had been no bond between you—'We wish we had been there with them to share the great gain!'". Verse 72 caught him at the disaster. Verse 73 catches him at the triumph.

### Phrase by phrase

**"if you return with Allah's bounties"** means victory, triumph and booty.

**"as if there had been no bond between you"** means as if he were not a follower of the religion, no acquaintance, friendship or tie of affection left, for he had already dropped the commitment to protect their lives, property and honour.

**"'We wish we had been there with them to share the great gain!'"** reveals the arithmetic: a share of the booty assigned and taken possession of. That is his ultimate aim, the great success being abundance and a good portion.

### The cry that convicts

The regret is real but its object convicts him. Had the lingering been principle, it would have kept him home at the triumph too. Instead he cries out as if no bond had ever existed, wishing to have marched only where marching paid. The reports of the passage, from Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān's reading to Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Jarīr's record of Ibn Ubayy's practice, and al-Qurṭubī's verdict on the verse, all describe the type. The jihād he avoided, and the path he would not walk, remain what they were, and the uḥud pattern of his hesitation stands recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs' picture of the type, as Ibn ʿAbbās's reading of the passage confirms.

### In short

- Booty turns the sigh of relief into the cry of regret, and both are confessions.
- The bond of religion he denies by his conduct was already dropped in his commitments.
- His great success is a share of the spoils, and the believer's great success is the path itself.

74.text:
The command that answers them both: "Let those who would sacrifice this life for the Hereafter fight in the cause of Allah. And whoever fights in Allah's cause—whether they achieve martyrdom or victory—We will honour them with a great reward". The lingerer wanted the Hereafter without risk. The fighter is defined by the opposite trade.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Let those who would sacrifice this life for the Hereafter fight"** carries two readings. One addresses the hypocrites: let those who sell this world for the next fight instead of lingering, they who trade their religion for the world's meager goods out of disbelief. The sounder reading addresses the sincere: those who rate the Hereafter above this world are the ones to fight in the way of Allah, elevating His religion, aspiring to the Hereafter alone, and paying this world's benefits and conveniences for progress along the path of God.

**"in the cause of Allah"** means purely for His cause, for the real struggle is the one waged purely for the sake of God, not for fame or the safety of lip service.

**"whether they achieve martyrdom or victory"** covers both ends: slain a martyr or triumphant over the enemy, the two outcomes are one.

**"We will honour them with a great reward"** means an immense compensation with Allah, the plentiful reward of Paradise and the pleasure of Allah.

### The two ends of one road

The guarantee stands over both: whoever fights in the cause of Allah, killed or victorious, earns the great wage, as the two Ṣaḥīḥs record, and the treatment of the fighting verses of 2:191 runs under the whole passage. Read inwardly, no jihād is sound while the fighter's lower self stands unslain within him. The heart's fear of death must go first, and the self be surrendered to it after. The great wage means that what remains of God after the fighter's passing serves him better than a lifetime spent through the lower self. Their speaker said: are You not my compensation for myself? That is honour enough. Besides You I have no goal, nor anything to request.

### In short

- The believer sells this life for the Hereafter, and the fight is the market of that sale.
- Martyrdom and victory are one wage, and the two Ṣaḥīḥs guarantee both ends of the road.
- Inwardly, the sound struggle begins with slaying the fear of death, and its wage is God Himself.

75.text:
The question that shames the hesitant: "And what is it with you? You do not fight in the cause of Allah and for oppressed men, women, and children who cry out, 'Our Lord! Deliver us from this land of oppressors! Appoint for us a saviour; appoint for us a helper—all by Your grace.'". Rather than a straight command, the Qur'an elected the interrogative of rebuke: what is wrong with you that you do not fight?

### Phrase by phrase

**"You do not fight in the cause of Allah"** speaks of fighting in His path, in obedience of Allah, against the people of Makkah, and the hint of the rebuke is that jihād under such conditions is a natural duty, not doing which is far from a reasonable man.

**"and for oppressed men, women, and children who cry out"** names the weak, ill-treated and oppressed left behind in Makkah, restless because of having to remain there, prevented by the disbelievers from emigrating. Ibn ʿAbbās and his father said: my mother and I were among them, as al-Bukhārī records.

**"'Our Lord! Deliver us from this land of oppressors!'"** identifies the town as Makkah, whose people are oppressors through unbelief, idolaters all. The like stands in the verse: "Many a town, stronger than your town which has driven you out" (47:13).

**"'Appoint for us a saviour; appoint for us a helper'"** asks for protectors and helpers, one to take charge of their affair and one to defend them against the oppressors, all by His grace.

### The left behind

The Muslims unable to migrate, for physical weakness or insufficiency of resources, were later stopped by the disbelievers themselves and hurt and harassed in every way to turn them from their faith. Their names are preserved in the exegetic works: Ibn ʿAbbās and his mother, Ṣuhaym ibn Hishām, al-Walīd ibn al-Walīd and Abū Jandal ibn Sahl, as al-Qurṭubī's record carries them. They faced tyranny and torture with unflinching faith, showing no sign of surrender, and kept praying to Allah Almighty for deliverance, which was finally accepted when He commanded the Muslims to wage jihād and rescue the oppressed from coercion and persecution.

### The two prayers answered

The supplication asked two things: rescue from the town, and a supporter and helper. Both were granted. Some were given the opportunity to move out, which set them on the path out, fulfilling the first wish, and some remained until the Conquest of Makkah, when the Holy Prophet ﷺ appointed ʿAttāb ibn Asīd, spelled Ibn Usayd in one reading, as their caretaker, who had the oppressed delivered from their oppressors and sought justice for the wronged from those who had wronged them. Allah answered their prayers and made the Prophet ﷺ their defender and ʿItāb their protecting friend. The prayer of the weak was thus one of the very reasons the command to fight came down, a lesson in itself: praying to Allah is the panacea for all hardships.

### In short

- The rebuke, not the command, opens the verse, for fighting for the oppressed needs no persuading of a reasonable man.
- The trapped believers of Makkah, from Ibn ʿAbbās and his mother to Abū Jandal ibn Sahl, prayed the two-part prayer under torture.
- Both parts were answered, the exit for some and ʿAttāb ibn Asīd's justice at the Conquest for the rest.

76.text:
The two banners named: "Believers fight for the cause of Allah, whereas disbelievers fight for the cause of the Devil. So fight against Satan's ˹evil˺ forces. Indeed, Satan's schemes are ever weak". Verse 75 asked why they do not fight. Verse 76 shows what each side is actually fighting for.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Believers fight for the cause of Allah"** means fighting in obedience to Allah and for His pleasure. The purpose of the believer's striving is that the Divine Law becomes operative in this world and the authority of Allah reigns supreme, for He is the master of all, the Creator of the universe in His infinite wisdom, whose Law is based on pure justice. When the rule of justice is established, there is peace which sustains.

**"whereas disbelievers fight for the cause of the Devil"** means obedience to Shayṭān, the Ṭāghūt of the earlier verses, Abū Sufyān and his companions battling for the idols. The disbelievers seek to spread the message of kufr and work for its ascendency, eager that satanic powers rule the world, so that kufr and shirk are enforced through the universal order, dressed with the sheen of the seemingly positive. Since kufr and shirk are the ways of Satan, the disbelievers end up helping Satan in doing his job.

**"So fight against Satan's ˹evil˺ forces"** names his friends, the supporters of his religion and the soldiers of the devil, and the believer defeats them with the strength drawn from God.

**"Indeed, Satan's schemes are ever weak"** — his deceptive plans are insubstantial and cannot harm true Muslims, for their helper is Allah Himself, and Satan's plotting cannot stand up to God's plotting against the disbelievers.

### Badr and the fleeing helper

This is what happened at the battle of Badr. Satan stood by the disbelievers, dishing out tall claims: nobody would overpower them that day, he was the helper at their side, and his armies would be there in support. When the actual fighting began, he did advance with his army, but at the first sight of the angels arriving to help the Muslims his whole design collapsed, and he turned in flight. The word he flung back at his accomplices severed the alliance: no responsibility rested on him for them, he saw what they could not see, and he feared Allah, whose punishment is severe, as al-Mazharī relates.

The feebleness is not unconditional. Two conditions emerge from verse 76 itself. The person against whom Satan tries his guile must be a believer, from the words "those who believe", and the effort he makes must be for the pleasure of Allah alone, with no selfish motive behind it, from "fight in the way of Allah". If either condition fails, the feebleness of Satan's guile is no longer guaranteed. Ibn ʿAbbās said: when you see Satan, do not think twice, attack him, and then recited this very verse of the feeble guile, in the record of al-Qurṭubī.

The servants of God know the pattern from within: a preacher who warns people of the perils of Hell and guides them toward Paradise, refraining from quarrels on materialistic or political issues, is still opposed and challenged by evil-doers, for his utterances assail their egos, and the spread of his message threatens them with economic and political danger. Finding no valid argument against his arguments, they resort to violence, the followers of the path of Satan fighting a servant of God for no crime but his truthfulness.

### The inner reading

Those sincerely devoted to God prefer nothing to God and hold nothing back from God, ever against their lower selves for His sake. The states of the disbelievers are the reverse. Therefore He strengthened and encouraged the believers with the command to fight the friends of Satan without fear of them, His own undertaking being the care of their affairs and their sufficiency against enemies.

### In short

- The believer fights for the reign of the Divine Law and lasting peace, the disbeliever for the ascendency of kufr dressed as progress.
- At Badr, Satan promised armies and fled at the sight of the angels, the proof of his feeble guile.
- The feebleness has two conditions, faith and sincerity of purpose, and without either the guarantee lifts, for the jihād of verse 76 is what the promise rides on.
- Ibn ʿAbbās's counsel, attack him on sight, rests on this verse, and the inward reading rests on God's own sufficiency.

77.text:
The verse remembers a moment of human weakness: "Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who had been told, 'Do not fight! Rather, establish prayer and pay alms-tax.'?" (4:77). It is addressed to men who had once begged for the very command they now dreaded. Two eras of the young community stand behind it, the years of patient endurance in Makkah and the years of strength after the Migration, and the verse asks what changed in a few hearts when the order they had prayed for finally came.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who had been told"** means to be told about, to know of. Those spoken of are Companions in Makkah, among them al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad, Qudāmah ibn Maẓʿūn, Ṭalḥah ibn ʿAbdullāh, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ and ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, as al-Kalbī names them. A gloss ties the verse to the expedition of the lesser Badr, when some of them disliked joining the Prophet ﷺ on the march.

**"Do not fight! Rather, establish prayer and pay alms-tax"** belongs to the Makkan years. The Muslims then lived under persecution: assault, ruin of their livelihoods, exclusion from the Kaʿbah, and pressure to abandon the new faith and return to ancestral religion. That oppression had, in principle, already made arms lawful against the oppressors, and they came again and again to the Prophet ﷺ asking leave to fight and put an end to the kāfir reign of terror. Rūḥ al-Maʿānī records this setting of the verse. He always held them back. He had not been commanded to fight, he told them, but to be patient, to forbear and forgive, and to keep the ṣalāh and the zakāh already given them, devoting themselves to these, for the charity comforted the poor among them. The restraint had its reasons. The Muslims were few against many, and their city was sacred ground, the most honoured spot on earth, which is why the command to fight was not revealed in Makkah. Premature and untimely action is not the way of Islam. A practical step waits until its preparations exist, and a clash of arms at that stage would have handed the Makkans a justification for open war instead of stray tyranny at the individual level. Until then the faithful carry the personal obligations that hold under all circumstances: to seek nearness to Allah, to pay others their rightful dues, and to endure hardship along the path of religion.

ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf and a group of his companions once came to the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah and complained:

> O Prophet of Allah, we were mighty when we were idolaters, but now that we are believers we have become humiliated.
>
> I am commanded to pardon. Do not fight these people.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded the report on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, and an-Nasāʾī and al-Ḥākim both collected it. The words about pardon were his answer in Makkah. When Allah moved him to Madinah, the command to fight the idolaters came, and some of them held back, and this verse came down about them.

**"Then once the order came to fight"** marks the change. After the Migration the community had a town of its own, strength, power and support, and jihād was legislated. The command was exactly what they had asked for through the years of harm. Yet when it arrived, a section of them grew weary and deeply afraid of facing the idolaters in battle.

**"a group of them feared those ˹hostile˺ people as Allah should be feared"**, or even more. They feared death at the hands of the Makkans as they feared the punishment of Allah, or with greater fear still. One reading counts Ṭalḥah ibn ʿAbdullāh among this group.

**"Our Lord! Why have You ordered us to fight? If only You had delayed ˹the order for˺ us for a little while!"** is the wish itself. They wanted postponement, a little more time to live and to enjoy, because fighting means bloodshed, orphans and widows. The Qur'ān had already described this wavering: "Those who believe say: 'Why is not a sūrah sent down for us?' But when a decisive sūrah is sent down and fighting is mentioned" (47:20), the eagerness drains away.

**"The enjoyment of this world is so little"** turns their eyes from the length of life to its worth. There is no gain in this world for one who has no share in the eternal abode from Allah. If it still attracts anyone, its enjoyment is short-lived and its decline is near, for once the eyes close in death, the Hereafter is there to see.

**"whereas the Hereafter is far better for those mindful ˹of Allah˺"** promises the person of taqwā a destination better than this whole life. Tafsir Kabīr sets out four differences between the two sets of blessings. This world's are few, while the Hereafter's are many. These perish, while those endure eternally. Worldly blessings come laced with every kind of botheration, while the blessings of the Hereafter come free of such impurity. And no one is certain of gaining the world's goods, while the blessings of the Hereafter most certainly reach everyone who fears Allah, the observer of taqwā.

**"And none of you will be wronged ˹even by the width of˺ the thread of a date stone"** seals the promise. The faṭīl is the thin thread upon the pit of a date. Not one deed will be cut short by even that much, and the full rewards will be earned. A promise of this kind pulls the believer's hope away from this life, makes him eager for the Hereafter, and steadies him for jihād.

### A wish, not a rebellion

The wish for delay was not an objection to the command of jihād. It was a benign and subtle complaint, and human nature explains it. People hurt past endurance burn to strike back, while people grown used to comfort lose the taste for marching out. In Makkah they had known nothing but pain from the disbelievers and looked forward most eagerly to the command. In Madinah they found the peace they had missed for long, and when the order came in that state it found them without their old fire, so they simply wished the call had not come at that hour. To read this as defiance, or to charge those Muslims with sin for it, is not correct. The excuse holds only if they pronounced the complaint aloud. If nothing passed their lips and it was only a thought crossing the mind, then the Sharīʿah of Islam simply does not count the passing thoughts and heart's doubts of this kind as sins. The word "they said" need not mean speech, for saying can happen within the hearts. This is abridged from the Bayān al-Qur'ān of Mawlānā Thanāʾī. Others say the verse speaks of the hypocrites, in which case no explanation is called for at all, as Tafsir Kabīr has it.

### Self-correction before reform

The verse keeps an order. First come the prescribed prayers and the fixed zakāh, the medium of self-correction. Then comes jihād, the medium of collective and political correction, through which the forces of coercion and injustice are eliminated and peace prevails in the country. The lesson is that well before worrying about correcting others, one should start correcting oneself. Seen by relative importance, the first duty is farḍ al-ʿayn, an absolute obligation on every individual, while jihād is farḍ al-kifāyah, an obligation which, when some perform it, absolves the rest, as al-Mazharī notes, which makes the precedence of self-correction obvious. The order also trains. Unless a person has trained himself to fight his own evil desires in obedience to Allah's command, and grown used to bearing pain and giving up wealth, joining jihād and staking his life will feel like a very difficult proposition to him. That is the wisdom of the Makkan years of prayer, charity and patience.

### The trifling world

The people of the heart hear the same words inwardly. He gave you power over this world and then pronounced the enjoyment of it trifling, of no account for you. Give alms from it as little as half a date and you would be saved from the Fire and reach the Garden. That is generosity beyond measure. Caring little about what comes to you for the sake of the Beloved is the strongest indicator of your relationship with Him. When He wants a servant to forsake the present world, He makes it seem meagre in his eyes so that abandoning it becomes easy. Since your share of it is smaller than the trifling whole, what is there for Him to dispute with you over the fine points of the permitted, the taḥlīl, while your covenant stays safe from change? If the world's worth is so small, then the cheapest of people are the ones who settle for what is cheap and let the precious go. The believer is torn from the worlds of being in degrees. First He seizes him from the present world by what comes next. Then He robs him of both worlds with the words of the verse: what is with Allah is better and more lasting (42:36).

### In short

- In Makkah the command was to hold back, pray, give zakāh and endure. Fighting waited for a town, strength and support, and came with the Migration.
- When the order finally arrived, some feared men as they should fear Allah and wished for delay. The wish was weakness rather than defiance, and a thought in the heart is no sin.
- The answer points to worth, not length: the world's enjoyment is little, the Hereafter far better for the mindful, and no deed is wronged by the width of a faṭīl.
- Prayer and charity correct the self before jihād corrects the world, and the trifling world is left behind degree by degree.

78.text:
Death stands behind the command: "Wherever you may be, death will overcome you" (4:78). The verse closes the escape route the deserters from jihād were quietly counting on, for some imagined that by dodging the battlefield they might also dodge death. The occasion was raw. When Muslims were martyred at Uḥud, the hypocrites who had failed to join the fighting said that if their killed brothers had remained with them, they would not have died or been killed. Ibn ʿAbbās, in a report through Abū Ṣāliḥ, narrates this setting.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Wherever you may be, death will overcome you"** addresses the sincere believers, at home or travelling, on dry land or at sea. Death keeps its appointment exactly where you happen to be, on the day fixed for it, and no one shall ever slip out of its reach. Every soul will taste death, whether it performed jihād or not, for everyone has an appointed time and a limited term of life: "Whatsoever is on it will perish" (55:26).

**"even if you were in fortified towers"** spells out the futility. The towers are entrenched, fortified, high and towering, and no caution or fortification can ever avert death. So there is no sense in backing out of fighting for fear of it.

**"When something good befalls them, they say, 'This is from Allah'"** turns to the hypocrites and the Jews of Madinah. The good is fertile years, produce, children and the like, in the gloss of Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū al-ʿĀliyah and as-Suddī, along with rainfall, lower prices and a good year. They credited all of it to Allah, adding that He knew they were good.

**"but when something evil befalls them, they say, 'This is from you.'"** names the other half of their arithmetic. The evil is drought, famine, shortage of fruits, the death of children and animals, hardship and high prices, as Abū al-ʿĀliyah and as-Suddī stated. "From you" means the blame is yours, that it comes of following you and embracing your religion. It was the ill omen they pinned on Muḥammad ﷺ and his Companions, as when the Jews of Madinah grumbled that their harvests and fields had done nothing but shrink since he arrived. The habit is ancient. Whenever good came to Firʿawn's people they claimed it as their own, and whenever evil struck them they laid it on the omens of Mūsā (Moses) and his people (7:131). The Qur'ān also sketches "the man who worships Allah as it were upon the edge", standing in doubt (22:11), and the hypocrites were of that make. Islam was on their tongues and dislike of it in their hearts, so each calamity that arrived was charged to their following of the Prophet ﷺ. After the setback at Uḥud the opportunists went further, blaming the debacle on his poor strategy and trying to turn people against his ability to lead, for they found the new instructions toward sacrifice disturbing to the pattern of their lives.

**"Say, 'Both have been destined by Allah.'"** corrects the whole account. Everything, hardship and blessing alike, occurs by the decision and decree of Allah, and His decision comes to pass for the righteous and the wicked, the faithful and the disbelievers. The people of the heart add that death, being unavoidable, is better submitted to willingly than endured under protest, and that death is joy to the believer, whose approaching end he greets as good news, because it carries him to his Lord. Whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him. The fault in these people runs deeper than a slip of logic. Their insight is feeble and their belief infirm, so good fortune wakes joy and gratitude in them, while evil fortune sends them anywhere but back to Allah. A Magian disposition flows in them, one that attributes the evil thing to something created. The reply names the true order: everything is from Allah, who creates and originates, produces and invents, decrees and makes easy.

**"So what is the matter with these people? They can hardly comprehend anything"** ends in wonder. The question is an interrogative of amazement at their extreme ignorance. To say they do not even come near to comprehending any word delivered to them is rhetorically more intense than saying they cannot understand it, and that is the force of the closing line.

### The Sword of Allah on his bed

The famous soldier and general of Islam, Khālid bin al-Walīd, was known as Saifullah, the Sword of Allah. Martyrdom in the way of Allah was the one thing he burned for, and he spent his whole life in the field, marching from one jihād to the next in the hope of falling in the heat of battle. He killed thousands of disbelievers on the field and lived daringly through trial after trial, all the while pleading to be spared a death in bed and granted the death of a fearless soldier. As decreed by Allah, he died nowhere else but on his own bed in the house. In the illness that preceded his death he spoke from his bed:

> I participated in battle after battle, and every part of my body sustained an injury from a stab or a shot. Yet here I am, I die in my bed. Let not the eyes of the cowards ever taste sleep.

### The woman and the spider

A story Mujāhid told, as Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim relate it, carries the same lesson at length. A woman of an earlier community gave birth to a girl and sent her servant out to fetch fire. At the door a man appeared suddenly and asked what the woman had borne. Told it was a baby girl, he said to remember this: the girl would sleep with a hundred men and finally die through a spider. The servant went back in with a knife, slit the infant's abdomen open, and fled believing her dead. Her mother stitched the skin closed, and the girl grew up so beautiful that she was called the jewel of the city. The servant escaped overseas, stayed long and assembled a fortune. When he planned to marry, he returned to his old city and told an old woman he wanted the most beautiful bride in town. She matched him with that very girl, and the rich returnee married his own unrecognised victim. As they came to know each other, the stories met. She learned who he was, showed him her abdomen, and the cut mark was still there. He then passed on the two prophecies. She confessed the first, saying she could not remember the number, and he told her the number was a hundred. For the second he had a grand palace built for her, absolutely free of spider webs. On a day of rest a spider appeared on the wall of their room. She asked whether this was the spider he frightened her with, sprang up, downed it on the floor and trampled it dead. Its poison spread into her feet and nails, and the sentence pronounced at her birth was carried out. Here was a woman in a new and spotless palace who died suddenly through a spider. Compare her with the many who spent a lifetime in battles and met no death there. The arrangement of life and death stays in the hands of the Creator, whose decisions are final. If He wills, He gives death on a luxury bed at the hands of a spider, and if He elects to save, He keeps a person alive amid swinging swords and roaring fires.

### In short

- Death meets every soul at its appointed term, in a fortress or on a battlefield. Staying behind the walls saves no one.
- The hypocrites and some Jews of Madinah credited the good to Allah and hung the evil on the Prophet ﷺ, as Firʿawn's people once hung it on Mūsā.
- Both good and evil come by Allah's decree, and the closing question marvels at people who come nowhere near understanding a word.
- Khālid the Sword of Allah died in bed after a body of wounds, and the bride of the spider-proof palace died by a spider. The term arrives regardless.

79.text:
The rule of attribution: "Whatever good befalls you is from Allah and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself" (4:79). The verse takes the two half-truths of the previous one and sorts them into a single account of where blessing and calamity come from, then widens into the mission of the one who brought it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whatever good befalls you is from Allah"** speaks of blessings, for the word of the verse means blessing in al-Mazharī's vocabulary. No blessing that reaches a person comes to him as a matter of right. It is nothing but the grace of Allah, His faḍl in the common terminology of Islam. No matter how much a person devotes himself to the acts of worship laid upon him, he cannot claim to deserve blessing on the strength of his deeds alone, for the simple reason that the very ability to engage in worship comes from none but Allah Himself, His tawfīq. And His blessings are beyond counting. No limited programme of worship could ever purchase them, least of all worship that falls short of the supreme mastery and power of the Lord of this universe and of the universes beyond it. The Prophet ﷺ said it in a hadith:

> No one shall enter Paradise unless it be with the mercy of Allah. The narrator asked: not you either? He said: yes, not me either.

**"and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself"** turns to the word that means muṣībah, calamity and misfortune, again in al-Mazharī's vocabulary. Although calamities are created by Allah, their cause lies nowhere else but in the misdeeds of man himself. as-Suddī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd read it as because of your errors. Qatādah read it as punishment for you, O son of Adam, because of your sins. What it means depends on who is struck. For the kāfir, the disbeliever, the evil that hits him in this mortal world is a mere foretaste of the punishment still stored up, which outweighs anything worldly by far. If the person is a believer, all his misfortunes become an expiation, a kaffārah, for his sins, and thereby the very cause of his salvation in the Hereafter. Two sayings of the Prophet ﷺ carry it:

> No evil ever touches a Muslim, but it becomes a source of forgiveness for him, even the pinch of a thorn in his feet.
>
> No hardship befalls a servant of Allah, be it light or tough, but it is always due to his sin, and the sins Allah forgives without afflicting with a calamity are much more.

Al-Mazharī relates both from at-Tirmidhī, the second reported by Abū Mūsā. The address, though spoken to the Prophet ﷺ, refers to mankind in general, for Allah addressed him while meaning his people. The readings then multiply. One reading takes it as a word of consolation: for the sake of your own purity, He is purifying you through it. Or the good means conquest and booty, an honour from Allah, and the bad means killing and defeat, such as befell at Uḥud, which came of the transgression of the Companions when they left their positions. Or the good is whatever you do by Allah's given success and help, and the evil whatever you commit by the transgression of your soul and His forsaking you. The inner teaching agrees in its own idiom: good is a bounty from Allah, and evil is from yourself through your own acquisition, your kasb, while both of them are created by Allah.

**"We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ as a messenger to ˹all˺ people"** states the reach of the mission. The Holy Prophet ﷺ was not simply a messenger for the Arabs alone. His prophethood is universal, addressed to every human being of this universe and to the jinn as well, to those alive now and to everyone still to come before the Qiyāmah, the fateful Last Day, as al-Mazharī reads it. His task is to convey the commandments of Allah to them, the acts He loves and approves, and the acts He rejects and refuses.

**"And Allah is sufficient as a Witness"** closes the account. Allah is sufficient as witness that He sent him, and He is witness over the messenger and over the people alike, with full knowledge of what is conveyed to them and of the disbelief and rebellion with which they respond to the truth. To any who demand a witness to testify that he is a messenger from Allah, Allah Himself is witness enough.

### Towers and trust

The towers of the previous verse leave a ruling behind them. Putting up a good, strong house to live in, made safe for one's person and property, goes against nothing in tawakkul, the trust in Allah, and nothing in the rules of the Sharīʿah either, as al-Qurṭubī judges. Trust in Allah does not demand open doors and paper walls. It demands a heart that knows the wall saves nothing unless He wills, which is exactly what the verse of the towers said.

### In short

- Blessing is never a wage. It arrives by grace, and even the strength to worship and so to earn is itself given.
- Calamity is created by Allah but caused by sin, a small foretaste for the kāfir and an expiation for the believer.
- The Prophet ﷺ was sent to all peoples, jinn and men, down to the Qiyāmah, and Allah is sufficient as witness.
- A strong and secure house contradicts neither trust nor law, for the term of death walks through walls.

80.text:
The right that follows the affirmation: "Whoever obeys the Messenger has truly obeyed Allah. But whoever turns away, then ˹know that˺ We have not sent you ˹O Prophet˺ as a keeper over them" (4:80). An earlier passage of this surah had affirmed the prophethood. This verse establishes its right, which is compulsory obedience, and then absolves the Prophet ﷺ of all responsibility for those who refuse it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Whoever obeys the Messenger has truly obeyed Allah"** carries a weighty principle bearing on the authority of Allah's Messenger. The opening statement of the verse equates obedience to the Prophet ﷺ with obedience to Allah. It follows that turning away from him is turning away from the command of Allah. And since obeying Allah is a duty even by reason, obeying His Messenger stands on the same footing of duty. Whatever the Messenger ﷺ utters is not of his own desire. It is revelation inspired to him, so his commands carry the command of Allah itself. Abū Hurayrah narrates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, in the record of Ibn Abī Ḥātim:

> Whoever obeys me, obeys Allah, and whoever disobeys me, disobeys Allah. Whoever obeys the amīr I set over him has obeyed me, and whoever disobeys that amīr has disobeyed me.

The hadith also stands in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs.

**"But whoever turns away"** is answered with comfort for the one refused. Do not worry about him. The job of the Prophet ﷺ is only to convey. Whoever obeys him acquires happiness and success, and a reward similar to the one he earns accrues to the Prophet ﷺ himself. As for the one who turns away, he gains failure and loss, and no burden of what he does falls upon the one he turned from. Another hadith states:

> Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger acquires guidance, and whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger will only harm himself.

**"then ˹know that˺ We have not sent you ˹O Prophet˺ as a keeper over them"** releases him from guard duty over hearts. He was sent as a warner, not as a watcher set over deeds, for their affair is Allah's to deal with and He will requite them. The statement belongs to the period before the command to fight them was revealed. ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy had drawn a crooked lesson from the earlier verse about messengers being sent to be obeyed by Allah's leave, objecting that Muḥammad ﷺ commands obedience to himself instead of obedience to Allah, and this verse came down as the answer. As Mawlānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānāvī explains in the Bayān al-Qur'ān, the Prophet of Allah is not duty-bound to see that people do not indulge in disbelief. He is not charged with stopping anyone from disbelieving. His mission is to deliver the message, and once that is done his duty as a prophet stands fulfilled. If they still go about disbelieving, that is their business, for which he is in no way accountable.

### The caller accepted or refused

To acknowledge Allah's caller is to accept a human being like oneself, and that is the hard part of faith. People may accept Allah yet never extend their acceptance to Allah's caller. The real test is to acknowledge him and stand at his side, for unless one takes him to be truly a messenger of Allah, one cannot be serious toward him. There is no point in agreeing to lend support to his face, then going one's own way afterwards, or spreading irresponsible rumours about him. No plea of ignorance will win exoneration in the Hereafter for people who treat him with such carelessness. His veracity, when pondered, is self-evident in his utterances, which are inspired by Allah.

### The inner reading

The verse also alludes to the gathering, the jamʿ, of the Messenger's own state, for the divine word runs:

> Obedience to him is obedience to Us. Whoever draws near to him draws near to Us. Whoever is accepted by him is accepted by Us, and whoever is rejected by him is rejected by Us.

### In short

- Obedience to the Prophet ﷺ is obedience to Allah, for he speaks only what is revealed to him, and so his obedience is as binding as Allah's own.
- His job is conveyance, not custody. The one who obeys gains success and earns him a like reward, and the one who turns away carries his own loss.
- Ibn Ubayy's objection, that the Prophet ﷺ sought obedience to himself, is answered here: the mission is delivery of the message, and disbelief after that is the disbeliever's own business.
- Nearness to him is nearness to Allah, and acceptance by him is acceptance by Allah.

81.text:
The two faces: "And they say, 'We obey,' but when they leave you, a group of them would spend the night contradicting what they said" (4:81). The verse condemns a settled policy of double-dealing. Some hypocrites would say one thing with their tongues and keep another hidden in their hearts. Verse 80 had made obedience obligatory and comforted the Prophet ﷺ for those who refuse. This verse shows the sort of people his mission now had to pass through.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And they say, 'We obey'"** catches them mid-performance. The hypocrites, ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy and his followers among them, would come face to face with the Holy Prophet ﷺ and declare themselves quite obedient, accepting whatever he had commanded them with. Their speech amounted to saying that his command stood obeyed, O Muḥammad, that he should command them with whatever he willed and they would comply.

**"but when they leave you, a group of them would spend the night contradicting what they said"** turns the coin over. Once departed from his company, a section of them would gather and conspire together through the night, planning other than what they pretended in his presence and working out how they could disobey him. This duplicity of theirs caused him great pain.

**"Allah records all their schemes"** holds the threat inside the comfort. Allah has full knowledge of the plots they try to hide, and He records them through His command to His scribes, the angels responsible for recording the actions of the servants, so that they will be requited for what they harbour, written in their scrolls of deeds. A verse of like import shows the same habit of speech: "We have believed in Allah and in the Messenger, and we obey" (22:47).

**"So turn away from them"** sets the instructed attitude. They are to be pardoned and borne with, neither punished nor exposed before the people, nor feared. The command is to turn aside in forgiveness, to ignore them and pay no attention, for they will not harm him at all.

**"and put your trust in Allah. And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs"** hands the whole matter over. For those who rely on Him and return to Him, He is enough as Protector, enough as Supporter and Helper, and He it is who grants triumph and sovereignty over such people. The Prophet ﷺ was told to surrender his affair to Allah and rely on Him alone, who would watch over his concerns and take care of him.

### The instruction for a leader

From here comes a lesson for anyone who leads people. Hardships of every sort come with leading people. Absurd allegations get levelled at a leader, and enemies sit near him dressed as friends and confidants. Through all of it he must stay firm and unshaken, giving himself to his mission in complete reliance on Allah. If his objective and orientation are right, he will, Allah willing, succeed.

### The inner reading

In the idiom of the inward path, their coming into his presence was a surrender to his witnessing, the mushādaha, but once they left, the light of drawing near, the iqbāl, was cut off and they returned to their darknesses. The saying of this path about their kind: each time he repents, he returns to his ignorance, just as the feeble one suffers a relapse of his illness.

### In short

- The hypocrites, Ibn Ubayy among them, pledged obedience to the face of the Prophet ﷺ and spent their nights plotting against his commands.
- Allah records the nightly schemes through His scribes, and requital for what is harboured is certain.
- The instructed response is pardon, forbearance, no exposure, no fear, and no punishment.
- The leader who keeps his orientation right outlasts allegations and false friends, for Allah is sufficient as Trustee of Affairs.

82.text:
The challenge to look closely: "Do they not then reflect on the Quran? Had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have certainly found in it many inconsistencies" (4:82). The verse is an open invitation to deliberate in the Qur'an, and it hides a proof inside the invitation, for a book that survives deep reflection unchanged can only be from the One who sees all.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do they not then reflect on the Quran?"** uses the word for pondering and deliberation, tadabbur, not the word for plain recitation. The choice carries a delicate hint. Looked at deeply, the Qur'an shows no discrepancy in its words and meanings, while reciting without deliberating, without thinking it through, a person may start seeing contradictions that were never there. The verse also shows that the Qur'an itself demands that every human being ponder its meanings, so supposing that pondering is the exclusive domain of its highest and ablest exponents is not correct. The levels of deliberation differ with the levels of knowledge. The deliberation of the great exponents deduces the solution of thousands of problems from a single verse. A common scholar's pondering extends only to grasping what those problems and their solutions are. When ordinary people recite the Book and think through its meanings via a translation and explanation in their own tongue, the greatness of Allah settles on their hearts, love for Him grows there, and concern for the life-to-come is planted. That is the master key to success. To stay safe from doubts along the way, the better course is to sit with an ʿālim and study the Qur'an lesson by lesson. If that cannot be done, take up some authentic and reliable tafsir instead. Should a doubt arise during such study, the wiser course is not to force a solution from personal opinion, but to consult expert scholars.

**"Had it been from anyone other than Allah"** faces the alternative squarely. The verse means: had it been fraudulent and made up, as the ignorant idolaters and the hypocrites assert in their hearts.

**"they would have certainly found in it many inconsistencies"** draws the conclusion. Nothing in the Qur'an wobbles. No inconsistency, no contradiction, no statements that conflict, no discrepancy, because the Book is revelation from the Most-Wise, Worthy of all praise, the truth that comes from the Truth. The Qur'an asks the same elsewhere: "Do they not then think deeply in the Qur'an, or are their hearts locked up from understanding it?" (47:24). One contradiction in one subject would have multiplied across many subjects into a great deal of contradiction, as the Bayān al-Qur'ān puts it, but the truth is that there is just no contradiction anywhere in it. This perfect uniformity cannot be found in the word of man. Its eloquence never tapers. It talks about the Oneness of Allah and about the disbelief of men, it lays down rules for the lawful and the unlawful, and no inconsistency enters the process. It offers information about the unseen, and not one bit of that information fails to match reality. Its order retains the quality of its diction all along, never touching a pitch that is low, while the speech and writing of man shifts with peace and distraction, happiness and sorrow. That is a clear proof of its being the word of Allah.

The sections of the Book belong together in this proof. Those firmly grounded in knowledge say of the clear and the unclear alike: "We believe in it, all of it" (3:7). Both kinds of section, the muhkam that lies entirely clear and the mutashabih that does not, are true. The grounded understand the unclear from the clear, and thus gain guidance. Those in whose hearts is the disease of hypocrisy do the reverse, understanding the muhkam from the mutashabih, and gain only misguidance. Allah praised those who have knowledge and criticised the wicked.

### Two gatherings that went wrong

The danger of mishandling the Book has a face in the reports. ʿAmr bin Shuʿayb relates from his father, from his grandfather, in the record of Imām Aḥmad:

> I and my brother were present in a gathering more precious to me than red camels. We came and found some of the leaders of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sitting close to one of his doors. Not liking to be separate from them, we sat near the room. They then mentioned an āyah and began disputing until they raised their voices. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came out so angry that his face was red. He threw sand on them and said: Behold, O people! This is how the nations before you were destroyed, because of their disputing with their Prophets and their contradicting parts of the Books with other parts. The Qur'an does not contradict itself. Rather, it testifies to the truth of itself. Whatever of it you have knowledge in, implement it, and whatever you do not know of it, refer it to those who have knowledge in it.

ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr reported the like: he went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ one day, and while they sat, a pair of men fell to disputing over an āyah until their voices rose. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> Verily, the nations before you were destroyed because of their disagreements over the Book.

Muslim and an-Nasāʾī recorded this hadith.

### Who may draw from the Book

No group or individual holds a monopoly on the exegesis of Qur'an and Sunnah, yet there are conditions for it, and the verse proves a rule on the way. When no explicit statement in the Qur'an and Sunnah covers a certain problem, the best of efforts must be made to find a solution by serious deliberation within them, a method technically known as qiyās, analogical deduction, as al-Qurṭubī notes. But the serious deliberation of a master mujtahid, which deduces solutions at the highest level, requires that the one pondering first acquaint himself with the basic rules of such deduction, so that his results are correct and sound. Without the basic postulates, with faulty education and training, without the qualifications that must be found in a mujtahid exponent, the results come out wrong, and better-equipped scholars may rightfully challenge and contradict them. Think of the man who never walked the corridors of a medical college, objecting that trained doctors hold a monopoly of medical treatment. Or the one who gags his reason and asks why canals, bridges and dams go only to expert engineers, when he as a citizen could render the service. Or the person devoid of reason who stands up asking why legal experts alone interpret the law of the land. To each it must be said that the right exists, but so do the years of education, training and experience, the enormous body of arts and sciences assimilated under expert teachers. Yet the moment the same analogy is laid on the reading and application of Qur'an and Sunnah, a task intricate and delicate beyond these, a barrage of taunts arrives claiming that the ʿulamā keep the job locked up for themselves. Does this work require no ability, no qualification? The claim is terrible.

### The outer proof

None of the statements of the Qur'an contradicts any established truth. It contains nothing against human nature. It conflicts with no fact known through the earlier divine books. No part of its content contradicts any fact verified by the body of knowledge established through observation and experimentation. That it conforms to factual reality at every point is the definite proof of its being Allah's revealed message. This freedom from contradiction appears to the one who ponders, for truth appears as truth to the sincerity with which it is sought, while one who does not ponder will ceaselessly raise baseless objections against the Book, and may do so until Doomsday ends the period of human trial.

### The inner reading

Pondering, tadabbur, alludes to meanings acquired through immersing oneself deeply in contemplation.

### In short

- The word is reflect, not merely recite. Deep looking finds no discrepancy, and careless looking invents them.
- Pondering the Qur'an is every human's right, at the level each can reach, best pursued under a guide, a reliable tafsir, or expert scholars when doubt strikes.
- Had the Book been man's invention, one contradiction would have bred many. Instead its law, reports of the unseen and diction hold one quality throughout.
- Disputing over the āyahs destroyed earlier nations, and the Prophet ﷺ forbade it with anger, sand thrown upon the disputers.
- Qiyās is licensed here: where no explicit text exists, deliberate within the texts, with the training of a mujtahid.

83.text:
The instruction about news: "And when they hear news of security or fear, they publicize it. Had they referred it to the Messenger or their authorities, those with sound judgment among them would have validated it" (4:83). The verse settles how rumour is to be handled in a community whose safety depends on truth, and it ends with a warning about how few would have stood upright without Allah's grace.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And when they hear news of security or fear"** speaks of tidings about the raiding parties sent by the Prophet ﷺ and what happened to them, security through victory or booty, fear through defeat and killing. According to Ibn ʿAbbās, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and Abū Muʿādh, the verse was revealed about the hypocrites, and according to Ḥasan and many others, about weak Muslims, as Rūḥ al-Maʿānī carries the two reports. Out of resentful envy, the hypocrites insisted on divulging such news, and the broadcasting sapped the courage of the believers and distressed the Prophet ﷺ.

**"they publicize it"** is the charge. They make it widely known before being sure of its truth, disclosing and spreading news that might not be true at all. Hearsay is not to be repeated without prior investigation into its credibility. In the introduction to his Ṣaḥīḥ, Imām Muslim recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> Narrating everything one hears is sufficient to make a person a liar.

The same narration was collected by Abū Dāwūd in the section on manners in his Sunan. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record from al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prohibited "It was said," and, "So-and-so said." The Ṣaḥīḥ also records:

> Whoever narrates a hadith while knowing it is false, then he is one of the two liars, the one who invents and the one who spreads the lie.

**"Had they referred it to the Messenger or their authorities"** gives the correct course. The word for the investigation that follows literally names the drawing out of water from the depth of a well, the mustambat water that oozes out first, and here it means getting to the bottom of something and finding out the truth of the matter, as al-Qurṭubī explains. As for those in authority, positions vary. Ḥasan, Qatādah and Ibn Abī Laylā say the expression refers to Muslim scholars and jurists. As-Suddī says it means rulers and officials. After reporting both statements, Abū Bakr al-Jassas takes the general view that the expression means both, which is the correct approach. Some scholars doubt that the jurists could be meant, since the expression in its literal sense names people whose orders are carried out administratively. The reality of the thing answers the doubt. The implementation of authority takes two forms. One works by force, coercion and oppression, and belongs to office holders. The other works by reliance and trust, and that stands reposed in the revered jurists alone, as the whole body of Muslims have shown in every age, taking the decisions of the religious scholars as the mandatory course in all matters of religion by their own free will. Under the precepts of the Sharīʿah, obedience to the rules the scholars set is obligatory, wājib, so the application of the term to them is correct, as the Aḥkām al-Qur'ān of al-Jaṣṣāṣ argues. Details of the subject appeared under the verse that says: "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you" (4:59). One gloss reads the authorities as those possessed of reason and understanding, Abū Bakr and his companions. The sense of referring is keeping quiet until fully informed.

**"those with sound judgment among them would have validated it"** names the people who follow the matter up and seek knowledge of it. They would have known from the Prophet ﷺ and the authorities whether the news ought to be broadcast or not. The sentence also proves something larger about prophethood itself. The command turns to two sources, first the Prophet ﷺ and then those in authority, and the injunction to investigate covers both parties alike, which shows that the Holy Prophet ﷺ too was obligated with the function of extracting, formulating and reasoning out injunctions with proofs, as the Aḥkām al-Qur'ān of al-Jasas demonstrates.

**"Had it not been for Allah's grace and mercy, you would have followed Satan—except for a few"** closes the warning, and the excepted few are the believers, as ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās. The bounty is Islam and the mercy is the Qur'ān, and but for them all would have followed Shayṭān in the abominations he commands. The truly Islamic society is one whose members have done enough self-analysis to acknowledge their shortcomings, ready to place their affairs in the charge of members more competent than themselves and to accept their leadership. That quality of self-assessment is what deters people from following the path of Satan. A person devoid of it jumps into the fray without the capacity to handle complicated issues, and brings destruction upon himself and his own people. In matters of collective application, silence matters more than speech, and a rumour spread on hearsay is help handed to Satan.

### The divorce rumour

The hadith of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, collected in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, is the one to weigh when considering the background of the verse. When ʿUmar was informed that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had divorced his wives, he left his house for the Masjid and found the people at its doorsteps already talking about the news. He said to himself that this was something which must first be investigated, went in to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him whether he had divorced his wives. He said: no.
